name: Pork Adobo
description: A classic Filipino dish made by simmering pork in soy sauce, vinegar, garlic, peppercorns, and bay leaves until tender and flavorful.
ingredients: 1 kg pork belly or pork shoulder, cut into serving pieces
steps: Combine the pork and soy sauce in a bowl. Marinate for at least 30 minutes.
Heat oil in a pot. Sauté garlic and onion until fragrant.
Add the marinated pork and cook until lightly browned.
Pour in the marinade, water, bay leaves, and peppercorns.
Bring to a boil, then lower the heat and simmer for 40–50 minutes or until the pork is tender.
Add vinegar. Let it simmer uncovered for 5 minutes without stirring.
Stir gently and continue cooking until the sauce reaches your preferred consistency.
Taste and adjust the seasoning before serving.
tips: Use pork belly for a richer, more flavorful adobo.
Avoid adding too much water if you prefer a concentrated sauce.
Refrigerate leftovers promptly in a covered container.

name: Pork Sinigang
description: A comforting Filipino sour soup made with tender pork, tamarind broth, and assorted vegetables.
ingredients: 1 kg pork ribs or pork belly
8–10 pieces string beans, cut into 2-inch pieces
steps: Place the pork and water in a pot. Bring to a boil and remove the scum that rises to the surface.
Add onion and tomatoes. Simmer for 45–60 minutes or until the pork is tender.
Add the sinigang mix and stir until dissolved.
Add radish and string beans. Cook for 3–5 minutes.
Add eggplant and green chilies. Simmer until the vegetables are tender.
Add kangkong last and cook for another 1–2 minutes.
Season with fish sauce according to taste.
Serve hot with steamed rice.
tips: Remove the scum regularly to keep the broth clear.
Add vegetables according to their cooking time to prevent overcooking.
Adjust the sourness gradually instead of adding the entire seasoning packet immediately.

name: Pork Menudo
description: A Filipino tomato-based stew made with pork, liver, potatoes, carrots, and hotdogs or sausage.
steps: Heat oil in a pan. Sauté garlic and onion until fragrant.
Add pork and cook until lightly browned.
Pour in soy sauce and tomato sauce. Stir to coat the pork.
Add water and bring to a boil. Lower the heat and simmer for 35–45 minutes until tender.
Add potatoes and carrots. Cook until almost tender.
Add liver and hotdogs. Simmer for 5–7 minutes.
Add green peas and bell pepper.
Season with salt and pepper. Simmer briefly before serving.
tips: Cut the ingredients into uniform sizes for even cooking.
Avoid overcooking the liver because it can become tough.
Add a little water if the sauce becomes too thick before the pork is tender.

name: Pork Caldereta
description: A rich Filipino tomato-based stew with tender pork, potatoes, carrots, bell peppers, and liver spread.
steps: Heat oil in a pot. Sauté garlic and onion.
Add pork and cook until lightly browned.
Pour in soy sauce and tomato sauce. Stir well.
Add water or broth and bring to a boil.
Lower the heat and simmer for 45–60 minutes until the pork is tender.
Stir in liver spread and tomato paste.
Add potatoes and carrots. Cook until tender.
Add bell peppers and green peas.
Season with salt and pepper. Simmer for another 3 minutes before serving.
tips: Liver spread gives caldereta its characteristic richness and thicker sauce.
Add bell peppers near the end to retain their color and texture.
Serve with rice or bread to enjoy the thick sauce.

name: Pork Mechado
description: A Filipino tomato-based pork stew traditionally flavored with soy sauce, calamansi, garlic, and vegetables.
steps: Combine pork, soy sauce, and calamansi juice. Marinate for 30 minutes.
Heat oil in a pot. Sauté garlic and onion.
Add pork and cook until browned.
Pour in the marinade, tomato sauce, tomato paste, water, and bay leaf.
Bring to a boil, then simmer for 45–60 minutes until tender.
Add potatoes and carrots. Cook until soft.
Adjust the seasoning with salt and pepper.
Simmer until the sauce thickens slightly.
tips: Pork shoulder is suitable because it becomes tender during slow cooking.
Brown the pork before simmering to develop deeper flavor.
Keep the heat low to prevent the tomato sauce from scorching.

name: Pork Paksiw na Pata
description: A savory and slightly sweet Filipino pork dish made with pork hock simmered in vinegar, soy sauce, garlic, and banana blossoms.
steps: Wash the pork pata thoroughly and drain.
Heat oil in a pot. Sauté garlic and onion.
Add pork pata and cook until lightly browned.
Pour in vinegar, soy sauce, and water.
Add bay leaves and peppercorns. Bring to a boil without stirring for the first few minutes.
Lower the heat and simmer for 1½–2 hours or until tender.
Add brown sugar and banana blossoms.
Continue simmering until the sauce is flavorful and slightly thickened.
tips: Use a pressure cooker to shorten the cooking time if available.
Soak dried banana blossoms before adding them to remove excess salt and impurities.
Cook until the pork is tender but still holds its shape.

name: Pork Bistek Tagalog
description: A Filipino-style pork steak cooked in soy sauce and calamansi, topped with tender onion rings.
ingredients: 750 g pork shoulder or pork loin, thinly sliced
steps: Combine soy sauce, calamansi juice, and black pepper.
Add the pork slices and marinate for 30 minutes.
Heat oil in a pan. Fry the onion rings until slightly softened. Remove and set aside.
In the same pan, sauté garlic.
Add the pork slices and cook until lightly browned.
Pour in the marinade and water.
Simmer for 15–20 minutes or until the pork is tender.
Return the onions to the pan and cook for another 2 minutes.
Serve with steamed rice.
tips: Slice the pork evenly so it cooks at the same rate.
Do not overcook thin pork slices because they can become dry.
Adjust the calamansi and soy sauce according to your preferred balance of sourness and saltiness.

name: Pork Giniling
description: A simple Filipino ground pork dish cooked with tomato sauce, potatoes, carrots, and peas.
steps: Heat oil in a pan. Sauté garlic and onion.
Add ground pork and cook until no longer pink.
Pour in soy sauce and stir.
Add tomato sauce and water. Bring to a simmer.
Add potatoes and carrots. Cover and cook until tender.
Add green peas and stir.
Season with salt and pepper.
Simmer until the sauce reaches your preferred consistency.
tips: Break up the ground pork while cooking to avoid large lumps.
Drain excess fat if the dish becomes too oily.
This dish is suitable for meal preparation because it reheats well when stored properly.

name: Pork Tocino
description: A sweet and savory Filipino cured pork dish commonly served for breakfast with garlic rice and egg.
ingredients: 750 g pork shoulder or pork belly, thinly sliced
steps: Combine brown sugar, pineapple juice, soy sauce, vinegar, garlic, pepper, salt, and annatto powder.
Add pork slices and mix until evenly coated.
Cover and refrigerate for at least 8 hours, preferably overnight.
Place the pork and marinade in a pan.
Add enough water to partially cover the pork.
Simmer until the liquid evaporates and the pork becomes tender.
Add a little oil if needed and cook until lightly caramelized.
Ensure the pork is thoroughly cooked before serving.
tips: Keep the pork refrigerated while marinating.
Slice the pork evenly for consistent cooking.
Use medium-low heat when caramelizing because the sugar can burn quickly.

name: Filipino Pork Longganisa
description: A Filipino sausage made from ground pork seasoned with garlic, vinegar, sugar, and spices. It can be sweet or savory depending on the preferred style.
ingredients: Sausage casing or food-safe plastic for shaping
steps: Combine ground pork, brown sugar, soy sauce, vinegar, garlic, salt, pepper, and paprika in a bowl.
Mix thoroughly until the seasonings are evenly distributed.
Cover and refrigerate for at least 4 hours.
Shape the mixture into small sausage links or patties. Use food-safe sausage casing if available.
Heat a pan over medium-low heat and add the longganisa.
Add a little water and cover the pan. Simmer until the water evaporates and the pork is cooked through.
Add oil if necessary and fry until browned.
Serve with garlic rice and egg.
tips: Keep the ground pork cold while preparing the mixture.
Do not overmix because this can make the sausage dense.
Cook thoroughly; ground pork should reach an internal temperature of 71°C.
PART 2: FRIED, GRILLED, AND SPECIAL PORK DISHES

name: Lechon Kawali
description: A popular Filipino dish made with boiled pork belly that is deep-fried until the skin becomes golden and crispy.
steps: Place pork belly in a pot with enough water to cover it.
Add salt, peppercorns, bay leaves, and garlic.
Bring to a boil, then simmer for 45–60 minutes or until tender.
Remove the pork and let it cool.
Pat the skin completely dry with paper towels.
Refrigerate uncovered for several hours or overnight to help dry the skin.
Heat cooking oil in a deep pot.
Carefully fry the pork until golden brown and crispy.
Drain excess oil and allow it to rest before slicing.
tips: Dry skin is essential for achieving crispiness.
Avoid overcrowding the pot when frying.
Use a splatter guard and lower the pork carefully into the oil.

name: Crispy Pata
description: A Filipino celebration dish made from pork leg that is boiled until tender and deep-fried until the skin becomes crunchy.
steps: Place the pork pata in a large pot and cover with water.
Add salt, peppercorns, bay leaves, garlic, and onion.
Simmer for 1½–2 hours or until tender.
Remove the pata and drain thoroughly.
Let it cool, then refrigerate uncovered until the skin is dry.
Heat oil in a deep pot.
Carefully deep-fry the pata until the skin is golden and crispy.
Drain excess oil and rest briefly before serving.
Combine all dipping sauce ingredients in a bowl.
Serve the crispy pata with the dipping sauce.
tips: Make sure the pata is completely dry before frying.
Use a large, deep pot to reduce oil splatter.
Do not leave the frying oil unattended.

name: Filipino Pork Barbecue
description: Skewered pork slices marinated in a sweet, savory, and slightly tangy mixture, then grilled until caramelized.
ingredients: 1 kg pork shoulder or pork kasim, thinly sliced
steps: Combine soy sauce, banana ketchup, calamansi juice, brown sugar, garlic, pepper, and oil.
Add pork slices and mix thoroughly.
Cover and refrigerate for at least 4 hours or overnight.
Thread the pork slices onto soaked bamboo skewers.
Preheat the grill to medium heat.
Grill the pork, turning occasionally.
Brush with the remaining marinade that has been boiled before use.
Continue grilling until the pork is cooked through and lightly caramelized.
Serve hot.
tips: Cut pork into evenly sized pieces for uniform cooking.
Soak bamboo skewers to prevent them from burning.
Never brush cooked meat with marinade that has touched raw pork unless it has been boiled first.

name: Inihaw na Liempo
description: Grilled pork belly marinated in a savory mixture of soy sauce, calamansi, garlic, and spices.
steps: Combine soy sauce, calamansi juice, garlic, brown sugar, pepper, and oil.
Add pork belly and marinate for at least 2 hours.
Preheat the grill to medium heat.
Grill the pork belly for approximately 5–8 minutes per side, depending on thickness.
Turn occasionally to prevent burning.
Continue grilling until fully cooked and lightly charred.
Combine the dipping sauce ingredients in a bowl.
Rest the pork briefly before slicing and serving.
tips: Avoid grilling over excessively high heat because pork belly fat can cause flare-ups.
Use a meat thermometer to check doneness.
Allow the meat to rest before slicing to retain its juices.

name: Pork Sisig
description: A popular Filipino sizzling dish made with chopped pork, onions, chilies, and calamansi, often served on a hot plate.
ingredients: 500 g pork face or pork belly, boiled
steps: Boil the pork until tender. Drain and allow it to cool.
Grill or pan-fry the pork until the outside becomes slightly crispy.
Chop the pork into small pieces.
Cook the liver thoroughly, then chop it finely.
Heat oil in a pan. Sauté garlic and half of the onion.
Add chopped pork and liver.
Season with soy sauce, calamansi juice, salt, and pepper.
Add chilies and stir well.
Mix in mayonnaise if desired.
Transfer to a sizzling plate and top with the remaining onion.
tips: Use a mixture of pork cuts for different textures.
Add calamansi gradually to control the sourness.
Make sure the liver is fully cooked before mixing it into the dish.

name: Pork Humba
description: A sweet and savory Visayan-style braised pork dish flavored with soy sauce, vinegar, brown sugar, black beans, and banana blossoms.
steps: Heat oil in a pot. Sauté garlic and onion.
Add pork belly and cook until lightly browned.
Pour in soy sauce and vinegar.
Add water, brown sugar, bay leaves, and peppercorns.
Bring to a boil, then lower the heat.
Simmer for 45–60 minutes or until the pork is tender.
Add black beans and banana blossoms.
Continue simmering until the sauce thickens and coats the pork.
Taste and adjust the sweetness or saltiness before serving.
tips: Rinse salted black beans briefly if they are excessively salty.
Simmer slowly to allow the pork to absorb the sauce.
Add water as needed to prevent the sauce from drying out too early.

name: Filipino Pork Asado
description: A Filipino-style braised pork dish cooked in a sweet and savory sauce made with soy sauce, sugar, garlic, and spices.
ingredients: 1 kg pork shoulder or pork kasim
steps: Heat oil in a pot. Sauté garlic and onion.
Add pork and brown on all sides.
Combine soy sauce, brown sugar, oyster sauce, water, and pepper.
Pour the mixture into the pot.
Add star anise and bring to a boil.
Lower the heat and simmer for 50–60 minutes or until tender.
Turn the pork occasionally to coat it evenly.
Remove the pork and slice.
Simmer the remaining sauce until slightly thickened.
Pour the sauce over the sliced pork before serving.
tips: Pork shoulder works well for braising because it remains moist.
Do not add too much sugar at the beginning; adjust after tasting.
Slice the pork against the grain for a more tender texture.

name: Pork Afritada
description: A Filipino tomato-based stew made with pork, potatoes, carrots, bell peppers, and tomato sauce.
steps: Heat oil in a pot. Sauté garlic and onion.
Add pork and cook until lightly browned.
Pour in soy sauce and tomato sauce.
Add water and bring to a boil.
Lower the heat and simmer for 40–50 minutes until tender.
Add potatoes and carrots. Cook until almost tender.
Add bell peppers and simmer for another 3–5 minutes.
Season with salt and pepper.
Serve hot with rice.
tips: Brown the pork before adding liquid to improve flavor.
Cut vegetables into similar sizes for even cooking.
Add bell peppers last to keep them from becoming too soft.

name: Pininyahang Baboy
description: A creamy Filipino pork dish cooked with pineapple chunks, vegetables, and milk or cream for a sweet and savory flavor.
steps: Heat oil in a pot. Sauté garlic and onion.
Add pork and cook until lightly browned.
Pour in pineapple juice and water.
Cover and simmer for 35–45 minutes or until the pork is tender.
Add carrots and pineapple chunks.
Pour in evaporated milk and stir gently.
Add bell pepper and simmer over low heat for 3–5 minutes.
Season with salt and pepper.
Avoid boiling vigorously after adding the milk.
tips: Use unsweetened evaporated milk if you prefer a less sweet sauce.
Add the milk near the end to reduce the risk of curdling.
Balance the sweetness with a little salt or pepper.

name: Pork Binagoongan
description: A savory Filipino pork dish cooked with shrimp paste, tomatoes, garlic, and chilies.
steps: Boil pork belly in water until tender. Drain and reserve some cooking liquid.
Heat oil in a pan and sauté garlic and onion.
Add tomatoes and cook until softened.
Add bagoong alamang and stir.
Add the boiled pork and mix until coated.
Pour in water and vinegar.
Simmer for 10–15 minutes.
Add chilies and brown sugar if desired.
Season with pepper and serve with rice.
tips: Taste the bagoong before adding more because its saltiness varies by brand.
Fry the boiled pork briefly before adding it for a richer flavor.
Pair with fresh vegetables to balance the salty taste.
PART 3: FILIPINO PORK SOUPS

name: Pork Nilaga
description: A simple Filipino boiled pork soup with cabbage, potatoes, corn, and other vegetables in a clear, savory broth.
ingredients: 1 kg pork ribs or pork shoulder
steps: Place pork and water in a pot.
Bring to a boil and remove the scum.
Add onion and peppercorns.
Simmer for 45–60 minutes until the pork is tender.
Add corn and potatoes. Cook until almost tender.
Add cabbage and pechay.
Season with fish sauce and salt.
Simmer for another 2–3 minutes and serve hot.
tips: Skim the broth regularly for a cleaner soup.
Add leafy vegetables last to preserve their color and texture.
Use pork ribs for a more flavorful broth.

name: Pork Bulalo-Style Soup
description: A comforting pork shank soup inspired by traditional bulalo, with tender meat, bone marrow, vegetables, and a clear broth.
steps: Place pork shanks in a large pot and cover with water.
Bring to a boil and remove the scum.
Add onion and peppercorns.
Simmer for 1½–2 hours or until the meat is tender.
Add corn and potatoes. Cook until tender.
Add cabbage and pechay.
Season with fish sauce and salt.
Simmer for a few minutes and serve hot.
tips: Slow cooking helps extract flavor from the bones.
Add more hot water if the broth reduces too much.
Refrigerate leftovers promptly and remove excess hardened fat if desired.

name: Pork Mami
description: A Filipino noodle soup made with pork broth, egg noodles, sliced pork, and vegetables.
ingredients: 500 g pork shoulder or pork bones
steps: Boil pork in water with onion and peppercorns until tender.
Remove the pork, slice it thinly, and set aside.
Strain the broth if necessary.
Heat oil in a separate pan and sauté garlic until golden.
Add the garlic and soy sauce to the broth.
Season with salt.
Cook egg noodles according to package instructions.
Place noodles in serving bowls and add sliced pork.
Pour hot broth over the noodles.
Top with pechay, boiled egg, and spring onions.
tips: Use pork bones for a richer broth.
Cook noodles separately to prevent the broth from becoming cloudy or starchy.
Prepare toppings before serving to keep the noodles from becoming soggy.

name: Pork Monggo
description: A nutritious Filipino mung bean stew cooked with pork, garlic, onion, tomatoes, and leafy vegetables.
steps: Rinse the mung beans thoroughly.
Place mung beans and water in a pot.
Boil for 30–40 minutes or until soft.
Heat oil in a separate pan. Sauté garlic, onion, and tomatoes.
Add pork and cook until lightly browned.
Add fish sauce and cook briefly.
Transfer the pork mixture to the cooked mung beans.
Simmer for 10–15 minutes.
Add malunggay or spinach leaves.
Season with salt and pepper before serving.
tips: Soaking mung beans for several hours can reduce cooking time.
Stir occasionally to prevent the beans from sticking to the bottom.
Add leafy vegetables near the end to retain their nutrients and color.

name: Pork Batchoy
description: A flavorful noodle soup inspired by La Paz batchoy, traditionally made with pork, liver, noodles, broth, and crunchy toppings.
steps: Heat oil in a pot. Sauté garlic and onion.
Add pork and cook until lightly browned.
Pour in pork broth and bring to a boil.
Add fish sauce, soy sauce, and black pepper.
Simmer until the pork is tender.
Add liver and cook thoroughly.
Cook the miki noodles according to package instructions.
Place noodles in serving bowls.
Pour hot broth and pork mixture over the noodles.
Top with crushed chicharon, fried garlic, and spring onions.
tips: Avoid overcooking the liver because it can become tough.
Prepare the noodles separately if they are likely to absorb too much broth.
Add chicharon immediately before serving to maintain its crunch.

name: Pork Sinampalukang Baboy
description: A sour Filipino pork soup made with tamarind, tomatoes, ginger, and leafy vegetables.
ingredients: 750 g pork ribs or pork shoulder
1 cup tamarind pulp or 1 packet tamarind soup mix
steps: Place pork and water in a pot. Bring to a boil and remove the scum.
Add ginger, onion, and tomatoes.
Simmer for 45–60 minutes or until the pork is tender.
Add tamarind pulp or soup mix and stir.
Add string beans and green chilies.
Simmer until the vegetables are nearly tender.
Add kangkong.
Season with fish sauce and salt.
Serve hot.
tips: Adjust the tamarind gradually to avoid making the soup too sour.
Fresh tamarind can be boiled and strained to make a more natural sour broth.
Avoid overcooking the leafy vegetables.

name: Pork Misua Soup
description: A light Filipino noodle soup made with thin misua noodles, ground pork, garlic, onion, and patola or sponge gourd.
steps: Heat oil in a pot. Sauté garlic and onion.
Add ground pork and cook until no longer pink.
Add fish sauce and black pepper.
Pour in water or broth and bring to a boil.
Add patola and cook until slightly tender.
Add misua noodles and stir gently.
Cook for 2–3 minutes or according to package instructions.
Adjust the seasoning.
Garnish with spring onions and serve hot.
tips: Add misua only near the end because it cooks quickly.
Use enough broth because misua absorbs liquid.
Serve immediately to prevent the noodles from becoming too soft.

name: Pork Sopas
description: A creamy Filipino macaroni soup made with pork, milk, cabbage, carrots, and elbow macaroni.
steps: Heat oil in a pot. Sauté garlic and onion.
Add pork and cook until lightly browned.
Pour in water or broth and bring to a boil.
Simmer until the pork is tender.
Add elbow macaroni and cook according to package instructions.
Add carrots and cook until tender.
Pour in evaporated milk and stir gently.
Add cabbage and simmer for 2–3 minutes.
Season with salt and pepper.
Serve while warm.
tips: Avoid overcooking macaroni because it continues absorbing liquid.
Add milk over low heat to prevent scorching.
Add more broth when reheating because the pasta thickens the soup.

name: Pork Upo Soup
description: A light and comforting Filipino soup made with pork, bottle gourd, garlic, onion, and a clear savory broth.
steps: Heat oil in a pot. Sauté garlic and onion.
Add pork and cook until lightly browned.
Add fish sauce and stir.
Pour in water and bring to a boil.
Simmer until the pork is tender.
Add sliced upo and cook for 5–8 minutes or until tender.
Season with black pepper.
Garnish with spring onions and serve hot.
tips: Avoid overcooking upo because it softens quickly.
Choose a fresh, firm bottle gourd.
Cut the upo into uniform pieces for even cooking.

name: Pork Sinabawang Repolyo
description: A simple Filipino cabbage soup with pork slices, garlic, onion, and a light savory broth.
steps: Heat oil in a pot. Sauté garlic and onion.
Add pork and cook until lightly browned.
Pour in water and bring to a boil.
Simmer until the pork is tender.
Add carrots and cook for 3–4 minutes.
Add cabbage and simmer until slightly softened.
Season with fish sauce and black pepper.
Serve hot.
tips: Add cabbage near the end to preserve its texture.
Use pork ribs or pork shoulder for a more flavorful broth.
Avoid cooking the cabbage for too long because it can become mushy.
PART 4: REGIONAL AND TRADITIONAL FILIPINO PORK DISHES

name: Bicol Express
description: A spicy Filipino dish from the Bicol region made with pork, coconut milk, chilies, and shrimp paste.
ingredients: 5–8 pieces red or green chilies, sliced
steps: Heat oil in a pan. Sauté garlic, onion, and ginger.
Add pork and cook until lightly browned.
Add bagoong alamang and stir.
Pour in coconut milk.
Bring to a gentle boil, then simmer for 30–40 minutes until the pork is tender.
Add chilies and coconut cream.
Continue simmering over low heat until the sauce thickens.
Adjust the seasoning and serve with rice.
tips: Adjust the number of chilies according to your preferred spice level.
Taste the bagoong before adding additional salt.
Simmer gently after adding coconut cream to prevent separation.

name: Laing with Pork
description: A traditional Bicolano dish made with dried taro leaves simmered in coconut milk, pork, chilies, and shrimp paste.
steps: Place pork, garlic, onion, ginger, and water in a pot.
Simmer until the pork is tender.
Add bagoong alamang and stir.
Pour in coconut milk.
Add dried taro leaves on top. Do not stir immediately.
Cover and simmer over low heat for 25–30 minutes.
Once the leaves have softened, stir gently.
Add chilies and coconut cream.
Continue simmering until the sauce thickens and the leaves are fully cooked.
Serve with steamed rice.
tips: Do not eat raw or undercooked taro leaves; cook them thoroughly to reduce irritating calcium oxalate crystals.
Avoid stirring the leaves too early because this can make the dish gritty.
Use low heat to prevent the coconut milk from scorching.

name: Pinakbet with Pork
description: A traditional Filipino vegetable stew made with pork, bagoong, squash, eggplant, okra, bitter melon, and other vegetables.
ingredients: 1 cup string beans, cut into portions
steps: Heat oil in a pot. Sauté garlic, onion, and tomatoes.
Add pork and cook until lightly browned.
Add bagoong alamang and stir.
Pour in water and bring to a simmer.
Add squash and string beans.
Cover and cook for 5 minutes.
Add eggplant, okra, and ampalaya.
Simmer until the vegetables are tender but not mushy.
Adjust the seasoning and serve.
tips: Add vegetables according to their cooking time.
Avoid excessive stirring to keep the vegetables intact.
Use fresh seasonal vegetables to make the dish more affordable.

name: Pork Dinakdakan
description: An Ilocano pork dish made with grilled or boiled pork parts, onions, chilies, vinegar, and a creamy dressing traditionally made with pig brain.
ingredients: 500 g pork belly or pork face
2 tbsp mayonnaise as an accessible alternative to traditional brain dressing
steps: Boil pork belly and pork ears in water until tender.
Drain and allow the pork to cool.
Grill or pan-fry the pork until lightly charred.
Slice the pork into bite-sized pieces.
In a bowl, combine vinegar, calamansi juice, soy sauce, and black pepper.
Add sliced pork, onion, and chilies.
Mix in mayonnaise if using.
Toss until evenly coated.
Adjust the seasoning and serve.
tips: Grill the pork for a smoky flavor.
Add the dressing gradually to avoid making the dish too sour or creamy.
Keep the prepared dish refrigerated if it will not be served immediately.

name: Bagnet
description: A traditional Ilocano deep-fried pork belly dish known for its crispy skin and tender meat.
steps: Place pork belly in a pot and cover with water.
Add salt, peppercorns, bay leaves, and garlic.
Simmer for 45–60 minutes until tender.
Remove the pork and drain thoroughly.
Let it cool, then refrigerate uncovered until the skin is dry.
Heat oil in a deep pot.
Carefully fry the pork until the skin becomes golden and crispy.
Drain excess oil and allow it to rest.
Combine the dipping sauce ingredients in a bowl.
Slice the bagnet and serve with the sauce.
tips: Drying the pork skin is important for crispiness.
Fry carefully because moisture on the pork can cause oil splattering.
Store leftovers in the refrigerator and reheat thoroughly.

name: KBL (Kadyos, Baboy, Langka)
description: A traditional Ilonggo soup made with pigeon peas, pork, and unripe jackfruit, often flavored with batwan or another souring ingredient.
ingredients: 500 g pork ribs or pork belly
4–6 pieces batwan or 1 packet sinigang mix
steps: Rinse the kadyos thoroughly.
Place pork, kadyos, and water in a pot.
Bring to a boil and remove the scum.
Simmer until the pork and beans are tender. This may take longer if the beans are not soaked.
Add onion and tomatoes.
Add unripe jackfruit and cook until tender.
Add batwan or souring mix.
Season with fish sauce and salt.
Simmer briefly and serve hot.
tips: Soak dried kadyos overnight to reduce cooking time.
Check the beans regularly because cooking time varies.
Add souring ingredients after the beans are tender to help control the flavor.

name: Pork Kilawin
description: A Filipino-style pork dish made with thoroughly cooked or grilled pork mixed with vinegar, onions, ginger, and chilies.
ingredients: 500 g pork belly or pork shoulder
steps: Boil the pork in water until fully cooked and tender.
Drain and allow it to cool.
Grill or pan-fry the pork until lightly browned.
Slice the pork into bite-sized pieces.
In a bowl, combine vinegar, calamansi juice, onion, ginger, chilies, and pepper.
Add the cooked pork and toss well.
Season with salt.
Allow the mixture to rest briefly in the refrigerator before serving.
tips: This version uses fully cooked pork rather than raw pork.
Keep the dish refrigerated and do not leave it at room temperature for extended periods.
Adjust the vinegar and calamansi according to your preferred sourness.

name: Pork Embutido
description: A Filipino steamed or baked meatloaf made with ground pork, vegetables, raisins, cheese, and hard-boiled eggs.
steps: Combine ground pork, carrot, raisins, cheese, breadcrumbs, raw eggs, onion, garlic, soy sauce, and pepper.
Mix until the ingredients are evenly distributed.
Lay a sheet of aluminum foil on a flat surface.
Spread a portion of the mixture over the foil.
Place hard-boiled egg halves and hotdog slices in the center.
Roll the mixture tightly into a log and seal the foil.
Steam for 45–60 minutes or until fully cooked.
Allow the embutido to cool before unwrapping and slicing.
Pan-fry slices if a browned exterior is desired.
tips: Avoid overmixing the meat to maintain a tender texture.
Wrap the embutido tightly to help it retain its shape.
Cool completely before slicing to prevent crumbling.

name: Lumpiang Shanghai
description: A popular Filipino appetizer made with seasoned ground pork and vegetables wrapped in thin spring roll wrappers, then deep-fried until crispy.
steps: Combine ground pork, carrot, onion, garlic, egg, soy sauce, pepper, and spring onions.
Mix until evenly combined.
Place a small amount of filling near the edge of each wrapper.
Fold the sides inward and roll tightly.
Moisten the edge with water to seal.
Heat cooking oil in a deep pan.
Fry the lumpia in batches until golden brown and fully cooked.
Drain on a wire rack or paper towels.
Serve with sweet chili sauce or banana ketchup.
tips: Avoid adding too much filling because it can cause the wrappers to break.
Keep unused wrappers covered with a damp cloth to prevent drying.
Ground pork filling must reach an internal temperature of 71°C.

name: Pork Siomai
description: A Filipino-Chinese-inspired dumpling made with seasoned ground pork, vegetables, and wonton wrappers, usually served with soy sauce and calamansi.
steps: Combine ground pork, shrimp, carrot, onion, garlic, soy sauce, oyster sauce, sesame oil, pepper, and egg.
Mix until evenly combined.
Place a spoonful of filling in the center of each wrapper.
Gather the sides of the wrapper around the filling, leaving the top open.
Arrange the siomai in a lightly greased steamer.
Steam for approximately 15–20 minutes or until the pork is fully cooked.
Remove carefully and serve with soy sauce, calamansi, and chili garlic sauce.
tips: Do not overfill the wrappers.
Leave enough space between dumplings to allow steam to circulate.
Keep uncooked siomai refrigerated or frozen until ready to cook.
PART 5: EVERYDAY AND SPECIAL-OCCASION PORK RECIPES

name: Pork Kilayin (Kapampangan)
description: A traditional Kapampangan pork dish made with pork, liver, and vinegar, cooked with garlic, onions, and spices. It has a savory and slightly tangy flavor.
ingredients: ¼ cup pork broth or water
½ tsp salt, or to taste
steps: Wash and prepare the pork and liver. Cut them into small, bite-sized cubes.
Heat cooking oil in a pan. Sauté the garlic and onion until fragrant and softened.
Add the pork and cook until lightly browned.
Pour in the vinegar and allow it to boil uncovered for about 2–3 minutes without stirring.
Add the soy sauce, water, pork broth, peppercorns, bay leaves, salt, and ground black pepper.
Cover and simmer for 35–45 minutes or until the pork becomes tender. Add water if the mixture becomes too dry.
Add the pork liver and cook for another 5–8 minutes or until fully cooked.
Adjust the seasoning according to taste. Continue simmering until the sauce reaches your preferred consistency.
Serve hot with steamed rice.
tips: Cut the pork and liver into similar-sized pieces for even cooking.
Avoid overcooking the liver because it can become tough.
Allow the vinegar to boil before stirring to reduce its sharp smell and taste.

name: Lucban Hardinera (Quezon)
description: A well-known dish from Lucban, Quezon, made with diced pork, vegetables, pineapple, and tomato sauce. The mixture is placed in a llanera or mould, topped with eggs, and steamed until firm.
ingredients: ½ cup pineapple chunks, drained and chopped
½ tsp salt, or to taste
steps: Heat cooking oil in a pan. Sauté the garlic and onion until fragrant.
Add the diced pork and cook until lightly browned.
Pour in the soy sauce, calamansi juice, tomato sauce, and water. Stir to combine.
Cover and simmer for 30–40 minutes or until the pork becomes tender.
Add the carrots and potatoes. Cook for about 5–7 minutes or until slightly tender.
Add the pineapple chunks, green peas, and raisins. Mix well and cook for another 3–5 minutes.
Season with salt and ground black pepper. Remove from heat and allow the mixture to cool slightly.
Lightly grease individual llaneras or a heatproof mould. Arrange the sliced hard-boiled eggs at the bottom.
Mix the beaten eggs into the cooled pork mixture. Transfer everything into the prepared moulds and press gently to remove air pockets.
Cover each mould with foil and steam for 30–40 minutes or until the mixture is firm and fully set.
Allow to rest for a few minutes before carefully unmoulding onto a serving plate.
Serve warm.
tips: Cut the pork and vegetables into small, uniform pieces for a better texture.
Drain the pineapple well to prevent the mixture from becoming too watery.
Grease the moulds properly to make unmoulding easier.

name: Adobong Tumbong ng Baboy
description: A Filipino-style adobo dish made with pork large intestines, thoroughly cleaned and simmered until tender in a savory and tangy mixture of vinegar, soy sauce, garlic, and spices.
ingredients: 1 kg pork large intestines (tumbong ng baboy), thoroughly cleaned
2 pcs red or green chili peppers (optional)
Salt and ground black pepper to taste
steps: Clean the pork intestines thoroughly under running water. Remove any unwanted residue and odor.
Place the intestines in a pot with enough water to cover them.
Boil for approximately 1½–2 hours or until tender. Add more water as needed.
Drain, allow to cool, and cut the intestines into bite-sized pieces.
Heat cooking oil in a pan.
Sauté garlic and onion until fragrant.
Add the boiled intestines and cook for a few minutes.
Pour in the soy sauce, vinegar, and beef broth.
Add oyster sauce, bay leaves, and peppercorns. Allow the vinegar to boil uncovered for 3–5 minutes before stirring.
Cover and simmer for 15–20 minutes to allow the flavors to blend.
Add chili peppers and brown sugar, if desired. Season with salt and ground black pepper.
Simmer for another 3–5 minutes or until the sauce reaches your preferred consistency.
Serve hot with steamed rice.
tips: Clean the pork intestines thoroughly before cooking to remove unwanted residue and odor.
Boil the intestines until tender before adding the adobo sauce.
Avoid adding too much salt because soy sauce and oyster sauce already provide saltiness.
Let the vinegar boil uncovered before stirring to develop a balanced adobo flavor.
Adjust the amount of chili depending on your preferred level of spiciness.
Refrigerate leftovers within two hours of cooking.

name: Filipino-Style Pork Curry
description: A Filipino-style curry made with tender pork, potatoes, carrots, bell peppers, curry powder, and coconut milk or evaporated milk.
ingredients: 1 cup coconut milk or evaporated milk
steps: Heat oil in a pot. Sauté garlic and onion.
Add pork and cook until lightly browned.
Add curry powder and stir until fragrant.
Pour in water or broth.
Simmer for 40–50 minutes or until the pork is tender.
Add potatoes and carrots.
Cook until the vegetables are nearly tender.
Pour in coconut milk or evaporated milk.
Add bell pepper and simmer gently until the sauce thickens.
Season with salt and pepper before serving.
tips: Add curry powder while sautéing to release its aroma.
Use coconut milk for a richer flavor.
Avoid boiling vigorously after adding milk.

name: Pork with Tausi
description: A savory Chinese-Filipino-inspired pork dish cooked with fermented black beans, garlic, onion, and a flavorful sauce.
ingredients: 1 tsp cornstarch mixed with 2 tbsp water
steps: Rinse the black beans briefly if they are very salty.
Heat oil in a pan.
Sauté garlic, onion, and ginger.
Add pork and cook until lightly browned.
Add black beans, soy sauce, and oyster sauce.
Pour in water or broth.
Simmer until the pork is tender.
Add the cornstarch mixture and stir until the sauce thickens.
Season with black pepper.
Serve with steamed rice.
tips: Black beans are naturally salty, so adjust the soy sauce accordingly.
Slice pork thinly to reduce cooking time.
Add the cornstarch slurry gradually to control the sauce consistency.

name: Sweet and Sour Pork with Pineapple
description: A popular sweet and sour pork dish made with crispy pork pieces coated in a tangy sauce with pineapple, bell peppers, and onions.
ingredients: 500 g pork shoulder, cut into bite-sized pieces
1 tbsp cornstarch mixed with 2 tbsp water
steps: Season pork with salt and pepper.
Dip the pork pieces in beaten egg.
Coat with flour and cornstarch.
Heat oil and fry the pork until golden brown and fully cooked.
Remove and drain excess oil.
In a separate pan, combine pineapple juice, vinegar, ketchup, sugar, water, and soy sauce.
Bring to a simmer.
Add pineapple chunks, bell peppers, and onion.
Add the cornstarch mixture and stir until the sauce thickens.
Add the fried pork and toss until coated.
Serve immediately.
tips: Fry the pork in batches to maintain the oil temperature.
Add the fried pork just before serving to preserve its crispiness.
Adjust the sugar and vinegar to achieve your preferred sweet-and-sour balance.

name: Sinantolan with Pork (Southern Luzon)
description: A traditional Southern Luzon dish made with grated or shredded santol rind, pork, coconut milk, and shrimp paste. It has a creamy, savory, and slightly tangy flavor, often with a spicy kick.
ingredients: 500 g santol, peeled and grated or finely shredded
2–3 pieces red or green chilies, sliced
steps: Peel the santol and remove the seeds. Grate or finely shred the flesh and rind, depending on the variety and local preparation.
Squeeze the shredded santol to remove some of its excess juice. Set aside.
Heat cooking oil in a pan. Sauté the garlic and onion until fragrant.
Add the pork belly and cook until lightly browned and some of its fat has rendered.
Add the bagoong alamang and stir for about 1–2 minutes.
Add the shredded santol and mix well with the pork.
Pour in the water and coconut milk. Stir to combine.
Cover and simmer for 20–30 minutes or until the pork is tender and the santol has softened.
Add the coconut cream, sliced chilies, and ground black pepper.
Continue cooking uncovered for 5–10 minutes until the sauce thickens.
Taste and adjust the seasoning. Add salt only if needed because the bagoong is already salty.
Serve hot with steamed rice.
tips: Squeeze the santol properly to reduce excess liquid and some of its bitterness.
Adjust the amount of bagoong according to your preferred saltiness.
Add more chilies if you prefer a spicier dish.
Use santol that is suitable for cooking; the flavor and texture can vary depending on its variety and ripeness.

name: Pork Hamonado
description: A Filipino sweet-style pork dish braised in pineapple juice, soy sauce, garlic, and sugar until tender and flavorful.
ingredients: 1 kg pork shoulder or pork belly
steps: Combine pineapple juice, soy sauce, brown sugar, and black pepper.
Marinate the pork in the mixture for at least 1 hour in the refrigerator.
Heat oil in a pot and sauté garlic and onion.
Add the pork and brown on all sides.
Pour in the marinade and add the bay leaf.
Bring to a boil, then simmer over low heat for 45–60 minutes or until tender.
Add water if the sauce becomes too concentrated before the pork is tender.
Add pineapple chunks during the last 10 minutes.
Simmer until the sauce thickens and coats the pork.
Slice and serve with the sauce.
tips: Pineapple juice helps give the dish its sweet and tangy flavor.
Do not add the pineapple chunks too early because they may become mushy.
Adjust the sugar according to the sweetness of the pineapple juice.

name: Sinantomas (Quezon)
description: A Quezon-style pork dish featuring tender pork ribs simmered in a sweet and savory sauce made with pineapple juice, banana ketchup, garlic, and spices. It is commonly served with rice during family meals and special occasions.
ingredients: 750 g pork ribs, cut into serving pieces
½ tsp salt, or to taste
steps: Wash and drain the pork ribs. Season them with salt and ground black pepper.
Heat cooking oil in a pot. Sauté the garlic and onion until fragrant.
Add the pork ribs and cook until lightly browned on all sides.
Pour in the pineapple juice, banana ketchup, soy sauce, and water. Stir until the sauce is evenly combined.
Bring to a boil, then lower the heat and cover the pot.
Simmer for 45–60 minutes or until the ribs become tender. Add a little water if necessary.
Add the potatoes and carrots. Continue cooking for 10–15 minutes or until the vegetables are tender.
Taste the sauce and adjust the seasoning as needed.
Add the grated cheese, if desired, and stir until incorporated.
Simmer uncovered for another 2–3 minutes until the sauce thickens slightly.
Transfer to a serving dish and serve hot with steamed rice.
tips: Brown the pork ribs first to develop a richer flavor.
Simmer over low heat to make the ribs tender without drying them out.
Adjust the sweetness by adding more or less banana ketchup.
Add the cheese sparingly so it does not overpower the sauce.

name: Pork Kare-Kare
description: A traditional Filipino stew made with tender pork, vegetables, and a rich peanut-based sauce, usually served with bagoong alamang.
ingredients: 1 kg pork pata or pork shoulder
¼ cup ground toasted rice or rice flour
1 tbsp annatto powder or annatto oil
1 cup string beans, cut into portions
steps: Place pork in a pot and cover with water.
Bring to a boil and remove the scum.
Simmer for 1–1½ hours or until the pork is tender. Reserve the broth.
Heat oil in a separate pot.
Sauté garlic and onion until fragrant.
Add annatto powder or annatto oil.
Add peanut butter and stir.
Gradually pour in 3–4 cups of reserved pork broth.
Add ground toasted rice or rice flour and stir until the sauce thickens.
Add the cooked pork and simmer for 10–15 minutes.
Cook the eggplant, string beans, banana blossom, and pechay separately or add them according to their cooking times.
Arrange the vegetables with the pork and peanut sauce.
Serve hot with bagoong alamang on the side.
tips: Add broth gradually to control the thickness of the peanut sauce.
Use unsweetened peanut butter for a more traditional savory flavor.
Serve bagoong separately so everyone can adjust the saltiness to taste.
Cook vegetables separately when possible to preserve their color and texture.
GENERAL MEAL MANAGEMENT AND FOOD SAFETY GUIDE
1. Menu Planning
Choose dishes based on the number of people, budget, available ingredients, and occasion.
Balance rich pork dishes with vegetables, fruits, and lighter side dishes.
Consider preparation and cooking time when planning meals.
Use ingredients that can be shared across multiple recipes to minimize food waste.
2. Food Selection and Purchasing
Buy pork from clean and reputable meat shops or suppliers.
Choose pork that is fresh-looking, properly chilled, and free from unpleasant odors.
Check the packaging and expiration or use-by dates of processed ingredients.
Select fresh vegetables that are firm, clean, and free from signs of spoilage.
3. Proper Food Storage
Store raw pork in sealed containers on the lowest refrigerator shelf to prevent its juices from dripping onto other food.
Separate raw pork from cooked food and ready-to-eat ingredients.
Thaw frozen pork in the refrigerator, in cold water using a sealed bag, or in the microwave—not on the kitchen counter.
4. Proper Cooking Temperatures
Whole cuts of pork: at least 63°C, followed by a 3-minute rest.
Ground pork: at least 71°C.
Leftovers: reheat to 74°C.
Use a food thermometer to check the internal temperature at the thickest part of the meat.
5. Portion Control and Healthy Eating
Serve appropriate portions based on the number of people.
Balance pork dishes with vegetables and fiber-rich foods.
Choose leaner cuts when preparing everyday meals.
Limit excessive amounts of salt, sugar, and cooking oil.
Use grilling, steaming, boiling, or braising as alternatives to frequent deep-frying.
6. Budget Management
Compare prices before purchasing ingredients.
Buy ingredients according to the planned number of servings.
Choose seasonal vegetables and locally available ingredients.
Use leftover ingredients in other dishes when they are still safe to consume.
Prepare a shopping list to avoid unnecessary purchases.
7. Kitchen Sanitation and Food Safety
Wash hands before and after handling raw pork.
Clean and sanitize knives, chopping boards, and countertops.
Use separate chopping boards for raw meat and vegetables when possible.
Never reuse raw pork marinade as a dipping sauce unless it has been thoroughly boiled.
Keep hot food hot and cold food cold.
Refrigerate perishable food promptly and discard food that shows signs of spoilage.

name: Bistek Tagalog (Filipino Beef Steak)
description: Bistek Tagalog is a classic Filipino beef dish made with thin slices of beef marinated in calamansi juice, soy sauce, and garlic. The beef is pan-fried and simmered in a savory, tangy sauce, then topped with tender onion rings. It is commonly served with steamed rice.
steps: Combine the soy sauce, calamansi juice, garlic, and black pepper in a bowl.
Add the beef slices and marinate in the refrigerator for 30 minutes.
Remove the beef from the marinade and reserve the liquid.
Heat the cooking oil in a skillet over medium-high heat. Sear the beef in batches for approximately 1–2 minutes per side, depending on thickness. Transfer to a plate.
In the same skillet, sauté the onion rings for 2–3 minutes until softened but still holding their shape. Remove some onion rings for garnish.
Pour the reserved marinade into the skillet and add the water. Bring to a boil, then simmer for 2–3 minutes.
Return the beef to the skillet. Cover and simmer over low heat until tender, adding water if necessary. Thin sirloin slices may need only a few minutes, while tougher cuts require longer cooking.
Taste the sauce and add sugar if a slightly sweeter flavor is desired. Arrange the beef and onion rings on a serving plate and spoon the sauce over them.
tips: Slice the beef across the grain to make it easier to chew.
Avoid overcrowding the skillet because the beef may release moisture and boil instead of sear.
For a more budget-friendly version, use a suitable braising cut and allow extra time for tenderizing.
Serve with steamed rice and sautéed vegetables for a more balanced meal.
Refrigerate leftovers promptly in a covered container and reheat thoroughly.

name: Classic Kalderetang Baka (Filipino Beef Caldereta)
description: Classic kalderetang baka is a Filipino tomato-based beef stew traditionally prepared with potatoes, carrots, bell peppers, and liver spread. This recipe represents the more familiar liver-spread version of caldereta, distinguishing it from the modern peanut-butter variation listed separately.
ingredients: 1 kg beef chuck, cut into 3–4 cm cubes
½ cup liver spread, approximately 120 g
½ teaspoon salt, or to taste
steps: Pat the beef dry with paper towels. This helps it brown more effectively.
Heat the oil in a heavy-bottomed pot over medium-high heat. Brown the beef in batches, turning the pieces to develop color on several sides.
Reduce the heat to medium. Sauté the onion until translucent, then add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds.
Stir in the tomato paste and cook for 1 minute to deepen its flavor.
Return the beef to the pot. Add the tomato sauce, beef broth, soy sauce, and black pepper.

Bring the mixture to a boil, then reduce the heat to low. Cover and simmer for approximately 1½–2 hours, stirring occasionally, until the beef is tender. Add more water if the sauce becomes too thick before the beef softens.
Stir in the liver spread until fully incorporated into the sauce.
Add the potatoes and carrots. Simmer for 12–15 minutes, or until nearly tender.
Add the bell peppers and olives. Continue cooking for another 5–8 minutes.
Taste and adjust the seasoning. Serve hot with steamed rice.
tips: Beef chuck is suitable for this recipe because its connective tissue softens during slow cooking.
Add the liver spread after the beef has begun to tenderize so that the sauce does not become excessively thick too early.
For a less oily version, skim excess fat from the surface before adding the vegetables.
Cut the potatoes and carrots into similar-sized pieces so they cook evenly.
If preparing the dish ahead for a gathering, refrigerate it promptly and reheat it thoroughly before serving.

name: Mechadong Baka (Filipino Beef Mechado)
description: Mechadong baka is a tomato-based Filipino beef stew known for its savory sauce and tender beef. It commonly includes potatoes, carrots, garlic, onions, and calamansi or lemon for acidity. Although traditional versions may use larded beef, a practical home-cooking version can be made with beef chuck.
ingredients: 1 kg beef chuck, cut into cubes
½ teaspoon salt, or to taste
steps: Combine the beef, soy sauce, calamansi juice, and black pepper in a bowl. Marinate for 20–30 minutes in the refrigerator.
Remove the beef from the marinade and reserve the liquid.
Heat the oil in a pot over medium-high heat. Brown the beef in batches and set aside.
In the same pot, sauté the onion until translucent. Add the garlic and cook until fragrant.
Add the tomato paste and stir for 1 minute.
Return the beef to the pot. Pour in the tomato sauce, reserved marinade, broth, and bay leaves.
Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer over low heat for 1½–2 hours, or until the beef is tender. Add water as needed.
Add the potatoes and carrots. Simmer for 12–15 minutes.
Add the bell pepper and cook for another 5 minutes.
Remove the bay leaves, taste the sauce, and adjust the seasoning before serving.
tips: Brown the beef before adding liquid to improve the flavor of the finished sauce.
For more concentrated tomato flavor, allow the sauce to reduce uncovered during the final few minutes.
Avoid cutting the vegetables too small because prolonged simmering can cause them to break apart.
Pair with steamed rice and a fresh cucumber or tomato salad.

name: Kare-Kare with Beef
description: Kare-kare is a traditional Filipino stew characterized by its thick, savory peanut sauce and assortment of vegetables. Beef shank, oxtail, or other suitable slow-cooking cuts are commonly used. The dish is typically served with bagoong on the side, which adds a salty, fermented contrast to the mild peanut flavor.
ingredients: 6 cups water, plus more as needed
¾ cup smooth peanut butter, approximately 190 g
¼ cup finely ground toasted rice, approximately 30 g
1 teaspoon annatto powder mixed with 2 tablespoons warm water
½ teaspoon salt, or to taste
200 g string beans, cut into 5 cm lengths
1 small banana heart or 1 small bundle of pechay, optional
¼ cup bagoong alamang, served separately
steps: Place the beef, quartered onion, peppercorns, and water in a large pot.
Bring to a boil and skim off the foam that forms on the surface.
Reduce the heat and simmer gently until the beef is tender, approximately 2–3 hours. Add water if necessary.
Remove the beef and reserve the broth. Strain the broth if desired.
Heat the cooking oil in a separate pot. Sauté the chopped onion until translucent, then add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds.
Stir in the peanut butter, annatto mixture, and 4 cups of reserved broth. Mix until smooth.
Add the ground toasted rice gradually while stirring to prevent lumps. Simmer for 5–10 minutes until the sauce thickens.
Add the cooked beef and simmer for another 10 minutes so it absorbs the sauce.
In a separate pot, blanch or simmer the string beans, eggplant, and pechay until tender but not mushy. Add the vegetables to the stew shortly before serving.
Transfer to a serving bowl and serve hot with bagoong on the side.
tips: Add the ground toasted rice gradually because the sauce thickens as it simmers.
Use natural peanut butter or a smooth commercial variety without excessive added sugar.
Cook the vegetables separately if you want to preserve their color and texture.
Because bagoong is high in sodium, serving it separately allows diners to control how much they use.
Check for peanut allergies before serving this dish to clients or guests.

name: Nilagang Baka (Filipino Boiled Beef Soup)
description: Nilagang baka is a comforting Filipino beef soup made by simmering beef with onions, peppercorns, and vegetables. Its clear broth has a mild, savory flavor, while the beef becomes tender through slow cooking. Potatoes, cabbage, pechay, and saba bananas are common additions.
ingredients: 1 kg beef shank or beef brisket
2 saba bananas, peeled and halved, optional
½ teaspoon salt, or to taste
steps: Place the beef in a large pot and cover with the water. Bring to a boil over medium-high heat.
Skim the foam from the surface to help keep the broth clear.
Add the onion and peppercorns. Reduce the heat and simmer gently for 2–3 hours, or until the beef is tender.
Add the potatoes and saba bananas. Simmer for 12–15 minutes, until the potatoes are almost tender.
Add the fish sauce and adjust the seasoning.
Add the cabbage and cook for 3–5 minutes.
Add the pechay and cook for another 1–2 minutes, just until wilted.
Transfer the beef and vegetables to a serving bowl. Ladle the hot broth over them and serve immediately.
tips: Maintain a gentle simmer rather than a vigorous boil to help produce a clearer broth.
Beef shank gives the soup a richer texture because of its connective tissue.
Add leafy vegetables near the end to prevent overcooking.
For budget-conscious meal planning, use the broth as part of the meal and serve with a measured portion of rice.

name: Bulalo (Beef Shank and Marrow Soup)
description: Bulalo is a well-known beef soup associated with Batangas and the Southern Tagalog region. It features beef shank and marrow bones slowly simmered until the broth becomes flavorful and the meat tender. Corn, cabbage, pechay, and peppercorns are commonly added.
ingredients: 1.5 kg beef shank with marrow bones
2 ears sweet corn, cut into thirds
½ teaspoon salt, or to taste
steps: Place the beef shank in a large pot and add the water. Bring to a boil.
Skim off the foam and excess impurities that rise to the surface.
Add the onion and peppercorns. Reduce the heat and simmer gently for approximately 3 hours, or until the meat is tender.
Add the corn and potatoes. Continue simmering for 15 minutes, or until the vegetables begin to soften.
Season with fish sauce and salt.
Add the cabbage and simmer for 3–5 minutes.
Add the pechay and cook for another 1–2 minutes.
Arrange the beef shank, marrow bones, and vegetables in a large serving bowl. Pour the hot broth over them and serve.
tips: Ask the butcher for shank pieces with marrow bones suitable for soup.
Slow simmering develops flavor and tenderizes the beef without making the broth excessively cloudy.
Refrigerate the soup after cooking if preparing it in advance. Once chilled, excess hardened fat can be removed from the surface.
Serve with calamansi, pepper, and a small dish of fish sauce on the side.

name: Beef Pares
description: Beef pares is a Filipino beef dish commonly served with garlic rice and clear soup. The beef is braised in a sweet-savory mixture of soy sauce, garlic, ginger, star anise, and other seasonings until tender. Its glossy sauce makes it a popular choice for rice meals and casual dining.
ingredients: 750 g beef brisket or chuck, cubed
steps: Pat the beef dry. Heat the cooking oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat.
Brown the beef in batches, turning the pieces to develop color. Transfer to a plate.
In the same pot, sauté the onion until softened.
Add the garlic and ginger. Cook for approximately 30–60 seconds.
Return the beef to the pot. Add the soy sauce, brown sugar, star anise, bay leaves, pepper, and water or broth.
Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat and cover. Simmer for 1½–2½ hours, or until the beef is tender.
Remove the lid during the final 10–15 minutes if the sauce needs to reduce. Stir occasionally to prevent sticking.
Remove the star anise and bay leaves.
Serve the beef with garlic rice, topped with spring onions and fried garlic if desired.
tips: Do not add excessive sugar at the beginning. Taste the sauce after the beef has softened and adjust if needed.
Use brisket or chuck for a tender, braised result.
Prepare the beef ahead of time to simplify service during busy meal periods.
Pair with a clear vegetable soup or fresh cucumber salad to complement the rich sauce.

name: Beef Tapa
description: Beef tapa consists of thinly sliced beef marinated in a savory mixture of soy sauce, garlic, calamansi, and pepper. It is commonly pan-fried and served as part of tapsilog, a Filipino breakfast combination of tapa, sinangag, and itlog. Its slightly salty, garlicky flavor pairs well with rice and eggs.
ingredients: 500 g beef sirloin or another suitable tender cut, thinly sliced
steps: In a bowl, combine the soy sauce, calamansi juice, garlic, brown sugar, and black pepper.
Add the beef and mix until the slices are evenly coated.
Cover and marinate in the refrigerator for at least 4 hours, preferably overnight.
Remove the beef from the marinade and let excess liquid drip off.
Heat the oil in a skillet over medium heat.
Cook the beef in batches, turning the slices as they brown. Thin slices generally cook within several minutes, depending on thickness.
If the beef needs more tenderizing, add 2–3 tablespoons of water, cover briefly, and simmer until tender. Remove the lid and allow excess liquid to evaporate.
Serve with garlic rice, eggs, tomato, and spiced vinegar if preparing tapsilog.
tips: Slice the beef across the grain for a more tender texture.
Avoid cooking all the beef at once because overcrowding can cause it to steam rather than brown.
For a lower-sodium version, reduce the soy sauce and increase the calamansi and garlic.
Keep the beef refrigerated while marinating. Do not reuse raw marinade as a dipping sauce unless it has been brought to a full boil.

name: Adobong Baka (Filipino Beef Adobo)
description: Adobong baka is a beef variation of the Filipino adobo cooking tradition. Beef is simmered with vinegar, soy sauce, garlic, bay leaves, and peppercorns until tender. The sauce may be left slightly brothy or reduced until it coats the beef.
steps: Combine the beef, soy sauce, garlic, bay leaves, and peppercorns in a bowl. Marinate in the refrigerator for 30 minutes.
Heat the cooking oil in a pot over medium-high heat.
Remove the beef from the marinade and brown it in batches. Reserve the marinade.
Add the onion and sauté until softened.
Return the beef to the pot. Add the reserved marinade, vinegar, and water.
Bring the mixture to a boil. Let it boil uncovered for approximately 3–5 minutes before stirring, allowing the sharp vinegar aroma to dissipate.
Reduce the heat, cover, and simmer for 1½–2½ hours, or until the beef is tender. Add water if needed.
Remove the lid and simmer for another 5–10 minutes to reduce the sauce.
Taste and add brown sugar if a slightly sweeter flavor is desired.
Serve hot with steamed rice.
tips: Choose beef chuck or brisket for braising.
Allow the vinegar to boil before stirring to help mellow its sharp aroma.
For a less salty preparation, use reduced-sodium soy sauce and adjust the quantity gradually.
Adobo generally develops flavor after resting, making it useful for planned meals. Refrigerate promptly and reheat thoroughly before serving.

name: Beef Afritada
description: Beef afritada is a Filipino tomato-based stew prepared with beef, potatoes, carrots, and bell peppers. It is related to other Filipino tomato-based dishes but is generally characterized by its straightforward tomato sauce and vegetable combination. The beef is simmered until tender before the vegetables are added.
ingredients: ½ teaspoon salt, or to taste
steps: Heat the oil in a pot over medium-high heat.
Brown the beef in batches, then transfer it to a plate.
In the same pot, sauté the onion until translucent. Add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds.
Stir in the tomato paste and cook for 1 minute.
Return the beef to the pot. Add the tomato sauce, broth, and black pepper.
Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat and simmer, covered, for 1–1½ hours or until the beef is tender. Add water if needed.
Add the potatoes and carrots. Simmer for 12–15 minutes.
Add the bell pepper and peas, if using. Cook for another 5 minutes.
Season with fish sauce or salt as desired.
Serve hot with rice.
tips: Brown the beef in batches to develop a richer flavor.
Add vegetables only after the beef has softened to prevent them from becoming mushy.
Use seasonal vegetables to keep ingredient costs manageable.
Serve with steamed rice and a side of sautéed leafy vegetables for a more balanced meal.

name: Menudong Baka (Filipino Beef Menudo)
description: Menudong baka is a tomato-based Filipino stew made with beef, potatoes, carrots, bell peppers, and sometimes beef liver. It is commonly served with rice and is suitable for family meals or celebrations. The combination of tender beef and slightly sweet tomato sauce gives the dish its familiar Filipino flavor.
ingredients: 750 g beef chuck, cut into small cubes
150 g beef liver, cut into cubes, optional
½ teaspoon salt, or to taste
steps: Heat the oil in a pot over medium-high heat. Brown the beef in batches and set aside.
Sauté the onion until softened. Add the garlic and tomato paste, then cook for 1 minute.
Return the beef to the pot. Add the tomato sauce, soy sauce, broth, and black pepper.
Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer over low heat for 1–1½ hours, or until the beef is tender.
Add the potatoes and carrots. Cook for 10–15 minutes.
If using beef liver, add it during the final 5–8 minutes and cook until fully done.
Add the bell pepper and raisins, if desired. Simmer for another 3–5 minutes.
Taste, adjust the seasoning, and serve hot.
tips: Cut the vegetables into evenly sized pieces to promote uniform cooking.
Add liver toward the end because prolonged cooking can make it firm.
Raisins are optional and can be omitted for a less sweet sauce.
Use lean beef and moderate the cooking oil to reduce the dish's fat content.

name: Beef Picadillo
description: Beef picadillo is a practical Filipino-style ground beef dish prepared with tomatoes, potatoes, carrots, and sometimes green peas or raisins. It is easy to prepare and can be served with rice, used as a filling for bread, or incorporated into other meals.
ingredients: ½ teaspoon salt, or to taste
steps: Heat the oil in a skillet over medium heat.
Sauté the onion until softened, then add the garlic and tomatoes.
Cook the tomatoes for 3–5 minutes, stirring until they soften.
Add the ground beef. Break it apart with a wooden spoon and cook until browned and no longer pink.
Stir in the tomato paste and soy sauce.
Add the diced potato, carrot, water, and black pepper.
Cover and simmer for 12–15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the vegetables are tender.
Add the green peas and cook for another 3–5 minutes.
Check that the ground beef is fully cooked. Adjust the seasoning and serve hot.
tips: Choose ground beef with a moderate fat content for flavor without excessive grease.
Drain excess fat if needed before adding the vegetables.
Prepare a larger batch and use the leftovers as filling for sandwiches or stuffed vegetables, provided they are cooled and stored safely.
Pair with steamed rice and a vegetable side dish.

name: Ginataang Baka (Beef in Coconut Milk)
description: Ginataang baka is a Filipino beef dish enriched with coconut milk. Depending on the household or regional variation, it may include ginger, garlic, chili, leafy vegetables, or other local produce. The coconut milk adds a creamy texture and balances the savory flavor of the beef.
ingredients: 200 g string beans, cut into 5 cm lengths
½ teaspoon salt, or to taste
steps: Heat the oil in a pot over medium-high heat. Brown the beef on several sides.
Add the onion, garlic, and ginger. Sauté until fragrant.
Pour in the water or broth. Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer over low heat for 1–2 hours, or until the beef is tender.
Add the coconut milk and fish sauce. Stir gently to combine.
Simmer uncovered over low heat for 10–15 minutes. Avoid vigorous boiling, which may cause the coconut milk to separate.
Add the string beans and green chilies. Cook for approximately 5–7 minutes.
Add the chili leaves or spinach and cook until wilted.
Season with black pepper and salt as needed. Serve hot.
tips: Use beef chuck or brisket because these cuts become tender during slow cooking.
Keep the heat low after adding coconut milk.
For a lighter preparation, replace part of the coconut milk with broth.
Serve with rice and a fresh vegetable side to complement the creamy sauce.

name: Sinigang na Baka (Sour Beef Soup)
description: Sinigang na baka is a Filipino sour soup featuring beef and vegetables in a tangy tamarind-based broth. Radish, eggplant, tomatoes, string beans, and kangkong are common additions. Its sour, savory flavor makes it a refreshing alternative to richer beef stews.
ingredients: 1 kg beef ribs or beef shank
100 g string beans, cut into 5 cm lengths
50 g tamarind paste, or a quantity of sinigang mix according to its package directions
steps: Place the beef in a pot and add the water. Bring to a boil and skim off the foam.
Add the onion and tomatoes. Reduce the heat and simmer for 2–3 hours, until the beef is tender.
Add the tamarind paste or prepared souring mixture. Stir and simmer for 5 minutes.
Add the radish and cook for 5–7 minutes.
Add the eggplant and string beans. Simmer until the vegetables are tender but still hold their shape.
Add the fish sauce and green chilies, if using.
Add the kangkong and cook for 1–2 minutes.
Taste the broth and adjust the sourness and seasoning before serving.
tips: Add the vegetables in stages according to their cooking times.
If using fresh tamarind, boil the pods until soft, mash them in a little broth, and strain the liquid into the soup.
Choose a souring agent according to your budget and availability.
Serve with rice and moderate the fish sauce if sodium intake is a concern.

name: Classic Beef Pochero
description: Classic beef pochero is a hearty Filipino stew influenced by Spanish culinary traditions. This version uses fresh tomatoes and tomato paste to build its broth, with beef, saba bananas, potatoes, cabbage, and chickpeas. It represents the standard family-style preparation in this collection.
steps: Heat the oil in a large pot. Brown the beef in batches and set aside.
Sauté the onion and garlic until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes and tomato paste. Cook for 3–5 minutes until the tomatoes soften.
Return the beef to the pot and add the water or broth.
Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat and simmer, covered, for 1½–2½ hours, or until tender.
Add the potatoes and saba bananas. Cook for 12–15 minutes.
Stir in the chickpeas and fish sauce. Simmer for another 5 minutes.
Add the cabbage and cook until just tender.
Add the pechay and simmer for 1–2 minutes.
Adjust the seasoning and serve hot with rice.
tips: Add saba bananas after the beef softens to prevent them from breaking apart.
Canned chickpeas are a convenient alternative to dried chickpeas that require soaking and longer cooking.
Choose firm saba bananas that will retain their shape during simmering.
Use the broth and vegetables to make the dish more filling without relying entirely on meat.

name: Beef Lauya
description: Lauya is a Filipino boiled meat dish associated with northern Luzon, including Ilocano cooking traditions. Beef versions commonly use shank or other bone-in cuts simmered with ginger, garlic, onions, and peppercorns. The result is tender meat served in a simple, aromatic broth.
ingredients: 1.2 kg beef shank or bone-in beef cuts
250 g cabbage, cut into wedges, optional
steps: Place the beef in a large pot and add the water.
Bring to a boil and skim off the foam.
Add the onion, ginger, garlic, and peppercorns.
Reduce the heat and simmer gently for 2½–3½ hours, depending on the cut, until the beef is tender.
Add fish sauce and taste the broth.
If using cabbage, add it during the final 5 minutes.
Add pechay during the last 1–2 minutes.
Transfer the beef to a serving bowl and pour the hot broth over it.
tips: Beef shank produces a flavorful broth because of its bones and connective tissue.
Keep the broth at a gentle simmer to reduce evaporation and preserve clarity.
Ginger provides aroma without requiring many expensive seasonings.
Serve with rice, calamansi, and a small amount of fish sauce on the side.

name: Beef Tinola (Adapted Version)
description: Beef tinola is an adaptation of the familiar Filipino tinola, which is traditionally prepared with chicken. This version uses beef simmered with ginger, garlic, onion, green papaya, and chili leaves to create a light, aromatic broth. It should be understood as a home-style beef adaptation, not the standard traditional chicken tinola.
ingredients: 300 g green papaya, peeled and sliced
1 cup chili leaves or malunggay leaves
steps: Heat the oil in a pot over medium heat.
Sauté the ginger, onion, and garlic until fragrant.
Add the beef and cook for 5–7 minutes, stirring to brown the outside.
Pour in the water and bring to a boil.
Reduce the heat and simmer, covered, for 1½–2 hours, or until the beef is tender.
Add the green papaya and simmer for 10–15 minutes, until soft but not falling apart.
Add fish sauce and black pepper.
Stir in the chili leaves or malunggay and cook for 1–2 minutes.
Taste, adjust the seasoning, and serve hot.
tips: Use ginger generously for a more aromatic broth.
Cut the papaya into uniform pieces so they cook evenly.
If using malunggay, add it just before serving to preserve its color.
For a quicker preparation, use thinly sliced beef that cooks faster, while ensuring it reaches a safe level of doneness.

name: Beef with Ampalaya
description: Beef with ampalaya combines tender beef strips with bitter melon, garlic, onions, and tomatoes. The beef provides savory flavor, while the ampalaya contributes a distinctive bitterness and crisp texture. It is a practical everyday dish that pairs well with rice.
steps: Cut the ampalaya lengthwise and remove the seeds and white pith. Slice thinly.
If desired, toss the ampalaya with ½ teaspoon salt, let it stand for 10 minutes, then rinse and drain.
Combine the beef with 1 tablespoon soy sauce and the black pepper. Marinate for 10 minutes.
Heat 1 tablespoon oil in a skillet over high heat. Sear the beef in batches until browned and cooked through. Transfer to a plate.
Add the remaining oil to the skillet. Sauté the garlic and onion until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes and cook until softened.
Add the ampalaya and stir-fry for 2–3 minutes.
Add the oyster sauce, remaining soy sauce, and water. Cook for another 2–3 minutes.
Return the beef to the skillet and toss until combined.
Taste and adjust the seasoning before serving.
tips: Do not overcook the ampalaya if you prefer it slightly crisp.
Searing beef in batches helps retain its texture.
Reducing the amount of oyster sauce and soy sauce can help moderate sodium.
Serve with rice and another vegetable dish to provide variety in the meal.

name: Beef with Broccoli, Filipino-Style
description: Beef with broccoli is a Filipino-style home and restaurant dish influenced by Chinese-style stir-frying. Thin beef strips are cooked with broccoli, garlic, onions, and a savory soy-based sauce. It is a Filipino-Chinese-influenced preparation rather than an indigenous traditional Filipino dish.
steps: Combine the beef with 1 tablespoon soy sauce, the black pepper, and ½ teaspoon cornstarch. Set aside for 10 minutes.
Mix the remaining soy sauce, oyster sauce, water, and remaining cornstarch in a small bowl.
Bring a pot of water to a boil. Blanch the broccoli for 1–2 minutes, then drain.
Heat the oil in a skillet or wok over high heat.
Sear the beef in batches until browned and cooked through. Transfer to a plate.
Add the garlic and onion to the skillet and sauté until fragrant.
Add the broccoli and stir-fry for 2 minutes.
Return the beef to the pan and pour in the sauce mixture.
Stir continuously for 1–2 minutes, until the sauce thickens and coats the ingredients.
Serve immediately with rice.
tips: Slice the beef across the grain for tenderness.
Blanching broccoli helps it retain its green color and shortens the stir-frying time.
Avoid adding too much cornstarch because the sauce should lightly coat the ingredients, not become pasty.
For budget-friendly meal planning, serve smaller portions of beef alongside generous portions of broccoli.

name: Simple Beef and Sayote Guisado
description: Simple beef and sayote guisado is a Filipino home-cooked dish centered on beef strips or ground beef and chayote, cooked with garlic, onion, and tomatoes. Sayote is the main vegetable in this straightforward version. For a more vegetable-rich variation that also includes carrots, see Recipe 50.
ingredients: 400 g beef strips or lean ground beef
½ cup water or beef broth
½ teaspoon salt, or to taste
steps: Peel the sayote, cut it in half, remove the seed, and slice into thin strips.
Heat the oil in a skillet over medium-high heat.
If using beef strips, sear them until browned. If using ground beef, cook while breaking it apart until browned and fully cooked.
Add the onion and garlic. Sauté until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes and cook until softened.
Stir in the soy sauce and black pepper.
Add the sayote and water or broth. Cover and simmer for 8–12 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Check that the sayote is tender but not mushy. Add a little more water if the pan becomes dry before the vegetables are cooked.
Adjust the seasoning and serve hot.
tips: Choose firm sayote without soft spots or deep blemishes.
Cut the sayote into evenly sized strips for consistent cooking.
Ground beef is convenient for a quick version, while beef strips offer a different texture.
This dish is budget-friendly because sayote adds volume and fiber without requiring a large amount of meat.

name: Giniling na Baka with Potatoes and Carrots
description: Giniling na baka is a familiar Filipino ground beef dish cooked with garlic, onions, tomatoes, potatoes, and carrots. Some versions use tomato sauce and green peas. Its versatility makes it suitable for rice meals, packed lunches, and fillings for bread or savory pastries.
ingredients: ½ teaspoon salt, or to taste
steps: Heat the cooking oil in a skillet over medium heat.
Add the onion and sauté until softened. Add the garlic and tomatoes, then cook until the tomatoes soften.
Add the ground beef. Break it into small pieces and cook until browned and no longer pink.
Stir in the soy sauce and tomato sauce.
Add the potato, carrot, water, and black pepper.
Cover and simmer for 12–15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the vegetables are tender.
Add the green peas and cook for another 3–5 minutes.
Confirm that the beef is fully cooked, then adjust the seasoning and serve.
tips: Dice the vegetables uniformly so they cook at the same rate.
Use lean ground beef and drain excess fat if necessary.
Portion leftovers into clean, shallow containers and refrigerate promptly.
Use leftover giniling as a filling for pandesal, omelets, or stuffed vegetables to reduce food waste.

name: Beef Embutido
description: Beef embutido is a variation of the Filipino steamed meatloaf commonly prepared for family celebrations. Ground beef is combined with vegetables, eggs, breadcrumbs, and seasonings, then shaped into a log and steamed. Hard-boiled eggs or sliced hotdogs can be added to the center.
ingredients: Aluminum foil or food-safe steaming wrappers
steps: Combine the ground beef, carrot, onion, breadcrumbs, beaten eggs, pickle relish, raisins, milk, soy sauce, and black pepper in a large bowl.
Mix until evenly combined, taking care not to compact the mixture excessively.
Divide the mixture into two portions.
Place each portion on a sheet of foil and shape it into a log. If desired, place a hard-boiled egg lengthwise in the center.
Roll the foil tightly around the mixture and twist the ends securely. Do not allow water to enter the wrapping.
Arrange the rolls in a steamer over boiling water.
Steam for approximately 40–50 minutes, depending on thickness, until the center reaches at least 71°C.
Remove the rolls and let them rest for 10 minutes before opening.
Slice into rounds and serve warm, or chill completely before slicing for a firmer texture.
tips: Grated carrot adds moisture and sweetness without requiring much added fat.
Steam one small test portion first if you want to check the seasoning before shaping the full batch.
For a leaner version, omit the raisins and use lean ground beef.
Cool leftovers promptly and refrigerate. Slice only what is needed for serving.

name: Beef Bola-Bola in Tomato Sauce
description: Beef bola-bola consists of seasoned ground beef shaped into small meatballs and cooked in tomato sauce. It is a practical Filipino-style family dish that can be served with rice or noodles. The meatballs can also be prepared in advance and frozen for future meals.
steps: Combine the ground beef, egg, breadcrumbs, garlic, onion, black pepper, and salt.
Mix gently and shape into approximately 20 meatballs, each about 3–4 cm in diameter.
Heat the cooking oil in a skillet over medium heat. Brown the meatballs in batches, turning them carefully. Transfer to a plate.
In the same skillet, sauté the chopped onion and garlic until fragrant.
Add the tomato sauce and water or broth. Bring to a gentle simmer.
Return the meatballs to the skillet and cover.
Simmer for approximately 15–20 minutes, turning the meatballs occasionally, until the centers reach 71°C.
Taste the sauce and add sugar if desired.
Garnish with spring onions and serve hot.
tips: Keep the meatball size consistent to ensure even cooking.
Avoid overmixing the ground beef because it can make the meatballs dense.
For easier preparation, form and freeze uncooked meatballs on a tray before transferring them to a freezer-safe container.
Serve with rice and steamed vegetables for a balanced meal.

name: Beef Siomai (Chinese-Filipino Style)
description: Beef siomai is a Chinese-influenced Filipino dumpling commonly enjoyed as a snack or meal accompaniment. This Filipino-style version uses seasoned ground beef mixed with finely chopped vegetables and wrapped in thin dumpling wrappers. The dumplings are steamed and commonly served with calamansi, soy sauce, and chili-garlic sauce.
steps: Combine the ground beef, carrot, onion, garlic, egg, soy sauce, sesame oil, black pepper, and salt in a bowl.
Mix until the ingredients are evenly distributed.
