Place approximately 1 tablespoon of filling in the center of each wrapper.
Gather the wrapper around the filling, leaving the top open. Press gently to secure the shape.
Arrange the siomai in a lightly oiled steamer basket, leaving space between pieces.
Steam over boiling water for approximately 15–20 minutes, depending on size, until the centers reach 71°C.
Remove carefully and serve hot with the dipping sauce.
tips: Keep unused wrappers covered with a clean, slightly damp cloth to prevent drying.
Do not overfill the wrappers because the dumplings may split during steaming.
Line the steamer with cabbage leaves or perforated parchment to prevent sticking.
Steam a test dumpling first if you are adjusting the seasoning for a larger batch.

name: Beef Mami
description: Beef mami is a Filipino noodle soup influenced by Chinese noodle traditions. It typically features tender beef, egg noodles, and a clear broth flavored with garlic, onion, and pepper. Spring onions and fried garlic add aroma and texture.
ingredients: ½ teaspoon salt, or to taste
steps: Place the beef and water in a large pot. Bring to a boil and skim off the foam.
Add the onion, garlic, and peppercorns.
Reduce the heat and simmer for 2–3 hours, until the beef is tender.
Remove the beef, slice it thinly, and set aside.
Strain the broth if desired. Season with fish sauce and salt.
Cook the egg noodles according to the package instructions, then drain.
Blanch the cabbage in the hot broth for 1–2 minutes.
Divide the noodles among four bowls. Add the sliced beef and cabbage.
Ladle the hot broth over the noodles.
Garnish with spring onions and fried garlic. Serve immediately.
tips: Simmer the broth gently to develop flavor without excessive cloudiness.
Cook the noodles separately to prevent excess starch from thickening the soup.
Slice the beef across the grain for easier chewing.
Refrigerate the broth and meat separately from the noodles if preparing the soup ahead.

name: Beef Pancit Bihon
description: Beef pancit bihon is a Filipino rice-noodle dish combining thin bihon noodles with beef, cabbage, carrots, and seasonings. It is a practical alternative to pork or chicken pancit and is suitable for family meals, gatherings, and packed lunches.
steps: Soak the bihon in room-temperature water for approximately 8–10 minutes, or according to the package instructions. Drain.
Heat the oil in a large wok or skillet over medium-high heat.
Sear the beef in batches until browned and cooked through. Transfer to a plate.
Add the onion and garlic to the wok. Sauté until fragrant.
Add the carrot and cabbage. Stir-fry for 2–3 minutes.
Pour in the beef broth, soy sauce, and black pepper. Bring to a simmer.
Add the drained bihon and toss with tongs until the noodles begin absorbing the liquid.
Return the beef to the wok and continue tossing until the noodles are tender and the liquid has been absorbed. Add a little more broth if necessary.
Stir in the calamansi juice.
Transfer to a serving platter and garnish with spring onions.
tips: Do not soak the noodles for too long because they may break during stir-frying.
Add broth gradually if you prefer firmer noodles.
Prepare and measure the vegetables before cooking to make the process more efficient.
Serve with calamansi wedges and a fresh vegetable side.

name: Beef Sotanghon Guisado
description: Beef sotanghon guisado is a Filipino glass-noodle dish prepared with beef, garlic, onions, and vegetables. Sotanghon noodles absorb the savory broth while retaining a delicate, springy texture. The dish is suitable for family meals and gatherings.
steps: Soak the sotanghon in warm water for 10–15 minutes, or follow the package instructions. Drain.
Heat the oil in a wok over medium-high heat.
Sear the beef in batches until cooked through. Set aside.
Sauté the onion and garlic until fragrant.
Add the carrot and cabbage and stir-fry for 2–3 minutes.
Pour in the broth and soy sauce. Bring to a simmer.
Add the drained sotanghon and toss gently.
Return the beef to the wok. Cook for approximately 5–8 minutes, or until the noodles are tender and have absorbed much of the broth.
Add the black pepper and adjust the seasoning.
Garnish with spring onions and serve hot.
tips: Check the noodle package for soaking instructions because brands vary.
Use tongs to separate the noodles gently without breaking them.
Keep a small amount of broth available in case the noodles absorb liquid too quickly.
Add vegetables that cook quickly near the end to maintain their texture.

name: Beef Sopas
description: Beef sopas is a variation of Filipino macaroni soup. It combines tender beef, elbow macaroni, cabbage, carrots, and milk in a creamy broth. This filling soup is suitable for cool weather, family lunches, and simple one-pot meals.
ingredients: 400 g beef chuck, cut into small cubes
steps: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat.
Sauté the onion and garlic until fragrant.
Add the beef and cook for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Pour in the broth and bring to a boil.
Reduce the heat and simmer, covered, for 30–45 minutes, or until the beef is tender.
Add the macaroni and cook according to the package instructions, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking.
Add the carrot and cabbage during the final 5–8 minutes of cooking.
Reduce the heat to low and pour in the evaporated milk.
Season with fish sauce, pepper, and salt. Heat gently for 2–3 minutes without allowing the milk to boil vigorously.
Serve hot.
tips: Cut the beef into small, uniform pieces to shorten the cooking time.
Cook the macaroni until just tender because it continues absorbing liquid while the soup stands.
Add extra broth when reheating because the pasta thickens the soup.
Refrigerate leftovers promptly and reheat thoroughly.

name: Beef Curry, Filipino-Style
description: Filipino-style beef curry combines tender beef, potatoes, carrots, bell peppers, and curry seasoning in a rich sauce. Depending on the household, the sauce may include coconut milk, evaporated milk, or broth. This version uses coconut milk for a creamy texture.
steps: Heat the oil in a pot over medium-high heat. Brown the beef in batches and set aside.
Sauté the onion, garlic, and ginger until fragrant.
Add the curry powder and cook for approximately 30 seconds, stirring constantly.
Return the beef to the pot and pour in the water or broth.
Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer for 1½–2 hours, until the beef is tender.
Add the potatoes and carrots. Simmer for 12–15 minutes.
Pour in the coconut milk and stir gently.
Add the bell pepper and fish sauce. Simmer over low heat for another 5–8 minutes.
Taste and adjust the seasoning.
Serve hot with rice.
tips: Blooming the curry powder in oil helps release its aroma.
Add coconut milk after the beef has softened to avoid unnecessarily prolonged cooking.
Use vegetables that are in season to manage costs.
Keep the curry at a gentle simmer after adding coconut milk.

name: Beef with Tausi (Fermented Black Bean Beef)
description: Beef with tausi is a Filipino-Chinese-style dish featuring beef strips cooked with fermented black beans, garlic, onions, and bell peppers. The fermented beans provide a deep, savory flavor, so the dish generally requires only a small amount of additional salty seasoning.
ingredients: 2 tablespoons fermented black beans, rinsed and lightly mashed
½ cup water or beef broth
1 teaspoon cornstarch mixed with 1 tablespoon water
steps: Slice the beef thinly across the grain.
Heat the oil in a wok or skillet over high heat.
Sear the beef in batches until browned and cooked through. Transfer to a plate.
Reduce the heat to medium. Sauté the garlic and onion until fragrant.
Add the rinsed fermented black beans and cook for 30 seconds.
Add the bell pepper and stir-fry for 2 minutes.
Pour in the water or broth, soy sauce, and oyster sauce.
Return the beef to the pan and stir to combine.
Add the cornstarch slurry and cook for 1–2 minutes, until the sauce lightly thickens.
Add the black pepper and serve immediately with rice.
tips: Rinse the fermented black beans to remove excess surface salt.
Avoid adding too much soy sauce before tasting because tausi is already salty.
Slice the beef uniformly for faster, more consistent cooking.
Serve with steamed vegetables or a fresh salad to balance the savory sauce.

name: Beef with Oyster Sauce and Pechay
description: This Filipino-Chinese-style beef dish combines tender beef strips with pechay, garlic, onions, and oyster sauce. The sauce adds a savory, slightly sweet flavor, while the pechay contributes freshness and a mild bitterness. It is suitable for quick lunches and dinners.
ingredients: 300 g pechay, washed and cut into manageable pieces
1 teaspoon cornstarch mixed with 1 tablespoon water
steps: Wash the pechay thoroughly and drain. Separate the thicker stems from the leaves.
Heat the oil in a wok over high heat.
Sear the beef in batches until browned and cooked through. Transfer to a plate.
Reduce the heat to medium. Sauté the garlic and onion until fragrant.
Add the pechay stems and stir-fry for 2 minutes.
Add the leaves and cook for another minute.
Combine the oyster sauce, soy sauce, water, and black pepper. Pour the mixture into the wok.
Return the beef and toss to combine.
Add the cornstarch slurry and stir for 1–2 minutes until the sauce lightly thickens.
Serve immediately with steamed rice.
tips: Separate the stems and leaves because the stems take longer to cook.
Choose pechay with firm stems and fresh-looking leaves.
Avoid overcooking the vegetables, which can cause them to release too much water.
Use reduced-sodium soy sauce if appropriate, and remember that oyster sauce also contributes sodium.

name: Beef with Upo (Bottle Gourd and Beef Guisado)
description: Beef with upo is a simple Filipino home-cooked dish combining beef with bottle gourd, garlic, onions, and tomatoes. The upo softens during cooking and absorbs the savory broth, making the dish economical and suitable for everyday meals.
ingredients: 400 g lean ground beef or thinly sliced beef
500 g upo, peeled and cut into cubes
½ cup water or beef broth
½ teaspoon salt, or to taste
steps: Peel the upo, cut it lengthwise, remove any large mature seeds, and dice the flesh.
Heat the oil in a skillet over medium heat.
If using ground beef, cook it while breaking it apart until browned and fully cooked. If using beef strips, sear until browned and cooked through.
Add the onion and garlic. Sauté until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes and cook for 3–5 minutes until softened.
Stir in the fish sauce and black pepper.
Add the upo and water or broth. Cover and simmer for 8–12 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Check that the upo is tender but still holds its shape.
Adjust the seasoning and serve hot with rice.
tips: Choose young, firm upo with smooth skin and no soft spots.
Avoid excessive simmering because the vegetable can become mushy.
Ground beef works well for a faster and more economical preparation.
The upo increases the vegetable content of the meal without requiring additional meat.

name: Beef Asado, Filipino-Style
description: Filipino-style beef asado is a savory-sweet braised beef preparation influenced by Chinese-Filipino cooking. Beef is slowly cooked with soy sauce, garlic, onions, star anise, and sugar until tender. The reduced sauce is glossy and flavorful, making the dish suitable for rice meals and special occasions.
steps: Pat the beef dry. Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat.
Brown the beef on all sides. Transfer to a plate.
Sauté the onion and garlic in the same pot until fragrant.
Return the beef to the pot. Add soy sauce, brown sugar, star anise, bay leaves, peppercorns, and water or broth.
Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer over low heat for approximately 2–3 hours, until the beef is tender.
Turn the beef occasionally to ensure even cooking.
Remove the beef and set aside to rest for 10 minutes.
Remove the star anise and bay leaves. Simmer the sauce uncovered until slightly thickened.
Add calamansi juice if desired.
Slice the beef across the grain and spoon the sauce over it.
tips: Choose brisket or chuck for a tender braised result.
Keep the heat low to prevent the sauce from evaporating before the beef becomes tender.
Slice the beef after resting to help retain its juices.
Serve with rice and steamed vegetables to balance the richness of the sauce.

name: Beef Sisig (Kapampangan-Inspired Beef Adaptation)
description: This recipe is a beef adaptation inspired by sisig, a dish strongly associated with Pampanga. Traditional Kapampangan sisig commonly uses pork, including parts such as the pig's face and ears. This version substitutes cooked beef, which is chopped and combined with onions, calamansi, chili, and seasonings before being heated on a skillet or sizzling plate.
ingredients: 500 g beef, preferably a mixture of tender cooked beef and suitable beef trimmings
steps: If using raw beef, simmer it in water until tender. Drain and allow it to cool enough to handle.
Chop the cooked beef into small pieces. For a mixture of textures, include some finely chopped, well-cooked trimmings.
Heat the oil in a skillet over medium-high heat.
Add the beef and cook for 5–8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until some pieces develop crisp edges.
Add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds.
Stir in the soy sauce and black pepper.
Add the onion and chili. Cook for 1–2 minutes while retaining some onion crunch.
Turn off the heat and mix in the calamansi juice.
If using mayonnaise, stir it in just before serving. Alternatively, serve it separately.
Transfer to a warm plate. Add a cooked egg on top if desired and serve immediately.
tips: Use fully cooked beef before chopping and crisping it.
Add calamansi near the end to preserve its bright, tangy flavor.
Serve mayonnaise separately if diners prefer a lighter version.
For food safety, keep cooked beef refrigerated until reheating and do not leave the finished dish at room temperature for extended periods.

name: Crispy Beef Tadyang (Crispy Beef Ribs)
description: Crispy beef tadyang is a practical Filipino-style preparation of beef ribs that are first simmered until tender and then roasted or air-fried to develop a crisp exterior. The meat is seasoned with garlic, pepper, and other simple spices and served with a vinegar-based dipping sauce.
steps: Place the ribs, water, garlic, onion, bay leaves, peppercorns, and salt in a pot.
Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat and simmer for 1½–2 hours, until the meat is tender.
Remove the ribs and drain well. Pat the surfaces dry with paper towels.
Preheat the oven to 220°C or the air fryer to 200°C.
Brush the ribs lightly with cooking oil.
Roast for approximately 20–30 minutes, turning halfway, or air-fry in batches for 12–20 minutes until the exterior is browned and crisp. Adjust the time to the size of the ribs and the equipment.
Meanwhile, combine the vinegar, garlic, onion, chili, and black pepper to make the dipping sauce.
Allow the ribs to rest for 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Drying the ribs before roasting is important for browning.
Do not overcrowd the air fryer because the ribs need space for hot air to circulate.
Roasting or air-frying can reduce the amount of added oil compared with deep-frying.
Serve in small portions with fresh vegetables and a vinegar dip.

name: Beef Barbecue Skewers
description: Beef barbecue skewers are a Filipino-style grilled dish featuring bite-sized beef marinated in soy sauce, calamansi, garlic, and brown sugar. The marinade gives the beef a savory, tangy, slightly sweet flavor. The skewers are suitable for outdoor gatherings, parties, and family meals.
ingredients: 600 g beef sirloin, cut into 2–3 cm cubes
1 medium red onion, cut into chunks
1 red bell pepper, cut into chunks
steps: If using wooden skewers, soak them in water for at least 30 minutes.
Combine the soy sauce, calamansi juice, garlic, brown sugar, oil, and black pepper.
Add the beef, cover, and marinate in the refrigerator for 2 hours.
Remove the beef from the marinade and reserve the liquid separately.
Thread the beef onto the skewers, alternating with onion and bell pepper pieces.
Preheat the grill to medium-high heat and lightly oil the grates.
Grill the skewers for approximately 3–5 minutes per side, turning as needed. Adjust the time according to the size of the pieces and desired doneness.
For whole cuts of beef, use a food thermometer to verify safe doneness. If basting, boil the reserved marinade thoroughly before using it.
Rest the skewers briefly and serve hot.
tips: Cut the beef into uniform pieces to help the skewers cook evenly.
Avoid pressing the beef against the grill because this can release juices.
Add vegetables between beef pieces, but leave enough space for heat to circulate.
Serve with rice, grilled vegetables, and calamansi for a complete meal.

name: Beef Inihaw with Calamansi and Garlic
description: Beef inihaw is a Filipino grilled beef preparation that relies on a flavorful marinade and direct heat. This version uses beef short ribs or thin steaks seasoned with calamansi, soy sauce, garlic, and pepper. Grilling develops a smoky aroma while allowing excess fat to drip away.
ingredients: 700 g beef short ribs or thin beef steaks
steps: Combine the soy sauce, calamansi juice, garlic, oil, pepper, and brown sugar.
Add the beef and marinate in the refrigerator for 2 hours.
Preheat the grill to medium-high heat. Clean and lightly oil the grates.
Remove the beef from the marinade and let excess liquid drip off.
Grill thin steaks for several minutes per side, adjusting the time to their thickness. Thicker short ribs may require lower heat and a longer cooking period.
Use a food thermometer to check doneness. For whole cuts of beef, the recommended minimum is 63°C followed by a 3-minute rest.
Combine the calamansi juice, soy sauce, and chopped onion to make a dipping sauce.
Rest the grilled beef before slicing and serve with the dipping sauce.
tips: Use a cut suitable for the chosen grilling method. Thin steaks cook quickly, while thick ribs may need slower cooking.
Do not pour raw marinade directly over cooked beef.
For a lighter meal, serve moderate beef portions alongside grilled eggplant, tomatoes, and rice.
Keep raw beef and ready-to-eat sides on separate plates.

name: Beef Dinakdakan-Inspired Dish
description: Dinakdakan is an Ilocano dish traditionally made with cooked pork parts, onions, ginger, chili, and a tangy dressing. This recipe is a clearly labeled beef adaptation inspired by those flavors, using tender beef cheek or another suitable beef cut. It is not the original traditional pork preparation.
ingredients: 700 g beef cheek or beef chuck
steps: Place the beef, water, quartered onion, garlic, ginger, and peppercorns in a pot.
Bring to a boil, then simmer until the beef is tender. Beef cheek may take approximately 1½–2 hours, depending on thickness.
Remove the beef and drain thoroughly.
Cut the cooked beef into bite-sized pieces.
Heat a grill pan or skillet over medium-high heat.
Grill or sear the beef pieces until lightly browned and crisp at the edges.
In a bowl, combine the sliced red onion, calamansi juice, vinegar, chilies, black pepper, and optional fish sauce.
Add the cooked beef and toss to combine.
Let the mixture stand for 3–5 minutes so the flavors blend.
Transfer to a serving plate and serve warm.
tips: Beef cheek gives a gelatin-rich texture, while chuck offers a more accessible alternative.
Cook the beef until tender before grilling to avoid a tough result.
Add the dressing after searing so the onions remain fresh and crisp.
Because this is a beef adaptation, identify it as such on a menu rather than presenting it as the original Ilocano version.

name: Beef Kilawin, Cooked Version
description: Kilawin is a Filipino preparation characterized by vinegar, citrus, onions, ginger, and chili. Traditional versions vary by region and may use seafood or other meats. This version uses fully cooked beef before adding the acidic dressing. The title specifies 'Cooked Version' to distinguish it from preparations that use raw or uncooked seafood or meat.
steps: Place the beef and water in a pot. Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat and simmer until the beef is tender and fully cooked.
Remove the beef, drain it, and allow it to cool slightly.
Slice the beef thinly across the grain.
In a clean bowl, combine the vinegar, calamansi juice, ginger, onion, chili, black pepper, and optional fish sauce.
Add the cooked beef and toss until evenly coated.
Cover and refrigerate for 20–30 minutes to allow the flavors to develop.
Taste and adjust the acidity and seasoning.
Garnish with spring onions if desired and serve chilled or cool.
tips: Vinegar and calamansi provide flavor but should not be relied upon to make raw beef safe.
Use a clean bowl and utensils after cooking the beef.
Refrigerate promptly and serve chilled if preparing ahead.
For a more tender result, slice across the grain and avoid overcooking the beef.

name: Beef Bopis-Inspired Guisado
description: Bopis is a Filipino dish commonly prepared with finely chopped pork lungs and heart, vinegar, garlic, onions, and spices. This version uses beef heart and, optionally, beef lungs from an inspected source. It is a beef-offal guisado inspired by bopis, not the traditional pork-offal preparation.
ingredients: 500 g beef heart, cleaned and finely chopped
250 g beef lungs, cleaned and finely chopped, optional
1 teaspoon annatto powder mixed with 2 tablespoons water
steps: Obtain the beef offal from a reputable, inspected source. Clean and prepare it according to safe food-handling practices.
Place the beef heart and optional lungs in a pot with enough water to cover. Bring to a boil and simmer until thoroughly cooked and tender.
Drain and allow the meat to cool enough to handle. Chop finely.
Heat the cooking oil in a skillet over medium heat.
Sauté the onion and garlic until fragrant, then add the tomatoes.
Add the chopped beef offal and cook for 5–8 minutes, stirring frequently.
Stir in the vinegar and allow it to boil for several minutes.
Add the soy sauce, annatto mixture, carrot, bell pepper, chilies, broth, and black pepper.
Simmer until the vegetables are tender and most of the liquid has evaporated.
Adjust the seasoning and serve hot.
tips: Purchase offal only from reputable suppliers and handle it separately from ready-to-eat foods.
Clean preparation surfaces and utensils thoroughly after contact with raw offal.
Chop the cooked ingredients uniformly for a consistent texture.
If offal is unavailable or unfamiliar to clients, offer a clearly labeled beef mince adaptation rather than claiming it is the traditional version.

name: Beef Caldereta with Peanut Butter (Modern Variation)
description: This modern home-cooking variation of beef caldereta incorporates peanut butter into its tomato-based sauce, creating a thicker consistency and richer flavor. Beef, potatoes, carrots, and bell peppers are simmered together until tender. It is distinct from the classic liver-spread kalderetang baka in Recipe 2 and should not be presented as a standardized traditional regional recipe.
ingredients: ¼ cup smooth peanut butter, approximately 65 g
steps: Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat.
Brown the beef in batches, then transfer it to a plate.
Sauté the onion and garlic in the same pot until fragrant.
Add the tomato paste and cook for 1 minute.
Return the beef to the pot. Add the tomato sauce, soy sauce, broth, and black pepper.
Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer over low heat for 1½–2 hours, until the beef is tender.
Stir the peanut butter into a small bowl containing several tablespoons of hot broth until smooth.
Add the peanut mixture to the pot and stir well.
Add the potatoes and carrots. Simmer for 12–15 minutes.
Add the bell pepper and cook for another 5 minutes. Adjust the seasoning and serve hot.
tips: Dissolve the peanut butter in warm broth before adding it to prevent lumps.
Add the peanut butter after the beef has softened so the sauce does not become too thick too early.
Check for peanut allergies before serving.
Serve with rice and vegetables to complement the rich sauce.

name: Beef with Ginisang Monggo
description: Beef with ginisang monggo combines tender mung beans with ground beef, tomatoes, garlic, onions, and leafy vegetables. It is a filling Filipino-style dish that provides protein from both beef and legumes. Malunggay leaves or spinach can be added near the end.
steps: Rinse the mung beans under running water and remove any damaged beans or debris.
Place the mung beans and water in a pot. Bring to a boil, then simmer for approximately 40–60 minutes, until tender. Add water if necessary.
Heat the cooking oil in a separate skillet over medium heat.
Sauté the onion and garlic until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes and cook until softened.
Add the ground beef and cook while breaking it apart until browned and fully cooked.
Transfer the beef mixture to the pot of cooked mung beans.
Add the fish sauce and black pepper. Simmer for 5–10 minutes to combine the flavors.
Stir in the malunggay leaves or spinach and cook for 1–2 minutes.
Taste, adjust the seasoning, and serve hot with rice.
tips: Soaking the mung beans for several hours can shorten their cooking time, although it is not essential.
Cook the beans until soft before combining them with the beef mixture.
Mung beans help stretch a smaller quantity of beef across more servings.
Refrigerate leftovers promptly because cooked legumes and meat are perishable.

name: Tomato-Rich Beef Pochero with Chickpeas (Variation)
description: This variation of Filipino beef pochero emphasizes a richer, tomato-forward sauce by using tomato sauce in addition to fresh tomatoes. It also includes chickpeas, saba bananas, potatoes, and cabbage. It is presented as a tomato-rich variation of the classic, fresher-tomato broth preparation in Recipe 15.
steps: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium-high heat.
Brown the beef in batches and set aside.
Sauté the onion and garlic until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes and cook for 3–5 minutes until softened.
Stir in the tomato sauce, then return the beef to the pot.
Pour in the water or broth. Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat and simmer, covered, for 1½–2½ hours, until the beef is tender.
Add the potatoes and saba bananas. Simmer for 12–15 minutes.
Add the chickpeas and fish sauce. Cook for another 5 minutes.
Add the cabbage and simmer until tender.
Taste, adjust the seasoning, and serve hot.
tips: Canned chickpeas reduce preparation time. Drain and rinse them before use.
Add the saba bananas carefully to prevent them from breaking apart.
Choose firm bananas and potatoes for better presentation.
Portion the beef and vegetables evenly so each serving contains a balanced mixture of ingredients.

name: Beef with Mushrooms and Gravy
description: Beef with mushrooms and gravy is a Filipino home-style dish influenced by familiar restaurant beef-and-gravy preparations. Beef strips are cooked with mushrooms, onions, garlic, and a savory brown sauce. It pairs well with rice or mashed potatoes and can be prepared relatively quickly using tender beef cuts.
ingredients: ½ teaspoon salt, or to taste
steps: Pat the beef dry and slice it thinly across the grain.
Heat the oil in a skillet over medium-high heat.
Sear the beef in batches until browned and cooked through. Transfer to a plate.
Reduce the heat to medium. Add the onion and sauté until softened.
Add the garlic and mushrooms. Cook for 4–5 minutes, until the mushrooms release moisture and begin to brown.
Sprinkle the flour over the mushroom mixture and stir continuously for 1 minute.
Gradually pour in the beef broth while stirring to prevent lumps.
Add the soy sauce and black pepper. Simmer for 3–5 minutes until the gravy thickens.
Return the beef to the skillet and stir to coat it with the gravy.
Add butter if desired, adjust the seasoning, and serve hot.
tips: Avoid overcrowding the skillet when searing beef.
Add the broth gradually to create a smooth gravy.
Fresh mushrooms should be firm and free from slimy patches.
For a lighter preparation, use less butter and serve with steamed vegetables.

name: Beef with Sitaw and Tomato
description: Beef with sitaw is a practical Filipino stir-fry or guisado that combines beef strips, yardlong beans, tomatoes, garlic, and onions. The vegetables provide a fresh texture and absorb the savory sauce. It is suitable for everyday meals and budget-conscious menu planning.
ingredients: 300 g sitaw, cut into 5 cm lengths
½ cup water or beef broth
½ teaspoon salt, or to taste
steps: Wash the sitaw and cut it into uniform lengths.
Heat the oil in a skillet over medium-high heat.
Sear the beef in batches until browned and cooked through. Transfer to a plate.
Add the onion and garlic to the skillet and sauté until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes and cook for 3–5 minutes until softened.
Stir in the soy sauce and black pepper.
Add the sitaw and water or broth. Cover and simmer for 5–8 minutes, until the beans are tender but still slightly crisp.
Return the beef to the skillet and toss to combine.
Taste and adjust the seasoning.
Serve hot with steamed rice.
tips: Choose firm, fresh sitaw without shriveled or discolored areas.
Cut the beans evenly to help them cook consistently.
Avoid overcooking the sitaw because it can become soft and lose its color.
Use seasonal vegetables and moderate the amount of beef to manage meal costs.

name: Beef with Talong and Tomato
description: Beef with talong is a Filipino home-style dish combining tender beef, eggplant, tomatoes, garlic, and onions. The eggplant absorbs the savory juices while contributing a soft texture. It is a practical way to incorporate vegetables into a beef-based meal.
ingredients: ½ cup water or beef broth
steps: Wash the eggplants and cut them into 2–3 cm pieces.
Heat 1 tablespoon of oil in a skillet over medium-high heat.
Sear the beef in batches until browned and cooked through. Transfer to a plate.
Add the remaining oil to the skillet.
Cook the eggplant pieces for 4–6 minutes, turning occasionally, until lightly browned and beginning to soften. Remove and set aside.
Sauté the onion and garlic until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes and cook until softened.
Stir in the soy sauce, black pepper, and water or broth.
Return the beef and eggplant to the skillet. Cover and simmer for 5–8 minutes until the eggplant is tender.
Adjust the seasoning and serve hot.
tips: Choose firm eggplants with smooth, glossy skin.
Cut the eggplant into similar-sized pieces to ensure even cooking.
Add the eggplant later in the cooking process to help it retain its shape.
Serve with rice and another vegetable side if additional variety is desired.

name: Beef with Kalabasa and Sitaw in Coconut Milk
description: This Filipino home-style dish combines beef, squash, string beans, and coconut milk. The kalabasa contributes natural sweetness and a soft texture, while the coconut milk creates a creamy sauce. It is inspired by the flavors of Filipino ginataan dishes.
ingredients: 200 g sitaw, cut into 5 cm lengths
steps: Heat the oil in a pot over medium-high heat.
Brown the beef in batches and set aside.
Sauté the onion, garlic, and ginger until fragrant.
Return the beef to the pot and add the water or broth.
Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer for 1½–2 hours, until the beef is tender.
Add the kalabasa and simmer for 8–10 minutes.
Pour in the coconut milk and stir gently.
Add the sitaw, fish sauce, black pepper, and optional chili.
Simmer over low heat for another 5–8 minutes, until the vegetables are tender and the sauce has thickened slightly.
Adjust the seasoning and serve hot with rice.
tips: Cut the squash into large, uniform cubes to reduce the risk of it breaking apart.
Add coconut milk after the beef has softened.
Stir gently once the squash is tender.
For a lighter sauce, replace part of the coconut milk with broth.

name: Beef with Corn and Potatoes
description: Beef with corn and potatoes is a Filipino home-style beef stew combining tender beef, sweet corn, potatoes, carrots, and a savory broth. It is a practical family meal that uses readily available ingredients and can be adapted to different household budgets.
ingredients: 2 ears sweet corn, cut into thirds
steps: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium-high heat.
Brown the beef in batches and set aside.
Sauté the onion and garlic until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes and cook for 3–5 minutes.
Return the beef to the pot and pour in the broth or water.
Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer over low heat for 1–1½ hours, until the beef is tender.
Add the corn and carrots. Simmer for 10 minutes.
Add the potatoes and cook for another 12–15 minutes, until tender.
Season with fish sauce, black pepper, and salt.
Transfer to a serving bowl and serve hot.
tips: Choose fresh corn with plump kernels and green husks, or use frozen corn for convenience.
Add the potatoes late enough to prevent them from breaking apart.
Use broth made from previous safe cooking preparations when available.
Serve the stew with rice and leafy vegetables for a more varied meal.

name: Beef with Pechay and Garlic
description: Beef with pechay and garlic is a quick Filipino home-style stir-fry featuring tender beef strips, leafy vegetables, garlic, onions, and a light soy-based sauce. It is suitable for busy households because it requires relatively little preparation and cooks quickly.
ingredients: 1 teaspoon cornstarch mixed with 1 tablespoon water, optional
steps: Wash the pechay thoroughly and drain. Separate the stems from the leaves.
Heat the oil in a wok or large skillet over high heat.
Sear the beef in batches until browned and cooked through. Transfer to a plate.
Reduce the heat to medium and sauté the garlic and onion until fragrant.
Add the pechay stems and stir-fry for 2 minutes.
Add the leaves and cook for another minute.
Combine the soy sauce, optional oyster sauce, water, and black pepper. Pour into the skillet.
Return the beef and toss to combine.
If a thicker sauce is desired, add the cornstarch slurry and stir for 1–2 minutes.
Serve immediately with rice.
tips: Do not wash vegetables until you are ready to prepare them if you need to store them first, as excess moisture can shorten their shelf life.
Use high heat for quick searing, but cook the beef in batches.
For a lower-sodium option, omit the oyster sauce and use less soy sauce.
This dish works well with steamed rice and fresh fruit as part of a simple family menu.

name: Beef and Vegetable Guisado with Sayote and Carrots
description: This Filipino home-cooked guisado is a more vegetable-rich variation featuring beef, sayote, carrots, garlic, onions, and tomatoes. Unlike the simpler sayote-centered dish in Recipe 20, this version includes carrots as a second main vegetable and cooks them in stages to achieve an even texture.
ingredients: 400 g beef strips or lean ground beef
½ teaspoon salt, or to taste
steps: Peel the sayote, cut it in half, remove the seed, and slice into uniform pieces.
Heat the cooking oil in a skillet over medium-high heat.
If using beef strips, sear them in batches until browned and cooked through. If using ground beef, cook while breaking it apart until browned and fully cooked.
Add the onion and garlic. Sauté until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes and cook until softened.
Stir in the soy sauce and black pepper.
Add the carrot and water or broth. Cover and simmer for approximately 5 minutes.
Add the sayote and continue simmering for another 8–12 minutes, until the vegetables are tender.
Taste and adjust the seasoning. Add a small amount of water if the pan becomes too dry before the vegetables are cooked.
Transfer to a serving dish and serve hot with rice.
tips: Choose fresh sayote and carrots that are firm and free from soft spots.
Add the sayote after the carrot if you want both vegetables to retain their texture.
Use whichever beef cut is economical and appropriate for the cooking time. Ground beef is convenient, while strips provide a different texture.
For meal management, measure the beef and vegetables before cooking so that portions can be divided consistently across servings.

name: Chicken Adobo
description: The Philippines' most iconic chicken dish, simmered in soy sauce, vinegar, garlic, and spices. The ingredients are cooked in stages so the chicken becomes tender and the sauce develops a balanced, well-rounded flavor.
steps: Marinate chicken in soy sauce and garlic for 30 minutes. Turn the pieces once so the seasoning coats them evenly, then keep the bowl covered in the refrigerator.
Brown chicken in oil. Arrange the pieces in a single layer and turn as needed so they color evenly without overcrowding the pan.
Add marinade, vinegar, water, bay leaves, and peppercorns. Stir gently and cook only until the leaves wilt, so they keep their color and do not become overly soft.
Simmer for 35 minutes. Keep the heat low to medium-low and maintain a gentle simmer rather than a vigorous boil; check that the chicken is becoming tender.
Reduce sauce and serve. Check that the chicken is fully cooked before serving; its thickest part should reach 74°C (165°F).
tips: Cut the chicken into similar-sized pieces so they cook evenly.
Keep the chicken refrigerated while marinating, and avoid reusing raw-chicken marinade unless it is boiled thoroughly.
Cook chicken until the thickest part reaches an internal temperature of 74°C (165°F).
Serve with steamed rice.

name: Chicken Tinola
description: A comforting ginger-based soup with chicken, papaya, and malunggay. Its broth is best kept at a gentle simmer to develop a clear, comforting flavor, with the vegetables added in stages so they retain their texture.
steps: Sauté garlic, onion, and ginger. Stir frequently over medium heat and cook just until the aromatics soften and release their fragrance; do not let the garlic burn.
Add chicken and fish sauce. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly arranged so they cook at a consistent rate.
Pour water and simmer for 30 minutes. Keep the heat low to medium-low and maintain a gentle simmer rather than a vigorous boil; check that the chicken is becoming tender.
Add papaya. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly arranged so they cook at a consistent rate.
When tender, add malunggay. Stir gently and cook only until the leaves wilt, so they keep their color and do not become overly soft.
Serve hot. Check that the chicken is fully cooked before serving; its thickest part should reach 74°C (165°F).
tips: Cut the chicken into similar-sized pieces so they cook evenly.
Keep the chicken refrigerated while marinating, and avoid reusing raw-chicken marinade unless it is boiled thoroughly.
Cook chicken until the thickest part reaches an internal temperature of 74°C (165°F).
Best enjoyed on cool or rainy days.

name: Chicken Surol
description: A Visayan chicken dish simmered in coconut milk and lemongrass. Slow, gentle cooking helps the chicken absorb the coconut-based sauce and allows the spices and local ingredients to blend.
ingredients: 1 kg chicken, cut into serving pieces
steps: Sauté garlic, onion, and ginger until fragrant. Stir frequently over medium heat and cook just until the aromatics soften and release their fragrance; do not let the garlic burn.
Add chicken and cook until lightly browned. Arrange the pieces in a single layer and turn as needed so they color evenly without overcrowding the pan.
Add lemongrass and coconut milk. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly arranged so they cook at a consistent rate.
Simmer until chicken becomes tender. Keep the heat low to medium-low and maintain a gentle simmer rather than a vigorous boil; check that the chicken is becoming tender.
Add malunggay leaves. Stir gently and cook only until the leaves wilt, so they keep their color and do not become overly soft.
Season with salt and pepper. Taste a small amount first and adjust gradually to avoid making the dish too salty.
Serve hot. Check that the chicken is fully cooked before serving; its thickest part should reach 74°C (165°F).
tips: Cut the chicken into similar-sized pieces so they cook evenly.
Keep the chicken refrigerated while marinating, and avoid reusing raw-chicken marinade unless it is boiled thoroughly.
Cook chicken until the thickest part reaches an internal temperature of 74°C (165°F).
Best served with steamed rice and fresh vegetables.

name: Chicken Kulma
description: A Filipino-Muslim chicken curry from Mindanao prepared with coconut milk and spices. Slow, gentle cooking helps the chicken absorb the coconut-based sauce and allows the spices and local ingredients to blend.
steps: Sauté garlic and onion until fragrant. Stir frequently over medium heat and cook just until the aromatics soften and release their fragrance; do not let the garlic burn.
Add chicken and cook until lightly browned. Arrange the pieces in a single layer and turn as needed so they color evenly without overcrowding the pan.
Stir in turmeric, cumin, and coriander. Mix gently until the ingredients are evenly distributed and the chicken is coated.
Pour coconut milk and bring to a simmer. Keep the heat low to medium-low and maintain a gentle simmer rather than a vigorous boil; check that the chicken is becoming tender.
Cook until chicken becomes tender. Cook evenly and check the thickest piece to make sure the chicken reaches an internal temperature of 74°C (165°F).
Season with salt and pepper. Taste a small amount first and adjust gradually to avoid making the dish too salty.
Serve warm. Check that the chicken is fully cooked before serving; its thickest part should reach 74°C (165°F).
tips: Cut the chicken into similar-sized pieces so they cook evenly.
Keep the chicken refrigerated while marinating, and avoid reusing raw-chicken marinade unless it is boiled thoroughly.
Cook chicken until the thickest part reaches an internal temperature of 74°C (165°F).
Serve with turmeric rice or steamed rice.

name: Chicken Menudo
description: A colorful stew featuring vegetables and raisins. The ingredients are cooked in stages so the chicken becomes tender and the sauce develops a balanced, well-rounded flavor.
steps: Sauté aromatics. Stir frequently over medium heat and cook just until the aromatics soften and release their fragrance; do not let the garlic burn.
Add chicken and brown. Arrange the pieces in a single layer and turn as needed so they color evenly without overcrowding the pan.
Pour in tomato sauce. Mix gently until the ingredients are evenly distributed and the chicken is coated.
Simmer. Keep the heat low to medium-low and maintain a gentle simmer rather than a vigorous boil; check that the chicken is becoming tender.
Add vegetables and raisins. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly arranged so they cook at a consistent rate.
Cook until tender. Cook evenly and check the thickest piece to make sure the chicken reaches an internal temperature of 74°C (165°F).
tips: Cut the chicken into similar-sized pieces so they cook evenly.
Keep the chicken refrigerated while marinating, and avoid reusing raw-chicken marinade unless it is boiled thoroughly.
Cook chicken until the thickest part reaches an internal temperature of 74°C (165°F).
Excellent with white rice.

name: Kinalas na Manok
description: A chicken noodle soup inspired by the flavors of Bicolano kinalas. Its broth is best kept at a gentle simmer to develop a clear, comforting flavor, with the vegetables added in stages so they retain their texture.
steps: Boil chicken in water until tender. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly arranged so they cook at a consistent rate.
Remove chicken and shred the meat. Allow the chicken to cool enough to handle safely, then cut or pull it into evenly sized pieces.
Strain the broth. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly arranged so they cook at a consistent rate.
Return broth to the pot and season. Taste a small amount first and adjust gradually to avoid making the dish too salty.
Cook noodles according to package instructions. Cook evenly and check the thickest piece to make sure the chicken reaches an internal temperature of 74°C (165°F).
Place noodles in bowls and top with shredded chicken. Allow the chicken to cool enough to handle safely, then cut or pull it into evenly sized pieces.
Pour hot broth over noodles. Mix gently until the ingredients are evenly distributed and the chicken is coated.
Garnish with spring onions. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly arranged so they cook at a consistent rate.
tips: Cut the chicken into similar-sized pieces so they cook evenly.
Keep the chicken refrigerated while marinating, and avoid reusing raw-chicken marinade unless it is boiled thoroughly.
Cook chicken until the thickest part reaches an internal temperature of 74°C (165°F).
Serve hot with calamansi and fried garlic.

name: Chicken Law-uy
description: A Visayan vegetable soup with chicken and assorted local vegetables. Its broth is best kept at a gentle simmer to develop a clear, comforting flavor, with the vegetables added in stages so they retain their texture.
ingredients: Salt or fish sauce to taste
steps: Bring water to a boil. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly arranged so they cook at a consistent rate.
Add onion and chicken. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly arranged so they cook at a consistent rate.
Simmer until chicken is cooked. Keep the heat low to medium-low and maintain a gentle simmer rather than a vigorous boil; check that the chicken is becoming tender.
Add squash and cook until half tender. Cook evenly and check the thickest piece to make sure the chicken reaches an internal temperature of 74°C (165°F).
Add remaining vegetables. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly arranged so they cook at a consistent rate.
Season with fish sauce or salt. Taste a small amount first and adjust gradually to avoid making the dish too salty.
Cook until vegetables are tender. Cook evenly and check the thickest piece to make sure the chicken reaches an internal temperature of 74°C (165°F).
Serve immediately. Check that the chicken is fully cooked before serving; its thickest part should reach 74°C (165°F).

Turn off heat, add calamansi, and serve. Transfer to a serving plate and serve while hot so the texture and aroma are at their best.
tips: Oysters cook quickly; avoid prolonged boiling.

name: Talaba with Garlic Butter
description: A Filipino-inspired baked oyster appetizer topped with garlic butter and cheese. Garlic, onion, and other familiar Filipino seasonings build a savory base that complements the natural sweetness of the seafood. Serve warm with steamed rice.
ingredients: 500 g fresh oysters in half shells
steps: Scrub oyster shells and discard cracked or unsafe oysters. Drain well and check each piece carefully; discard any shellfish with cracked shells or an unpleasant odor. For shell-on mussels or clams, cook until the shells open and discard any that remain closed.

Arrange oysters level on a baking tray. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly distributed so they cook consistently. For shell-on mussels or clams, cook until the shells open and discard any that remain closed.
Mix butter, garlic, calamansi, and pepper. Mix until the ingredients are evenly distributed, scraping the sides of the bowl so the seasonings are incorporated.

Spoon garlic butter over oysters and sprinkle with cheese. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly distributed so they cook consistently. For shell-on mussels or clams, cook until the shells open and discard any that remain closed.
Bake at 200°C until cooked and topping bubbles. Cook in batches if needed and turn or reposition carefully so the food browns evenly without burning.
Garnish with spring onion. Transfer to a serving plate and serve while hot so the texture and aroma are at their best.
tips: Buy oysters from a safe source, keep chilled, and cook thoroughly.

name: Tinolang Halaan
description: A Filipino clam soup cooked with ginger, garlic, onion, and leafy greens. The broth develops a savory flavor from the seafood and aromatics, while the vegetables add freshness and texture. Serve it hot with steamed rice.
ingredients: 1 kg halaan clams, scrubbed and purged
steps: Purge clams in clean salted water, then rinse and drain. Drain well and check each piece carefully; discard any shellfish with cracked shells or an unpleasant odor. For shell-on mussels or clams, cook until the shells open and discard any that remain closed.
Sauté garlic, onion, and ginger in oil. Stir over medium heat until the aromatics soften and smell fragrant, taking care not to brown or burn the garlic.
Add water and bring to a boil. Adjust the heat to maintain a steady, gentle simmer and watch the liquid so it does not reduce too quickly.

Add clams, cover, and cook until shells open. Spread the seafood evenly in the pan so it cooks at a consistent rate; avoid overcrowding. For shell-on mussels or clams, cook until the shells open and discard any that remain closed.

Discard clams that remain closed; add greens and season. Taste a small amount first, then adjust the seasoning gradually to keep the flavors balanced. For shell-on mussels or clams, cook until the shells open and discard any that remain closed.
tips: Purge clams carefully to remove sand and discard any that do not open.

name: Halaan sa Gata
description: A Filipino-inspired clam dish simmered in coconut milk with ginger, garlic, and chilies. The broth develops a savory flavor from the seafood and aromatics, while the vegetables add freshness and texture. Serve it hot with steamed rice.
steps: Sauté garlic, onion, and ginger in oil. Stir over medium heat until the aromatics soften and smell fragrant, taking care not to brown or burn the garlic.
Add coconut milk and fish sauce; simmer gently. Adjust the heat to maintain a steady, gentle simmer and watch the liquid so it does not reduce too quickly.

Add clams and chilies, then cover. Spread the seafood evenly in the pan so it cooks at a consistent rate; avoid overcrowding. For shell-on mussels or clams, cook until the shells open and discard any that remain closed.
Cook until shells open; discard any that remain closed. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly distributed so they cook consistently.
Stir in malunggay and simmer briefly; serve. Adjust the heat to maintain a steady, gentle simmer and watch the liquid so it does not reduce too quickly.
tips: Keep coconut milk at a gentle simmer and discard unopened clams.

name: Clam and Corn Soup
description: A Filipino home-style soup combining fresh clams, sweet corn, ginger, and malunggay. The broth develops a savory flavor from the seafood and aromatics, while the vegetables add freshness and texture. Serve it hot with steamed rice.
steps: Sauté garlic, onion, and ginger in oil. Stir over medium heat until the aromatics soften and smell fragrant, taking care not to brown or burn the garlic.
Add water and corn; simmer until corn is tender. Adjust the heat to maintain a steady, gentle simmer and watch the liquid so it does not reduce too quickly.

Add clams and cover. Spread the seafood evenly in the pan so it cooks at a consistent rate; avoid overcrowding. For shell-on mussels or clams, cook until the shells open and discard any that remain closed.
Cook until shells open and discard any that remain closed. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly distributed so they cook consistently.
Add malunggay, season, and serve hot. Taste a small amount first, then adjust the seasoning gradually to keep the flavors balanced.
tips: Purge clams carefully to avoid grit in the soup.

name: Inihaw na Tahong
description: A Filipino grilled mussel appetizer seasoned with garlic, calamansi, and butter. The cooking method creates a browned, flavorful exterior while keeping the seafood tender inside. Serve freshly cooked for the best texture.
steps: Steam mussels until shells open and discard unopened ones. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly distributed so they cook consistently. For shell-on mussels or clams, cook until the shells open and discard any that remain closed.

Remove one shell half and arrange mussels on a grill-safe tray. Cook in batches if needed and turn or reposition carefully so the food browns evenly without burning. For shell-on mussels or clams, cook until the shells open and discard any that remain closed.
Mix butter, garlic, calamansi, and pepper. Mix until the ingredients are evenly distributed, scraping the sides of the bowl so the seasonings are incorporated.

Spoon mixture over mussels. Mix until the ingredients are evenly distributed, scraping the sides of the bowl so the seasonings are incorporated. For shell-on mussels or clams, cook until the shells open and discard any that remain closed.
Grill briefly until aromatic and lightly browned. Cook in batches if needed and turn or reposition carefully so the food browns evenly without burning.
Garnish and serve. Transfer to a serving plate and serve while hot so the texture and aroma are at their best.
tips: Steam mussels first and discard unopened shells before grilling.

name: Ginisang Tahong with Kamatis
description: A Filipino home-style sauté of mussels with tomatoes, garlic, onion, and ginger. Garlic, onion, and other familiar Filipino seasonings build a savory base that complements the natural sweetness of the seafood. Serve warm with steamed rice.
steps: Clean mussels and discard cracked or unsafe shells. Drain well and check each piece carefully; discard any shellfish with cracked shells or an unpleasant odor. For shell-on mussels or clams, cook until the shells open and discard any that remain closed.
Sauté garlic, onion, ginger, and tomatoes in oil. Stir over medium heat until the aromatics soften and smell fragrant, taking care not to brown or burn the garlic.
Add water and fish sauce; bring to a simmer. Adjust the heat to maintain a steady, gentle simmer and watch the liquid so it does not reduce too quickly.

Add mussels and cover until shells open. Spread the seafood evenly in the pan so it cooks at a consistent rate; avoid overcrowding. For shell-on mussels or clams, cook until the shells open and discard any that remain closed.

Discard mussels that remain closed; season with pepper and serve. Taste a small amount first, then adjust the seasoning gradually to keep the flavors balanced. For shell-on mussels or clams, cook until the shells open and discard any that remain closed.
tips: Cook mussels only until they open and discard unopened shells.

name: Ginataang Alimasag
description: A Filipino crab dish simmered in coconut milk with squash, sitaw, and aromatics. Slow simmering allows the seafood to absorb the fragrant coconut sauce, creating a creamy, comforting dish with a balance of savory and mildly sweet flavors.
steps: Sauté garlic and onion. Stir over medium heat until the aromatics soften and smell fragrant, taking care not to brown or burn the garlic.
Add coconut milk, squash, and fish sauce; simmer. Adjust the heat to maintain a steady, gentle simmer and watch the liquid so it does not reduce too quickly.

Add cleaned crabs and sitaw, cover, and cook until crabs are fully done. Drain well and check each piece carefully; discard any shellfish with cracked shells or an unpleasant odor. Cook until the crab meat is opaque and fully cooked near the thickest part of the body.
tips: Clean crabs thoroughly and cook until fully done. Keep the pot covered while simmering.

name: Rellenong Alimango
description: A Filipino stuffed crab preparation with crab meat, vegetables, egg, and breadcrumbs, baked in the shells. The mixture combines the natural sweetness of the seafood with vegetables and seasonings for a hearty Filipino-style dish.
steps: Cook crabs thoroughly and extract meat; reserve clean shells. Drain well and check each piece carefully; discard any shellfish with cracked shells or an unpleasant odor. Cook until the crab meat is opaque and fully cooked near the thickest part of the body.

Sauté onion and carrot; mix with crab meat, peas, egg, breadcrumbs, and seasonings. Stir over medium heat until the aromatics soften and smell fragrant, taking care not to brown or burn the garlic. Cook until the crab meat is opaque and fully cooked near the thickest part of the body.
Fill shells and bake until filling is hot and set. Cook in batches if needed and turn or reposition carefully so the food browns evenly without burning.
tips: Cook crabs thoroughly before extracting the meat. Use clean reserved shells and bake until the filling is hot and set.

name: Chili Crab Filipino-Style
description: A Filipino-inspired crab dish simmered in a sweet, savory, mildly spicy tomato-chili sauce. Garlic, onion, and other familiar Filipino seasonings build a savory base that complements the natural sweetness of the seafood. Serve warm with steamed rice.
steps: Sauté garlic, onion, and ginger in oil. Stir over medium heat until the aromatics soften and smell fragrant, taking care not to brown or burn the garlic.
Add tomato sauce, banana ketchup, soy sauce, chilies, and water. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly distributed so they cook consistently.
Bring sauce to a simmer. Adjust the heat to maintain a steady, gentle simmer and watch the liquid so it does not reduce too quickly.

Add crab, cover, and cook until crab is fully done. Spread the seafood evenly in the pan so it cooks at a consistent rate; avoid overcrowding. Cook until the crab meat is opaque and fully cooked near the thickest part of the body.
Pour in beaten egg while stirring gently. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly distributed so they cook consistently.
Serve immediately. Transfer to a serving plate and serve while hot so the texture and aroma are at their best.
tips: Use properly cleaned crab and cook until the meat is fully done.

name: Tortang Alimango
description: A Filipino-style crab omelet made with cooked crab meat, eggs, onion, and spring onion. The mixture combines the natural sweetness of the seafood with vegetables and seasonings for a hearty Filipino-style dish.
ingredients: 250 g cooked crab meat, checked for shell fragments
steps: Beat eggs and mix with crab meat, onion, garlic, spring onion, flour, and seasonings. Mix until the ingredients are evenly distributed, scraping the sides of the bowl so the seasonings are incorporated. Cook until the crab meat is opaque and fully cooked near the thickest part of the body.
Heat oil in a nonstick pan. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly distributed so they cook consistently.
Pour mixture into the pan and spread evenly. Mix until the ingredients are evenly distributed, scraping the sides of the bowl so the seasonings are incorporated.
Cook until the bottom is set and golden. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly distributed so they cook consistently.
Flip carefully and cook until fully set. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly distributed so they cook consistently.
Slice and serve. Transfer to a serving plate and serve while hot so the texture and aroma are at their best.
tips: Check crab meat for shell fragments and cook the egg mixture completely.

name: Crab Lumpia
description: A Filipino party appetizer filled with crab meat, vegetables, and seasonings, wrapped and fried. The seafood adds a savory taste to the noodles or filling, while vegetables provide color and texture. This makes a satisfying dish for family meals or gatherings.
steps: Combine crab meat, cabbage, carrot, onion, garlic, egg, breadcrumbs, and soy sauce. Mix until the ingredients are evenly distributed, scraping the sides of the bowl so the seasonings are incorporated. Cook until the crab meat is opaque and fully cooked near the thickest part of the body.
Place filling on each wrapper and roll tightly. Keep the portions even and seal the edges firmly to prevent the filling from leaking during cooking.
Seal edges with water. Keep the portions even and seal the edges firmly to prevent the filling from leaking during cooking.
Fry in batches until golden and filling is hot throughout. Cook in batches if needed and turn or reposition carefully so the food browns evenly without burning.
Drain and serve with sweet chili sauce. Transfer to a serving plate and serve while hot so the texture and aroma are at their best.
tips: Use well-drained crab meat and seal wrappers securely.

name: Ginataang Alimango with Aligue
description: A rich Filipino crab dish cooked in coconut cream with crab-fat paste, garlic, ginger, and chilies. Slow simmering allows the seafood to absorb the fragrant coconut sauce, creating a creamy, comforting dish with a balance of savory and mildly sweet flavors.
steps: Sauté garlic, onion, and ginger in oil. Stir over medium heat until the aromatics soften and smell fragrant, taking care not to brown or burn the garlic.
Stir in aligue until fragrant. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly distributed so they cook consistently.
Pour in coconut cream and simmer gently. Adjust the heat to maintain a steady, gentle simmer and watch the liquid so it does not reduce too quickly.

Add crab and chilies; cover and cook until crab is fully done. Spread the seafood evenly in the pan so it cooks at a consistent rate; avoid overcrowding. Cook until the crab meat is opaque and fully cooked near the thickest part of the body.
Season lightly and serve. Taste a small amount first, then adjust the seasoning gradually to keep the flavors balanced.
tips: Use aligue moderately because it is rich and salty; cook crab thoroughly.

name: Crispy Shrimp and Crab Cakes
description: A Filipino-inspired appetizer combining shrimp and crab meat with aromatics, egg, and breadcrumbs. The cooking method creates a browned, flavorful exterior while keeping the seafood tender inside. Serve freshly cooked for the best texture.
steps: Combine shrimp, crab, onion, garlic, egg, breadcrumbs, mayonnaise, calamansi, and seasonings. Mix until the ingredients are evenly distributed, scraping the sides of the bowl so the seasonings are incorporated. Shrimp are ready when they turn opaque and firm; remove them from the heat promptly to avoid a rubbery texture.
Shape into small flat patties. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly distributed so they cook consistently.
Chill for 15 minutes. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly distributed so they cook consistently.
Pan-fry in a thin layer of oil until golden on both sides and cooked through. Cook in batches if needed and turn or reposition carefully so the food browns evenly without burning.
Drain and serve with calamansi dip. Transfer to a serving plate and serve while hot so the texture and aroma are at their best.
tips: Chill patties before frying and cook the center thoroughly.

name: Ginataang Kuhol
description: A Filipino snail dish simmered in coconut milk with aromatics, malunggay, and green chilies. Slow simmering allows the seafood to absorb the fragrant coconut sauce, creating a creamy, comforting dish with a balance of savory and mildly sweet flavors.
steps: Sauté garlic, onion, and ginger. Stir over medium heat until the aromatics soften and smell fragrant, taking care not to brown or burn the garlic.
Add coconut milk and fish sauce. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly distributed so they cook consistently.
Add properly cleaned kuhol and simmer until thoroughly cooked. Drain well and check each piece carefully; discard any shellfish with cracked shells or an unpleasant odor.
Add malunggay and chilies. Add the vegetables in the order of their cooking time so firmer pieces soften while leafy vegetables stay bright.
tips: Use only correctly identified edible kuhol from a safe source. Clean and cook it thoroughly before serving.

name: Camaron Rebosado
description: A Filipino-Chinese-style appetizer of shrimp dipped in light batter and fried until golden. The cooking method creates a browned, flavorful exterior while keeping the seafood tender inside. Serve freshly cooked for the best texture.
ingredients: 500 g large shrimp, peeled and deveined with tails on
steps: Pat shrimp dry and season with salt and pepper. Drain well and check each piece carefully; discard any shellfish with cracked shells or an unpleasant odor. Shrimp are ready when they turn opaque and firm; remove them from the heat promptly to avoid a rubbery texture.
Whisk flour, cornstarch, egg, and cold water into a smooth batter. Mix until the ingredients are evenly distributed, scraping the sides of the bowl so the seasonings are incorporated.
Heat oil over medium heat. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly distributed so they cook consistently.

Dip shrimp in batter and fry in batches until golden and fully cooked. Cook in batches if needed and turn or reposition carefully so the food browns evenly without burning. Shrimp are ready when they turn opaque and firm; remove them from the heat promptly to avoid a rubbery texture.
Drain and serve with sweet chili sauce. Transfer to a serving plate and serve while hot so the texture and aroma are at their best.
tips: Keep the batter cold and avoid overcrowding the pan.

name: Mussels Sisig
description: A Filipino-style sisig variation made with chopped mussel meat, onion, chilies, and calamansi. The combination of aromatics, chilies, and calamansi gives the dish a savory, tangy flavor with a little heat. Serve immediately while hot.
ingredients: 400 g cooked mussel meat, drained and chopped
steps: Sauté garlic in oil. Stir over medium heat until the aromatics soften and smell fragrant, taking care not to brown or burn the garlic.

Add mussel meat and cook briefly. Spread the seafood evenly in the pan so it cooks at a consistent rate; avoid overcrowding. For shell-on mussels or clams, cook until the shells open and discard any that remain closed.
Stir in soy sauce and pepper. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly distributed so they cook consistently.
Add onion and chilies; toss while keeping some crunch. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly distributed so they cook consistently.
Turn off heat and mix in mayonnaise and calamansi. Mix until the ingredients are evenly distributed, scraping the sides of the bowl so the seasonings are incorporated.
Serve hot. Transfer to a serving plate and serve while hot so the texture and aroma are at their best.
tips: Drain mussels thoroughly and add calamansi at the end.

name: Seafood Pancit Bihon (No Fish)
description: A Filipino noodle dish with shrimp, squid, mussels, and vegetables, without finfish ingredients. The seafood adds a savory taste to the noodles or filling, while vegetables provide color and texture. This makes a satisfying dish for family meals or gatherings.
steps: Soak bihon according to package instructions and drain. Transfer to a serving plate and serve while hot so the texture and aroma are at their best.

Steam mussels until shells open; discard unopened ones and remove meat. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly distributed so they cook consistently. For shell-on mussels or clams, cook until the shells open and discard any that remain closed.
Sauté garlic and onion in oil. Stir over medium heat until the aromatics soften and smell fragrant, taking care not to brown or burn the garlic.

Add shrimp and squid and cook briefly. Spread the seafood evenly in the pan so it cooks at a consistent rate; avoid overcrowding. Shrimp are ready when they turn opaque and firm; remove them from the heat promptly to avoid a rubbery texture.
Pour in stock and soy sauce, then add bihon and toss. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly distributed so they cook consistently.

Add carrot, cabbage, and mussel meat; cook until noodles and seafood are done. Add the vegetables in the order of their cooking time so firmer pieces soften while leafy vegetables stay bright. For shell-on mussels or clams, cook until the shells open and discard any that remain closed.
Serve with calamansi. Transfer to a serving plate and serve while hot so the texture and aroma are at their best.
tips: Use shrimp or vegetable stock, not fish stock; this recipe contains no finfish.

name: Seafood Kare-Kare (Shellfish and Shrimp)
description: A Filipino-inspired kare-kare made with shrimp, mussels, and squid in peanut sauce, with no finfish. Its thick peanut sauce gives the dish a rich, nutty flavor that pairs well with vegetables and a small serving of bagoong on the side.
steps: Steam mussels until shells open; discard unopened ones and set meat aside. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly distributed so they cook consistently. For shell-on mussels or clams, cook until the shells open and discard any that remain closed.
Sauté garlic and onion in annatto oil. Stir over medium heat until the aromatics soften and smell fragrant, taking care not to brown or burn the garlic.
Add stock and peanut butter; stir until smooth. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly distributed so they cook consistently.
Add string beans and eggplant and simmer until nearly tender. Adjust the heat to maintain a steady, gentle simmer and watch the liquid so it does not reduce too quickly.

Add squid briefly, then shrimp and mussel meat. Spread the seafood evenly in the pan so it cooks at a consistent rate; avoid overcrowding. Shrimp are ready when they turn opaque and firm; remove them from the heat promptly to avoid a rubbery texture.
Cook until all seafood is fully done. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly distributed so they cook consistently.
Add pechay, thicken with slurry, and serve with bagoong. Transfer to a serving plate and serve while hot so the texture and aroma are at their best.
tips: Use shellfish or vegetable stock and cook each seafood according to its cooking time.

name: Mutya ng Cavite (No-Finfish Version)
description: A Filipino-inspired Cavite-style seafood soup with shrimp, crab, mussels, and squid in a creamy broth, without finfish. Garlic, onion, and other familiar Filipino seasonings build a savory base that complements the natural sweetness of the seafood. Serve warm with steamed rice.
steps: Steam mussels until shells open; discard unopened ones and reserve liquid. Transfer to a serving plate and serve while hot so the texture and aroma are at their best. For shell-on mussels or clams, cook until the shells open and discard any that remain closed.

Cook crab in water until fully done and reserve broth. Transfer to a serving plate and serve while hot so the texture and aroma are at their best. Cook until the crab meat is opaque and fully cooked near the thickest part of the body.
Melt butter and stir in flour to make a light roux. Stir over medium heat until the aromatics soften and smell fragrant, taking care not to brown or burn the garlic.
Gradually add shellfish broth and evaporated milk, stirring until smooth. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly distributed so they cook consistently.
Add onion, carrot, and celery; simmer until nearly tender. Adjust the heat to maintain a steady, gentle simmer and watch the liquid so it does not reduce too quickly.

Add crab, mussels, squid, and shrimp in order of cooking time. Spread the seafood evenly in the pan so it cooks at a consistent rate; avoid overcrowding. Shrimp are ready when they turn opaque and firm; remove them from the heat promptly to avoid a rubbery texture.
Season and serve warm. Taste a small amount first, then adjust the seasoning gradually to keep the flavors balanced.
tips: Use shellfish stock rather than fish stock to keep the dish free of finfish.

name: Seafood Sotanghon Soup (No Fish)
description: A Filipino noodle soup with sotanghon, shrimp, squid, and mussels in a light garlic broth. The broth develops a savory flavor from the seafood and aromatics, while the vegetables add freshness and texture. Serve it hot with steamed rice.
steps: Soak sotanghon until softened and drain. Transfer to a serving plate and serve while hot so the texture and aroma are at their best.

Steam mussels until shells open; discard unopened ones. Work gently and keep the pieces evenly distributed so they cook consistently. For shell-on mussels or clams, cook until the shells open and discard any that remain closed.
Sauté garlic and onion in oil. Stir over medium heat until the aromatics soften and smell fragrant, taking care not to brown or burn the garlic.
Add broth and fish sauce and bring to a boil. Adjust the heat to maintain a steady, gentle simmer and watch the liquid so it does not reduce too quickly.

Add carrot, shrimp, and squid; simmer until cooked. Adjust the heat to maintain a steady, gentle simmer and watch the liquid so it does not reduce too quickly. Shrimp are ready when they turn opaque and firm; remove them from the heat promptly to avoid a rubbery texture.

Add sotanghon and mussel meat; simmer until noodles are tender. Adjust the heat to maintain a steady, gentle simmer and watch the liquid so it does not reduce too quickly. For shell-on mussels or clams, cook until the shells open and discard any that remain closed.
Garnish with spring onion and serve. Transfer to a serving plate and serve while hot so the texture and aroma are at their best.
tips: Use shrimp or vegetable broth, not fish stock, and add seafood near the end.
