name: Fish Adobo
description: A Filipino-style fish dish simmered briefly in soy sauce, vinegar, garlic, peppercorns, and bay leaves. The fish gently absorbs the sharp, savory flavors of the cooking liquid while remaining tender and moist.
ingredients: 1 kg firm fish (tanigue, maya-maya, or tilapia), cut into serving pieces
steps: Pat the fish dry and season lightly with pepper. Remove any remaining scales, blood, or visible bones, then dry the surface well so the seasoning adheres.
Heat oil in a wide pan. Sauté garlic and onion until fragrant. The oil is ready when it shimmers lightly; avoid letting it smoke.
Add soy sauce, vinegar, water, bay leaves, and peppercorns. Bring to a gentle boil without stirring for 2 minutes. Watch the pot closely and adjust the heat once steady bubbles appear.
Lower the heat and add the fish pieces in a single layer. Work gently so the fish pieces remain intact and cook evenly.
Cover and simmer gently for 5–8 minutes, depending on thickness, until the fish is just cooked. Keep the liquid at a gentle simmer rather than a rolling boil, which can break the fish apart.
Turn the pieces carefully once if needed. Spoon sauce over the fish. Work gently so the fish pieces remain intact and cook evenly.
Taste the sauce and adjust with water or a little sugar if desired. Make small adjustments a little at a time so the sauce or broth remains balanced.
Serve hot with steamed rice. Transfer carefully to a warm serving dish and spoon a little of the sauce or broth over the fish.
tips: Use firm-fleshed fish so the pieces hold their shape.
Avoid vigorous stirring after adding the fish.
Do not overcook; fish cooks much faster than pork.

name: Fish Sinigang sa Sampalok
description: A sour Filipino fish soup with tamarind broth, tomatoes, radish, and leafy vegetables. Its broth balances a refreshing sourness with the natural sweetness of the fish and vegetables, making it best served piping hot with steamed rice.
ingredients: 1 kg fish (bangus, maya-maya, or tilapia), cut into serving pieces
1 packet sinigang sa sampalok mix or ½ cup fresh tamarind pulp
8–10 pieces string beans, cut into 2-inch pieces
steps: Bring water, onion, and tomatoes to a boil in a pot. Watch the pot closely and adjust the heat once steady bubbles appear.
Add radish and string beans. Simmer until partly tender. Work gently so the fish pieces remain intact and cook evenly.
Stir in the tamarind mix or strained tamarind pulp. Stir until the ingredients are evenly distributed and no dry seasoning remains.
Lower the heat and add the fish pieces carefully. Work gently so the fish pieces remain intact and cook evenly.
Simmer gently for 5–8 minutes or until the fish is cooked through. Keep the liquid at a gentle simmer rather than a rolling boil, which can break the fish apart.
Add eggplant and green chilies; cook until tender. Work gently so the fish pieces remain intact and cook evenly.
Add kangkong last and cook for 1 minute. Add the vegetables in stages according to how quickly they soften so they retain their color and texture.
Season with fish sauce and serve hot. Rub the seasoning evenly over all sides, including any cuts or crevices.
tips: Add fish only after the vegetables are partly cooked.
Keep the broth at a gentle simmer to prevent the fish from breaking.
Adjust sourness gradually.

name: Fish Paksiw sa Suka
description: A traditional Filipino dish in which fish is gently simmered in vinegar with ginger, garlic, and spices. The fish gently absorbs the sharp, savory flavors of the cooking liquid while remaining tender and moist.
ingredients: 1 kg bangus or another firm fish, cleaned and sliced
steps: Arrange ginger, garlic, onion, and peppercorns in a pot. Work gently so the fish pieces remain intact and cook evenly.
Place the fish pieces over the aromatics. Work gently so the fish pieces remain intact and cook evenly.
Pour in vinegar and water. Add salt and chilies. Pour slowly around the fish rather than directly onto one piece to keep the arrangement intact.
Bring to a boil uncovered for 3–4 minutes without stirring. Watch the pot closely and adjust the heat once steady bubbles appear.
Lower the heat, cover, and simmer for 8–10 minutes until the fish is cooked. Keep the liquid at a gentle simmer rather than a rolling boil, which can break the fish apart.
Add ampalaya or eggplant during the last few minutes, if using. Work gently so the fish pieces remain intact and cook evenly.
Taste and adjust the seasoning. Make small adjustments a little at a time so the sauce or broth remains balanced.
Serve with steamed rice. Transfer carefully to a warm serving dish and spoon a little of the sauce or broth over the fish.
tips: Do not stir immediately after adding vinegar; allow it to boil first.
Use a pot wide enough to arrange the fish in one layer.
Choose fresh fish for a clean-tasting paksiw.

name: Inihaw na Bangus
description: Milkfish marinated with calamansi, garlic, and pepper, stuffed with tomato and onion, then grilled. Grilling adds a lightly smoky aroma and a browned exterior while keeping the inside moist and flaky.
steps: Rinse the butterflied bangus and pat it dry. Work gently so the fish pieces remain intact and cook evenly.
Combine calamansi juice, garlic, soy sauce, pepper, and a little salt. Stir until the ingredients are evenly distributed and no dry seasoning remains.
Rub the mixture over the fish and inside the cavity. Marinate for 20–30 minutes. Keep the fish covered in the refrigerator while it marinates.
Mix tomato and onion, then place the mixture inside the fish. Stir until the ingredients are evenly distributed and no dry seasoning remains.
Brush the grill grate with oil and preheat to medium heat. Avoid moving the fish too soon; allow the surface to brown and release naturally before turning.
Grill the fish for about 8–12 minutes per side, depending on thickness. Avoid moving the fish too soon; allow the surface to brown and release naturally before turning.
Turn carefully and cook until the flesh is opaque and flakes easily. Work gently so the fish pieces remain intact and cook evenly.
Serve with calamansi-soy dipping sauce. Transfer carefully to a warm serving dish and spoon a little of the sauce or broth over the fish.
tips: Use a fish grilling basket to make turning easier.
Avoid very high heat, which can burn the skin before the center cooks.
Make sure the thickest part is fully cooked.

name: Daing na Bangus
description: Butterflied milkfish marinated in vinegar, garlic, and pepper, then pan-fried until crisp. The fish is cooked gently with familiar Filipino aromatics and seasonings to create a balanced, rice-friendly main dish.
steps: Combine vinegar, garlic, peppercorns, and salt in a bowl. Stir until the ingredients are evenly distributed and no dry seasoning remains.
Place the bangus in the marinade, coating both sides. Work gently so the fish pieces remain intact and cook evenly.
Cover and refrigerate for 4–8 hours. Work gently so the fish pieces remain intact and cook evenly.
Remove the fish and drain well; pat the surface dry. Work gently so the fish pieces remain intact and cook evenly.
Heat enough oil in a pan over medium heat. Work gently so the fish pieces remain intact and cook evenly.
Fry the bangus skin-side down until crisp and golden. Avoid moving the fish too soon; allow the surface to brown and release naturally before turning.
Turn carefully and fry the other side until cooked through. Avoid moving the fish too soon; allow the surface to brown and release naturally before turning.
Drain on a rack or paper towels and serve. Transfer carefully to a warm serving dish and spoon a little of the sauce or broth over the fish.
tips: Marinate in the refrigerator, not at room temperature.
Dry the fish before frying to reduce oil splatter.
Fry over medium heat so the fish cooks evenly.

name: Pritong Tilapia
description: A simple Filipino fried fish seasoned with salt and pepper and cooked until the skin is crisp. It is cooked until the outside is golden and crisp while the fish inside remains tender and fully cooked.
steps: Rinse the tilapia and pat completely dry. Work gently so the fish pieces remain intact and cook evenly.
Make two or three shallow diagonal cuts on each side. Work gently so the fish pieces remain intact and cook evenly.
Rub with salt, pepper, and calamansi juice, if using. Work gently so the fish pieces remain intact and cook evenly.
Heat oil in a frying pan over medium heat. The oil is ready when it shimmers lightly; avoid letting it smoke.
Carefully place the fish in the hot oil. Work gently so the fish pieces remain intact and cook evenly.
Fry for 6–8 minutes per side, depending on size, until golden and cooked through. Avoid moving the fish too soon; allow the surface to brown and release naturally before turning.
Drain excess oil and serve with tomatoes and a vinegar dip. Transfer carefully to a warm serving dish and spoon a little of the sauce or broth over the fish.
tips: Dry fish thoroughly before frying.
Do not overcrowd the pan; fry in batches if needed.
Use medium heat to crisp the skin without burning it.

name: Escabecheng Isda
description: A Filipino sweet-and-sour fish dish topped with sautéed vegetables and a bright vinegar-based sauce. The sauce combines savory seasoning with a bright, tangy finish that pairs well with steamed rice.
ingredients: 1 large whole lapu-lapu or maya-maya, cleaned
1 tbsp cornstarch mixed with 2 tbsp water
steps: Season the fish with salt and pepper, then lightly coat with flour. Rub the seasoning evenly over all sides, including any cuts or crevices.
Heat oil and fry the fish until golden and cooked through. Set aside. The oil is ready when it shimmers lightly; avoid letting it smoke.
In another pan, sauté garlic and onion until fragrant. Stir occasionally and cook until the aromatics soften and release their fragrance, without allowing the garlic to burn.
Add carrot and bell peppers; cook briefly so they remain slightly crisp. Add the vegetables in stages according to how quickly they soften so they retain their color and texture.
Pour in vinegar, water, soy sauce, and sugar. Bring to a boil. Watch the pot closely and adjust the heat once steady bubbles appear.
Stir in the cornstarch slurry and cook until the sauce thickens. Work gently so the fish pieces remain intact and cook evenly.
Taste and adjust the sweet-and-sour balance. Make small adjustments a little at a time so the sauce or broth remains balanced.
Place the fried fish on a serving platter and pour the sauce and vegetables over it. Pour slowly around the fish rather than directly onto one piece to keep the arrangement intact.
tips: Use a wide pan when frying a whole fish.
Add the sauce just before serving to preserve some crispness.

name: Bistek na Isda
description: Fish steaks cooked in a Filipino bistek-inspired sauce of soy sauce, calamansi, and onions. The sauce combines savory seasoning with a bright, tangy finish that pairs well with steamed rice.

Add onion rings and cook until softened; remove some for topping. Work gently so the fish pieces remain intact and cook evenly.
Add the fish steaks and sear briefly on both sides. Work gently so the fish pieces remain intact and cook evenly.
Pour in the marinade and water. Simmer gently until the fish is cooked through. Keep the liquid at a gentle simmer rather than a rolling boil, which can break the fish apart.
Taste the sauce and add a little sugar if desired. Make small adjustments a little at a time so the sauce or broth remains balanced.

tips: Use thick fish steaks that will not break easily.

Cover and bring to a gentle simmer. Watch the pot closely and adjust the heat once steady bubbles appear.
Cook over low heat until tomatoes break down and fish is cooked through. Work gently so the fish pieces remain intact and cook evenly.
Add calamansi juice instead of kamias if using, then taste. Make small adjustments a little at a time so the sauce or broth remains balanced.
Add chilies and simmer for 1 minute. Work gently so the fish pieces remain intact and cook evenly.
Serve hot. Transfer carefully to a warm serving dish and spoon a little of the sauce or broth over the fish.
tips: Use ripe tomatoes for a naturally thick sauce.
Add calamansi near the end to preserve its fresh sourness.
Keep the heat low to prevent the fish from breaking.
General Fish Preparation and Food-Safety Notes
Buy fish from a reputable seller. Fresh fish should have a mild smell, firm flesh, and clear, bright eyes when sold whole.
Keep raw fish refrigerated and separate from ready-to-eat foods. Wash hands, utensils, and surfaces after handling raw fish.
Cook fish thoroughly. The flesh should turn opaque and separate easily with a fork; a food thermometer can help verify safe doneness.

For recipes served raw or cured with calamansi and vinegar, use fish specifically sourced and handled for raw consumption. Acid does not reliably eliminate parasites or pathogens. When uncertain, cook the fish fully.
Check carefully for pin bones, especially when preparing fish for children.

name: Ensaladang Talong (Filipino Eggplant Salad)
description: Ensaladang talong is a traditional Filipino vegetable salad made with grilled or boiled eggplants mixed with tomatoes, onions, and vinegar. It has a smoky, slightly sour, and refreshing flavor that pairs well with fried fish, grilled pork, and other savory dishes.
steps: Wash the eggplants thoroughly and pat them dry.
Grill the eggplants over medium heat for 10–12 minutes, turning occasionally until the skin is charred and the flesh becomes soft.
Allow them to cool, then peel off the charred skin while keeping the stems intact.
Flatten the eggplants gently using a fork and arrange them on a serving plate.
Combine the tomatoes, onions, vinegar, fish sauce, pepper, and sugar in a bowl.
Pour the mixture over the eggplants and allow the flavors to blend for 5 minutes before serving.
tips: Choose firm, glossy eggplants without bruises.
Grilling gives the salad a distinctive smoky flavor. Boiling or steaming is a practical alternative.
Serve with grilled bangus, fried tilapia, or pork barbecue.
Refrigerate leftovers in a covered container and consume within 2–3 days.

name: Ginisang Kangkong (Sautéed Water Spinach)
description: Ginisang kangkong is a simple Filipino vegetable dish made by sautéing water spinach with garlic, onions, tomatoes, and seasonings. Its tender leaves and slightly crunchy stems make it an excellent everyday accompaniment to fried fish, grilled meat, and rice meals.
steps: Wash the kangkong thoroughly under running water. Remove damaged leaves and cut the stems into 5 cm pieces.
Heat cooking oil in a pan over medium heat.
Sauté garlic until fragrant, followed by onions and tomatoes.
Cook for 2–3 minutes until the tomatoes soften.
Add the kangkong stems and stir-fry for 2 minutes.
Add the leaves, fish sauce, pepper, and water.
Toss gently for another 2–3 minutes until the leaves wilt and the stems are tender but still slightly crisp.
Transfer to a serving dish.
tips: Avoid overcooking to preserve the vegetable's color and texture.
Select fresh kangkong with bright green leaves and firm stems.
Add sliced tofu for additional protein if desired.
Serve with fried fish, chicken adobo, or grilled pork.
Wash leafy vegetables carefully because soil may collect around their stems.

name: Chopsuey (Filipino Mixed Vegetable Stir-Fry)
description: Chopsuey is a popular Filipino vegetable dish featuring a colorful combination of cabbage, carrots, cauliflower, broccoli, bell peppers, and other vegetables cooked in a savory sauce. It offers different textures and flavors, making it a nutritious accompaniment to fried or roasted meat.
ingredients: 100 g green beans, cut into 5 cm pieces
steps: Wash and prepare all vegetables. Mix the cornstarch with 2 tablespoons of water to make a slurry.
Heat oil in a wok over medium-high heat.
Sauté garlic and onions until fragrant.
Add carrots, sayote, cauliflower, and young corn. Stir-fry for 3 minutes.
Pour in the chicken stock and oyster sauce. Cover and cook for 3 minutes.
Add broccoli, green beans, and bell peppers. Cook for another 2–3 minutes.
Add cabbage and black pepper.
Pour in the cornstarch mixture while stirring continuously until the sauce thickens.
Remove from heat and serve immediately.
tips: Add vegetables according to their cooking time to prevent overcooking.
Choose firm, brightly colored vegetables without soft spots.
Substitute water for chicken stock for a vegetable-based preparation.
Pair with fried chicken, pork chops, or steamed fish.
Refrigerate leftovers promptly and consume within 3–4 days.

name: Pinakbet Ilocano
description: Pinakbet Ilocano is a traditional vegetable dish from the Ilocos region made with native vegetables such as bitter melon, eggplant, okra, squash, and string beans. It is flavored with fermented fish sauce or bagoong isda, producing a savory and distinctly regional taste.
ingredients: 150 g string beans, cut into 5 cm pieces
steps: Wash all vegetables thoroughly and cut them into uniform pieces.
Place the tomatoes, onions, garlic, and water in a cooking pot.
Bring to a boil over medium heat.
Add the squash and cook for 5 minutes.
Add the bitter melon, eggplant, string beans, and okra.
Add bagoong isda and gently mix to distribute the seasoning.
Cover and simmer for 8–10 minutes until the vegetables are tender but retain their shape.
Avoid excessive stirring, then transfer to a serving dish.
tips: Traditional Ilocano pinakbet uses bagoong isda rather than sweet-style bagoong alamang.
Use fresh, young vegetables for better texture.
Avoid adding too much water because the vegetables naturally release moisture.
Serve with grilled fish, fried pork, or steamed rice.
Adjust the bagoong carefully because its saltiness varies by brand.

name: Laing (Taro Leaves In Coconut Milk)
description: Laing is a well-known Bicolano vegetable dish prepared using dried taro leaves simmered in coconut milk with ginger, garlic, onions, and chilies. It has a rich, creamy, and mildly spicy flavor that complements grilled seafood and fried meat.
steps: Inspect the dried taro leaves and remove any foreign materials. Use properly prepared, food-grade dried taro leaves.
In a pot, combine coconut milk, water, ginger, garlic, onions, and shrimp paste.
Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat.
Add the dried taro leaves, pressing them gently into the liquid. Do not stir vigorously.
Cover and simmer over low heat for 30–40 minutes until the leaves are thoroughly cooked and tender.
Pour in the coconut cream and add the chilies.
Continue simmering uncovered for 10–15 minutes until the sauce becomes thick and creamy.
Stir gently and serve hot.
tips: Never eat raw or inadequately cooked taro leaves because they contain irritating calcium oxalate crystals.
Follow the preparation and cooking instructions for the dried leaves and cook them thoroughly.
Avoid using fresh, improperly prepared taro leaves as a quick substitute.
Serve with grilled fish, fried chicken, or roasted pork.
Refrigerate leftovers promptly and reheat thoroughly.

name: Ginataang Kalabasa At Sitaw
description: Ginataang kalabasa at sitaw is a Filipino vegetable dish combining sweet squash and crunchy string beans in a creamy coconut milk sauce. Its naturally sweet and savory flavor makes it a comforting accompaniment to fried fish, grilled meat, and rice.
ingredients: 200 g string beans, cut into 5 cm pieces
steps: Wash, peel, and cut the squash into uniform cubes. Wash and trim the string beans.
Heat cooking oil in a pot over medium heat.
Sauté garlic, onions, and ginger until fragrant.
Add the squash and coconut milk.
Simmer for 8–10 minutes until the squash is almost tender.
Add the string beans, fish sauce, and black pepper.
Pour in the coconut cream and simmer for another 5–7 minutes.
Stir gently until the sauce thickens and the vegetables are fully cooked.
tips: Choose mature but firm squash with deep orange flesh.
Cut the squash evenly to ensure uniform cooking.
Do not boil coconut milk too vigorously because it may separate.
Pair with grilled tilapia, fried bangus, or chicken barbecue.
Use freshly opened coconut milk for the best flavor.

name: Atsarang Papaya (Pickled Green Papaya)
description: Atsarang papaya is a traditional Filipino pickled vegetable side dish made from shredded unripe papaya, carrots, ginger, onions, and bell peppers preserved in a sweet-and-sour vinegar mixture. Its crisp texture and refreshing flavor balance rich and fatty dishes.
steps: Peel the green papaya, remove the seeds, and grate the flesh.
Mix the grated papaya with 1 tablespoon salt and let it stand for 30 minutes.
Squeeze out the excess liquid and rinse briefly with clean water. Drain thoroughly.
Combine vinegar, sugar, peppercorns, and 2 teaspoons salt in a saucepan.
Bring to a boil and stir until the sugar dissolves. Remove from heat.
Add the carrots, bell peppers, onions, ginger, and raisins to the papaya.
Pour the cooled pickling solution over the vegetables.
Transfer into clean, heat-safe jars and allow to cool.
Refrigerate and let the flavors develop for at least 24 hours before serving.
tips: Use firm, completely unripe papaya for a crisp texture.
Drain the papaya thoroughly to prevent a watery pickling solution.
Use clean utensils when serving to avoid contamination.
Keep refrigerated and consume within approximately 2 weeks for best quality.
Serve with lechon, fried fish, grilled pork, or chicken barbecue.

name: Ensaladang Mangga (Green Mango Salad)
description: Ensaladang mangga is a refreshing Filipino salad made with unripe green mangoes, tomatoes, and onions. Its combination of sour, sweet, and savory flavors makes it a popular accompaniment to fried seafood and grilled dishes.
steps: Wash the mangoes thoroughly and peel off the skin.
Slice the mangoes into thin strips or small cubes.
Wash and dice the tomatoes and slice the onions.
In a small bowl, combine bagoong alamang, calamansi juice, sugar, and black pepper.
Add the mangoes, tomatoes, and onions to a mixing bowl.
Pour the dressing over the ingredients and toss gently.
Chill for 10 minutes before serving.
tips: Choose firm green mangoes with a distinctly sour flavor.
Adjust the sugar depending on the natural acidity of the mangoes.
Use cooked or commercially prepared bagoong from a reliable source.
Serve with grilled fish, fried shrimp, or pork barbecue.
Prepare shortly before serving to maintain the mangoes' crisp texture.

name: Tortang Talong (Filipino Eggplant Omelette)
description: Tortang talong is a popular Filipino vegetable side dish made with grilled eggplants dipped in beaten eggs and pan-fried until golden brown. It has a soft interior and lightly crisp exterior, making it a satisfying accompaniment to rice and meat dishes.
steps: Wash the eggplants and grill them over medium heat for 10–12 minutes until soft.
Allow them to cool, then peel off the charred skin.
Flatten each eggplant gently using a fork while keeping the stem attached.
Beat the eggs in a bowl and season with salt and black pepper.
Dip one eggplant into the beaten eggs, coating both sides.
Heat cooking oil in a frying pan over medium heat.
Fry each eggplant for approximately 2–3 minutes per side until golden brown and the egg is fully cooked.
Drain excess oil on a rack or paper towels and serve warm.
tips: Choose long, firm eggplants for easier preparation.
Do not fry over excessively high heat because the egg coating may brown before the interior cooks.
Serve with banana ketchup or a vinegar-garlic dipping sauce.
Pair with pork adobo, fried fish, or grilled chicken.
Ensure the egg coating is fully cooked before serving.

name: Adoboong Kangkong
description: Adobong kangkong is a vegetable variation of the classic Filipino adobo. Water spinach is cooked with soy sauce, vinegar, garlic, and peppercorns, creating a savory, tangy, and slightly garlicky dish that pairs well with rice and grilled or fried foods.
steps: Wash the kangkong thoroughly and separate the stems from the leaves.
Heat oil in a pan over medium heat.
Sauté garlic until lightly golden.
Add soy sauce, vinegar, water, peppercorns, and brown sugar.
Bring to a boil without stirring for approximately 2 minutes.
Add the kangkong stems and simmer for 2 minutes.
Add the leaves and cook for another 1–2 minutes until wilted.
Toss gently, adjust seasoning, and serve immediately.
tips: Add the leaves last to prevent them from becoming overly soft.
Avoid overcooking the kangkong.
Reduce the soy sauce if using a particularly salty brand.
Pair with grilled pork, fried chicken, or steamed fish.
Keep cooked leftovers refrigerated and reheat thoroughly.

name: Ginisang Sayote
description: Ginisang sayote is a simple Filipino sautéed vegetable dish prepared with chayote, garlic, onions, and tomatoes. Its mild sweetness and tender-crisp texture make it a practical everyday side dish for meat, fish, and poultry.
steps: Wash the sayote, peel it, remove the seed, and cut it into thin strips.
Heat cooking oil in a pan over medium heat.
Sauté garlic until fragrant.
Add onions and tomatoes. Cook until the tomatoes soften.
Add the sliced sayote and stir-fry for 3 minutes.
Pour in the water and fish sauce.
Cover and simmer for 5–7 minutes until tender but not mushy.
Season with black pepper and serve warm.
tips: Select firm sayote without wrinkles or soft spots.
Cut the pieces uniformly for even cooking.
Avoid adding too much water because sayote naturally releases moisture.
Serve with fried tilapia, chicken inasal, or pork barbecue.
Wear kitchen gloves when peeling if the sap irritates your skin.

name: Lumpiang Gulay (Filipino Vegetable Spring Rolls)
description: Lumpiang gulay is a Filipino fried vegetable roll filled with sautéed cabbage, carrots, bean sprouts, and other vegetables wrapped in thin lumpia wrappers. Its crispy exterior and savory filling make it a versatile side dish for rice meals.
ingredients: 2 tablespoons water mixed with 1 tablespoon flour (for sealing)
steps: Wash and drain all vegetables thoroughly.
Heat 2 tablespoons of oil in a pan over medium heat.
Sauté garlic and onions until fragrant.
Add carrots and green beans. Cook for 2 minutes.
Add cabbage, bean sprouts, soy sauce, and black pepper.
Stir-fry for 2–3 minutes until the vegetables are slightly tender.
Remove from heat and allow the filling to cool completely.
Place approximately 2 tablespoons of filling on each wrapper.
Fold the sides inward and roll tightly. Seal the edge with the flour mixture.
Heat frying oil to approximately 170–180°C.
Fry the rolls in batches for 3–4 minutes until golden brown and crispy.
Drain on a wire rack before serving.
tips: Drain the vegetable filling well to prevent soggy wrappers.
Allow the filling to cool before wrapping to prevent the wrappers from tearing.
Avoid overcrowding the pan because it lowers the oil temperature.
Serve with vinegar-garlic dip or sweet chili sauce.
Keep uncooked rolls refrigerated and fry promptly; do not leave perishable filling at room temperature for extended periods.

name: Inihaw Na Okra (Grilled Okra)
description: Inihaw na okra is a simple grilled vegetable side dish made by cooking fresh okra over direct heat until lightly charred and tender. Its mild earthy flavor and slightly crisp texture complement grilled fish, pork barbecue, and other Filipino dishes.
steps: Wash the okra thoroughly and dry with a clean towel.
Trim the tough ends without cutting into the pods.
Toss the okra with cooking oil, salt, and black pepper.
Preheat a grill to medium heat.
Place the okra directly on the grill.
Cook for approximately 3–4 minutes per side, turning occasionally until lightly charred and tender.
Combine the vinegar, soy sauce, garlic, and chili to make the dipping sauce.
Arrange the grilled okra on a platter and serve with the sauce.
tips: Choose small to medium-sized okra because they are usually more tender.
Dry the pods before grilling to encourage light browning.
Avoid overcooking because the pods may become excessively soft.
Serve alongside grilled bangus, pork liempo, or chicken inasal.
Use clean tongs and utensils when handling grilled food.

name: Ukoy Na Gulay (Filipino Vegetable Fritters)
description: Ukoy na gulay is a traditional Filipino crispy fritter made with shredded vegetables, usually bean sprouts and squash or sweet potato, mixed in a light flour batter and deep-fried. Its crunchy texture and savory flavor make it an excellent accompaniment to rice meals.
steps: Wash the vegetables thoroughly and drain well.
Combine flour, cornstarch, egg, water, salt, and pepper in a mixing bowl.
Mix until a smooth but slightly thick batter forms.
Fold in the bean sprouts, squash, and sweet potato.
Heat oil in a deep pan to approximately 170–180°C.
Spoon portions of the mixture into the hot oil and flatten gently.
Fry for 3–4 minutes per side until golden brown and crisp.
Drain on a wire rack.
Mix the dipping sauce ingredients and serve alongside the fritters.
tips: Use cold water to help create a crispier batter.
Drain vegetables properly to avoid thinning the batter.
Fry in small batches to maintain the oil temperature.
Serve with fried fish, grilled chicken, or steamed rice.
Allow the oil to cool completely before disposing of or storing it safely.

name: Ginisang Ampalaya (Sautéed Bitter Melon)
description: Ginisang ampalaya is a traditional Filipino vegetable preparation featuring sliced bitter melon sautéed with garlic, onions, and tomatoes. It has a distinctive bitter taste balanced by the sweetness of onions and tomatoes, making it a flavorful accompaniment to grilled and fried dishes.
steps: Wash the ampalaya, slice lengthwise, and remove the seeds and white pith.
Cut into thin half-moon slices.
Heat oil in a pan over medium heat.
Sauté garlic and onions until fragrant.
Add tomatoes and cook until softened.
Add ampalaya and stir-fry for 2 minutes.
Pour in the water and fish sauce.
Cover and cook for 3–4 minutes until tender-crisp.
Season with black pepper and serve.
tips: Select firm, bright green ampalaya.
Removing the white pith helps reduce bitterness.
Avoid excessive cooking to retain a pleasant texture.
Serve with grilled pork, fried bangus, or chicken adobo.
Do not rely on excessive salt to remove bitterness, as this may make the dish too salty.

name: Ensaladang Pako (Fiddlehead Fern Salad)
description: Ensaladang pako is a traditional Filipino salad made from young fiddlehead ferns mixed with tomatoes, onions, and a tangy vinegar dressing. It is especially popular in several rural communities and offers a refreshing, slightly crunchy vegetable accompaniment.
steps: Select young, fresh pako from a reliable food supplier.
Remove tough stems and damaged portions.
Wash thoroughly under running water.
Blanch the pako in boiling water for 1–2 minutes.
Transfer immediately to a bowl of clean cold water, then drain thoroughly.
Combine tomatoes, onions, vinegar, calamansi juice, fish sauce, sugar, and pepper.
Add the pako and toss gently.
Chill briefly and serve fresh.
tips: Purchase correctly identified, edible fiddlehead ferns from reputable sellers.
Never eat unidentified wild ferns raw.
Blanching provides an additional food-safety measure while preserving texture.
Serve with grilled fish, pork barbecue, or fried chicken.
Prepare the salad close to serving time for the best freshness.

name: Ensaladang Lato (Sea Grape Salad)
description: Ensaladang lato is a refreshing coastal Filipino salad made with edible sea grapes, tomatoes, onions, and a light vinegar or calamansi dressing. Its naturally salty flavor and delicate, popping texture make it an excellent partner for grilled seafood and fried fish.
steps: Purchase fresh, food-grade edible sea grapes from a reliable seafood vendor.
Separate damaged or discolored branches.
Rinse briefly using clean drinking water. Avoid soaking for too long.
Dice the tomatoes and thinly slice the onions.
Combine calamansi juice, vinegar, fish sauce, and black pepper.
Arrange the lato, tomatoes, and onions in a serving bowl.
Add the dressing immediately before serving.
Toss gently and serve fresh.
tips: Avoid prolonged soaking because it can cause sea grapes to lose their characteristic texture.
Select sea grapes that look fresh and have intact, rounded beads.
Omit additional fish sauce if the lato is already very salty.
Pair with grilled tuna, inihaw na pusit, or fried fish.
Keep refrigerated and follow the supplier's storage instructions.

name: Kilawing Labanos (Filipino Pickled Radish)
description: Kilawing labanos is a Filipino vegetable side dish made from radish cooked or marinated in vinegar with garlic, onions, ginger, and seasonings. It has a sharp, refreshing, and slightly peppery flavor that balances rich pork and grilled seafood dishes.
ingredients: 500 g white radish, peeled and sliced
steps: Wash, peel, and slice the radish into thin rounds.
Heat cooking oil in a saucepan over medium heat.
Sauté garlic, onions, and ginger until fragrant.
Add the radish and stir-fry for 2 minutes.
Pour in the vinegar and water.
Bring to a boil without stirring for approximately 2 minutes.
Add fish sauce, sugar, and black pepper.
Simmer for 5–7 minutes until the radish is tender but still holds its shape.
Transfer to a serving bowl and allow to cool slightly.
tips: Choose firm radishes without soft or damaged areas.
Slice uniformly to ensure even cooking.
Adjust vinegar and sugar according to your preferred balance of flavors.
Pair with lechon kawali, fried fish, or grilled pork.
Store leftovers in a covered container in the refrigerator.

name: Ginisang Repolyo (Sautéed Cabbage)
description: Ginisang repolyo is an economical Filipino vegetable side dish made by sautéing cabbage with garlic, onions, and tomatoes. Its mild sweetness and tender-crisp texture make it a practical accompaniment to everyday rice meals.
steps: Remove damaged outer cabbage leaves and wash the remaining cabbage thoroughly.
Cut into bite-sized pieces.
Heat oil in a pan over medium heat.
Sauté garlic, onions, and tomatoes until softened.
Add the cabbage and stir-fry for 2 minutes.
Pour in water and fish sauce.
Cover and cook for 3–4 minutes until the cabbage is tender-crisp.
Season with black pepper and serve warm.
tips: Avoid overcooking because cabbage releases moisture and becomes soft quickly.
Choose compact heads with crisp leaves.
Add carrots for additional color and nutrients.
Serve with fried chicken, pork chops, or grilled fish.
This is a budget-friendly recipe that makes good use of inexpensive seasonal vegetables.

name: Adobog Sitaw (String Beans Adobo)
description: Adobong sitaw is a simple Filipino side dish made from string beans cooked in soy sauce, vinegar, garlic, and pepper. Its savory and tangy flavor complements rice meals, especially grilled pork, fried fish, and roasted chicken.
steps: Wash the string beans thoroughly and cut into 5 cm pieces.
Heat oil in a pan over medium heat.
Sauté garlic and onions until fragrant.
Add the string beans and stir-fry for 2 minutes.
Pour in soy sauce, vinegar, water, peppercorns, and sugar.
Bring to a boil without stirring for 2 minutes.
Lower the heat and simmer for 5–7 minutes until the beans are tender but slightly crisp.
Adjust the seasoning and serve.
tips: Select bright green, firm string beans that snap easily.
Avoid overcooking to retain their texture.
Reduce the soy sauce if you prefer a less salty preparation.
Serve with grilled chicken, fried bangus, or pork barbecue.
Refrigerate leftovers promptly.

name: Ginisang Togue (Sautéed Bean Sprouts)
description: Ginisang togue is a popular Filipino vegetable side dish made with fresh mung bean sprouts sautéed with garlic, onions, carrots, and seasonings. It is light, inexpensive, and quick to prepare, making it suitable for everyday family meals.
steps: Remove damaged sprouts and rinse thoroughly under running water.
Heat cooking oil in a wok over medium-high heat.
Sauté garlic and onions until fragrant.
Add carrots and cook for 2 minutes.
Add the bean sprouts, soy sauce, fish sauce, and black pepper.
Stir-fry for 2–3 minutes until the sprouts are thoroughly heated and tender-crisp.
Add water if needed and toss gently.
Serve immediately.
tips: Purchase fresh, refrigerated bean sprouts from reliable suppliers.
Because raw sprouts may carry harmful bacteria, cook them thoroughly rather than serving them raw.
Avoid overcrowding the pan to prevent excessive moisture.
Pair with fried fish, chicken adobo, or grilled pork.
Use the sprouts promptly after purchase.

name: Ginataang Puso Ng Saging (Banana Blossom In Coconut Milk)
description: Ginataang puso ng saging is a traditional Filipino vegetable dish featuring banana blossom simmered in coconut milk with ginger, garlic, and onions. It has a creamy, mildly sweet, and savory flavor that makes it a satisfying accompaniment to grilled and fried dishes.
ingredients: 1 tablespoon salt for treating the banana blossom
steps: Remove the tough outer bracts of the banana blossom and finely slice the tender inner portion.
Place the slices in a bowl of water with 1 tablespoon salt and let stand for 15 minutes.
Drain, rinse thoroughly, and squeeze out excess liquid.
Heat oil in a pot and sauté garlic, onions, and ginger.
Add the banana blossom and stir-fry for 3 minutes.
Pour in the coconut milk and fish sauce.
Simmer for 15 minutes until the banana blossom softens.
Add coconut cream and black pepper.
Simmer for another 5 minutes until creamy and fully cooked.
tips: Wear gloves when slicing banana blossom because its sap can stain.
Choose fresh, tightly closed banana blossoms.
Properly remove sap and bitterness through soaking and rinsing.
Serve with fried tilapia, grilled pork, or steamed rice.
Refrigerate leftovers promptly because coconut-based dishes spoil easily at room temperature.

name: Ginisang Upo (Sautéed Bottle Gourd)
description: Ginisang upo is a light Filipino vegetable dish prepared by sautéing bottle gourd with garlic, onions, and tomatoes. Its mild flavor and soft texture make it a suitable everyday side dish, particularly when served with savory meat and seafood preparations.
steps: Wash, peel, and cut the upo into thin slices. Remove mature seeds if necessary.
Heat oil in a pan over medium heat.
Sauté garlic, onions, and tomatoes until softened.
Add the sliced upo and stir-fry for 2 minutes.
Add fish sauce and water.
Cover and simmer for 7–9 minutes until tender.
Season with black pepper.
Transfer to a serving bowl and serve warm.
tips: Choose young upo with smooth, firm skin.
Do not add excessive water because the vegetable releases moisture during cooking.
Add sliced carrots for extra color.
Serve with fried fish, chicken barbecue, or pork adobo.
Avoid using bitter bottle gourd, as unusually bitter gourds should be discarded.

name: Ginisang Pechay
description: Ginisang pechay is a quick Filipino vegetable side dish made with Chinese cabbage or bok choy sautéed with garlic, onions, and tomatoes. Its tender leaves and crisp stalks create a light, savory accompaniment to heavier rice meals.
steps: Separate the pechay leaves and stalks. Wash thoroughly, especially around the base.
Heat oil in a pan over medium heat.
Sauté garlic and onions until fragrant.
Add tomatoes and cook until soft.
Add the stalks first and stir-fry for 2 minutes.
Add the leaves, fish sauce, and water.
Cook for another 2–3 minutes until the leaves wilt and the stalks soften.
Season with black pepper and serve immediately.
tips: Choose pechay with crisp stalks and bright green leaves.
Separate the stalks and leaves to achieve even cooking.
Avoid excessive heat and prolonged cooking.
Serve with fried chicken, pork chops, or steamed fish.
Wash leafy vegetables thoroughly to remove dirt and insects.

name: Dinengdeng (Ilocano Boiled Vegetables)
description: Dinengdeng is an Ilocano vegetable dish featuring assorted local vegetables simmered in a light broth flavored with fermented fish paste or bagoong isda. Its simple preparation highlights the natural flavors of vegetables and makes it a traditional accompaniment to grilled fish.
ingredients: 150 g string beans, cut into pieces
steps: Wash and prepare all vegetables.
Bring water to a boil in a cooking pot.
Add the bagoong isda, tomatoes, and onions.
Simmer for 3 minutes to release the flavors.
Add the squash and cook for 5 minutes.
Add the string beans, okra, eggplant, and bitter melon.
Simmer for another 7–8 minutes until the vegetables are tender.
Add malunggay leaves during the final 2 minutes.
Taste and adjust the seasoning before serving.
tips: Traditional dinengdeng uses locally available vegetables, so the combination can vary by season.
Add vegetables according to their firmness.
Avoid excessive stirring to prevent delicate vegetables from breaking.
Serve with grilled tilapia, fried bangus, or grilled pork.
Adjust bagoong carefully because it is naturally salty.

name: Bulanglang Kapampangan (Sour Vegetable Broth)
description: Bulanglang is a traditional Kapampangan vegetable preparation featuring assorted vegetables cooked in a light, refreshing broth flavored with tomatoes and fermented fish or shrimp paste. Some versions use guava to provide natural sourness. It is a light accompaniment to fried and grilled main dishes.
ingredients: 100 g string beans, cut into pieces
steps: Wash and prepare all vegetables.
Place water, tomatoes, onions, and guava in a cooking pot.
Bring to a boil and simmer for 5 minutes.
Add bagoong isda and stir gently.
Add squash and cook for 5 minutes.
Add string beans, eggplant, and okra.
Simmer for another 5–7 minutes until the vegetables are tender.
Add malunggay leaves and cook for 2 minutes.
Remove from heat and serve hot.
tips: Guava adds a natural sour flavor; omit it if a milder broth is preferred.
Do not overcook the vegetables.
Use fresh seasonal produce for better flavor and affordability.
Pair with fried tilapia, grilled fish, or roasted chicken.
Serve immediately and refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Gising-Gising (Spicy Ground Vegetable Dish)
description: Gising-gising is a popular Filipino vegetable dish traditionally made with chopped green beans cooked in coconut milk, shrimp paste, garlic, onions, and chilies. It has a creamy, savory, and spicy flavor that pairs well with grilled meat and plain steamed rice.
steps: Wash the green beans and cut into small pieces.
Heat oil in a pan over medium heat.
Sauté garlic and onions until fragrant.
Add shrimp paste and cook for 1 minute.
Add the chopped green beans and stir-fry for 3 minutes.
Pour in the coconut milk and simmer for 8–10 minutes.
Add the coconut cream and chilies.
Continue cooking for 3–5 minutes until creamy and the vegetables are fully tender.
Season with black pepper and serve.
tips: Finely chopped beans provide the characteristic texture of this dish.
Adjust the number of chilies according to spice preference.
Use fresh coconut milk for richer flavor.
Serve with grilled pork, fried fish, or chicken inasal.
Reduce the shrimp paste if you prefer a less salty dish.

name: Law-Uy (Cebuano Mixed Vegetable Soup)
description: Law-uy is a traditional Visayan vegetable dish prepared by simmering assorted local vegetables in a light broth. It commonly features squash, okra, eggplant, string beans, and leafy vegetables. Its mild flavor makes it a nutritious accompaniment to fried fish and grilled meat.
ingredients: 100 g string beans, cut into pieces
steps: Wash and prepare all vegetables.
Bring water to a boil in a cooking pot.
Add garlic, onions, and tomatoes.
Simmer for 3 minutes.
Add squash and cook for 5 minutes.
Add string beans, okra, and eggplant.
Season with fish sauce and black pepper.
Simmer for 6–8 minutes until the vegetables are tender.
Add malunggay leaves during the last 2 minutes.
Serve hot in a bowl.
tips: Law-uy varies among Visayan households depending on available vegetables.
Use fresh seasonal produce for better quality.
Add leafy vegetables near the end to retain their color.
Serve with grilled fish, fried pork, or steamed rice.
Use a clean pot and refrigerate leftover soup promptly.

name: Utan Bisaya (Visayan Vegetable Medley)
description: Utan Bisaya is a traditional Visayan vegetable dish made from a combination of squash, eggplant, okra, string beans, and leafy vegetables simmered in a light broth. It is valued for its simple preparation and natural vegetable flavors.
ingredients: 100 g string beans, cut into pieces
steps: Wash all vegetables under running water and cut into uniform pieces.
Bring water to a boil in a pot.
Add garlic, onion, and tomato.
Simmer for 3 minutes.
Add squash and cook for 5 minutes.
Add eggplant, okra, and string beans.
Season with fish sauce and black pepper.
Simmer for 6–8 minutes.
Add alugbati leaves and cook for another 2 minutes.
Serve hot.
tips: Use young and tender vegetables for better texture.
Alugbati may be replaced with malunggay or other edible leafy vegetables.
Avoid prolonged boiling because it can make the vegetables mushy.
Serve with grilled bangus, fried tilapia, or pork barbecue.
Use drinking-quality water for the broth.

name: Ensaladang Talbos Ng Kamote
description: Ensaladang talbos ng kamote is a traditional Filipino salad made with boiled sweet potato leaves mixed with tomatoes, onions, and a sour vinegar dressing. It has a mild earthy flavor and tender texture, making it a refreshing side dish for fried and grilled foods.
ingredients: 300 g young sweet potato leaves and tender stems
steps: Remove damaged leaves and tough stems from the sweet potato tops.
Wash thoroughly under running water.
Bring water to a boil in a pot.
Add the leaves and blanch for 2–3 minutes until tender.
Drain and cool using clean utensils. Squeeze out excess water gently.
Combine tomatoes, onions, vinegar, calamansi juice, fish sauce, and black pepper.
Add the cooked leaves and toss gently.
Transfer to a serving plate and serve.
tips: Choose fresh young leaves with bright green color.
Avoid overboiling to preserve texture.
Add roasted peanuts for a crunchy variation.
Serve with grilled fish, fried chicken, or pork barbecue.
Cook leafy vegetables thoroughly and avoid leaving the prepared salad at room temperature for extended periods.

name: Burong Mustasa (Fermented Mustard Greens)
description: Burong mustasa is a traditional Filipino preserved vegetable preparation made by fermenting mustard leaves with salt and rice. It has a distinctive sour, salty flavor and is commonly served as an accompaniment to fried fish, grilled meat, and other rich dishes.
steps: Remove damaged leaves and wash the mustard greens thoroughly.
Drain and pat dry using clean kitchen towels.
Mix the mustard leaves with salt and gently massage until slightly softened.
Combine the cooled cooked rice with the boiled and cooled water.
Place the mustard leaves and rice mixture in a clean, food-grade fermentation container.
Press the mixture down so the leaves remain submerged in the liquid.
Cover and ferment in a cool, controlled environment according to a tested fermentation process for approximately 3–5 days. Monitor acidity and discard the batch if there are signs of spoilage.
Once properly fermented, heat oil in a pan and sauté garlic, onions, and tomatoes.
Add the fermented mustard greens and cook for approximately 5 minutes.
Serve as a tangy vegetable accompaniment.
tips: Fermentation requires clean equipment, correct salt concentration, and controlled conditions. Use a tested food-safety fermentation recipe rather than relying on time alone.
Do not consume a batch with mold, unusual discoloration, or unpleasant rotten odors.
Use clean utensils when handling fermented vegetables.
Serve with fried bangus, grilled pork, or steamed rice.
Refrigerate the finished product and use clean utensils when serving.

name: Ensaladang Pipino (Cucumber Salad)
description: Ensaladang pipino is a refreshing Filipino cucumber salad prepared with sliced cucumbers, tomatoes, onions, and a light vinegar dressing. Its crisp texture and refreshing acidity make it an excellent accompaniment to grilled and fried main dishes.
steps: Wash the cucumbers thoroughly and peel partially if desired.
Slice the cucumbers into thin rounds.
Wash and dice the tomatoes and slice the onions.
Combine vinegar, calamansi juice, sugar, salt, and black pepper in a bowl.
Add the vegetables and toss gently.
Refrigerate for 10–15 minutes before serving.
Transfer to a chilled serving bowl.
tips: Select firm cucumbers without soft spots.
Remove excess seeds if the cucumbers are particularly watery.
Prepare close to serving time to maintain crispness.
Pair with grilled liempo, fried fish, or chicken inasal.
Refrigerate leftovers in a covered container and consume within 1–2 days.

name: Kamatis At Itlog Na Maalat Salad
description: Kamatis at itlog na maalat is a popular Filipino side salad combining ripe tomatoes, salted duck eggs, and onions. Its combination of juicy sweetness, saltiness, and mild sharpness creates a refreshing accompaniment to grilled fish and fried seafood.
steps: Wash the tomatoes and onions thoroughly.
Boil the salted duck eggs for approximately 10–12 minutes to ensure they are fully cooked.
Cool, peel, and slice the eggs.
Cut the tomatoes into wedges and slice the onions thinly.
Arrange the tomatoes, eggs, and onions on a serving plate.
Combine calamansi juice, vinegar, black pepper, and sugar.
Drizzle the dressing over the salad.
Serve immediately or keep chilled until serving.
tips: Choose ripe but firm tomatoes.
Adjust the dressing because salted eggs already contain considerable sodium.
Add cucumber for additional crunch.
Pair with grilled bangus, fried tilapia, or pork barbecue.
Keep the prepared salad refrigerated because it contains cooked eggs.

name: Inihaw Na Talong (Grilled Eggplant)
description: Inihaw na talong is a simple Filipino grilled vegetable side dish made from whole eggplants cooked over direct heat until tender and lightly smoky. It can be served plain with vinegar or accompanied by a tomato-onion dipping mixture.
steps: Wash the eggplants thoroughly and pat dry.
Brush lightly with cooking oil.
Preheat a grill over medium heat.
Place the eggplants directly on the grill.
Cook for 10–12 minutes, turning occasionally until the skin is charred and the flesh becomes soft.
Remove from the grill and allow to cool slightly.
Peel off the charred skin and arrange the eggplants on a plate.
Combine the dipping sauce ingredients and serve alongside.
tips: Select medium-sized eggplants with smooth skin.
Do not peel before grilling because the skin protects the flesh.
Avoid excessively high heat that burns the exterior before the interior softens.
Serve with grilled pork, fish, or chicken.
Grilled eggplant can also be used as a base for ensaladang talong.

name: Crispy Kangkong (Fried Water Spinach)
description: Crispy kangkong is a popular Filipino vegetable preparation made by coating kangkong leaves in seasoned batter and frying them until light and crunchy. It offers a crispy texture and mild vegetable flavor that complements grilled meat and rice meals.
ingredients: 200 g large kangkong leaves with tender stems
steps: Separate the leaves and tender stems from the kangkong.
Wash thoroughly and dry completely using clean towels.
Combine flour, cornstarch, garlic powder, salt, and black pepper.
Add egg and cold water, mixing until a smooth batter forms.
Dip each leaf into the batter, allowing excess mixture to drip off.
Heat cooking oil to approximately 170–175°C.
Fry the coated leaves in small batches for 1–2 minutes until crisp and lightly golden.
Remove using a slotted spoon and drain on a wire rack.
Serve immediately with vinegar or garlic mayonnaise.
tips: Ensure leaves are completely dry before dipping to reduce oil splattering.
Cold batter helps produce a lighter, crispier coating.
Avoid overcrowding the pan.
Serve with grilled chicken, pork barbecue, or fried fish.
Drain on a wire rack instead of stacking to preserve crispness.

name: Pritong Talong (Fried Eggplant)
description: Pritong talong is a straightforward Filipino side dish made by slicing eggplants and frying them until golden brown and tender. Its soft interior and lightly crisp exterior make it an economical and flavorful accompaniment to rice meals.
ingredients: ½ cup cooking oil for frying
steps: Wash the eggplants thoroughly and remove the stems.
Slice lengthwise into strips approximately 1 cm thick.
Season lightly with salt and pepper.
Heat oil in a frying pan over medium heat.
Fry the eggplant slices for 2–3 minutes per side until golden brown and tender.
Remove from the pan and drain on a wire rack.
Combine the vinegar, garlic, salt, and pepper to prepare the dipping sauce.
Arrange the eggplants on a serving plate and serve warm.
tips: Choose fresh eggplants with firm, glossy skin.
Slice evenly to ensure uniform cooking.
Do not use excessively high heat because eggplant absorbs oil quickly.
Serve with fried fish, pork adobo, or grilled chicken.
Use a wire rack to prevent the fried slices from becoming soggy.

name: Fried Tokwa With Garlic Vinegar Sauce
description: Fried tokwa is a popular Filipino soybean-based accompaniment made by frying firm tofu until golden and crisp. It is served with a savory garlic-vinegar sauce and provides a plant-based protein option alongside vegetable, meat, and rice dishes.
steps: Remove tofu from its packaging and drain the liquid.
Pat dry with clean paper towels and cut into bite-sized cubes.
Season lightly with salt and pepper.
Heat oil in a frying pan over medium heat.
Fry the tofu in batches for 4–5 minutes, turning occasionally until golden brown.
Remove and drain on a wire rack.
Combine vinegar, soy sauce, garlic, onions, sugar, and chili in a bowl.
Arrange the tofu on a serving plate and serve with the sauce.
tips: Choose firm tofu to prevent the cubes from breaking.
Pat tofu dry before frying to reduce oil splattering.
Serve immediately to preserve the crisp exterior.
Pair with grilled vegetables, rice meals, or sautéed leafy greens.
Store leftover tofu and sauce separately in refrigerated containers.

name: Ginataang Langka (Young Jackfruit In Coconut Milk)
description: Ginataang langka is a traditional Filipino vegetable dish made from young unripe jackfruit simmered in coconut milk with garlic, onions, and ginger. It has a creamy, mildly sweet flavor and tender texture that complements grilled and fried main dishes.
ingredients: 500 g young jackfruit, peeled and chopped, or drained canned young jackfruit
steps: If using fresh jackfruit, remove the tough core and seeds and cut the flesh into small pieces. Use gloves when handling its sticky sap.
Wash and drain the prepared jackfruit. If using canned jackfruit, rinse and drain.
Heat oil in a pot over medium heat.
Sauté garlic, onions, and ginger until fragrant.
Add the jackfruit and stir-fry for 3 minutes.
Pour in coconut milk and fish sauce.
Cover and simmer for 15–20 minutes until tender.
Add coconut cream, chilies, and black pepper.
Simmer uncovered for another 5 minutes until the sauce thickens.
Serve warm.
tips: Use young, unripe jackfruit rather than ripe sweet jackfruit.
Canned young jackfruit is a convenient alternative for home cooking.
Simmer gently to prevent coconut milk from separating.
Serve with grilled fish, fried chicken, or pork barbecue.
Refrigerate leftovers promptly.

name: Ginataang Mais At Malunggay (Corn And Moringa In Coconut Milk)
description: Ginataang mais at malunggay is a Filipino vegetable preparation featuring sweet corn kernels and malunggay leaves cooked in coconut milk. Its mild sweetness and creamy texture make it a comforting side dish for grilled fish and savory meat preparations.
steps: Remove corn kernels from the cob and wash thoroughly.
Separate malunggay leaves from their stems and rinse well.
Heat cooking oil in a pot over medium heat.
Sauté garlic and onions until fragrant.
Add the corn kernels and stir-fry for 2 minutes.
Pour in coconut milk and simmer for 10–12 minutes until the corn is tender.
Add coconut cream, salt, and black pepper.
Stir gently and add the malunggay leaves.
Cook for another 2–3 minutes until the leaves wilt.
Transfer to a serving bowl.
tips: Choose fresh, sweet corn with plump kernels.
Frozen corn may be used when fresh corn is unavailable.
Add malunggay at the end to preserve its color.
Serve with grilled tilapia, fried fish, or roasted chicken.
Use unsweetened coconut milk to maintain the savory character of the dish.

name: Ginisang Malunggay
description: Ginisang malunggay is a simple Filipino vegetable dish made by sautéing fresh moringa leaves with garlic, onions, and tomatoes. It has a mild earthy flavor and soft texture, making it an easy and affordable accompaniment to everyday meals.
steps: Remove the malunggay leaves from their stems and wash thoroughly.
Heat oil in a pan over medium heat.
Sauté garlic and onions until fragrant.
Add tomatoes and cook until softened.
Add water and fish sauce.
Bring the mixture to a gentle simmer.
Add the malunggay leaves and stir gently.
Cook for 3–4 minutes until the leaves are tender.
Season with black pepper and serve.
tips: Use fresh malunggay leaves without yellowing or damaged portions.
Avoid prolonged cooking to retain the leaves' texture.
Add sliced mushrooms for a variation.
Serve with grilled fish, fried chicken, or pork barbecue.
Wash the leaves thoroughly to remove dust and insects.

name: Ginisang Sayote Tops
description: Ginisang sayote tops is a traditional home-style Filipino vegetable side dish made by sautéing young chayote leaves and tender shoots with garlic, onions, and tomatoes. It has a mild flavor and soft texture that complements rich and savory main dishes.
ingredients: 300 g young sayote leaves and shoots
steps: Remove tough stems and damaged leaves.
Wash the young leaves and shoots thoroughly.
Heat oil in a pan over medium heat.
Sauté garlic and onions until fragrant.
Add tomatoes and cook until softened.
Add the sayote tops and stir gently.
Pour in water and fish sauce.
Cover and simmer for 3–5 minutes until tender.
Season with black pepper and serve warm.
tips: Select young, tender leaves rather than mature fibrous shoots.
Wash thoroughly because leafy shoots may contain soil and insects.
Do not overcook to preserve their texture.
Serve with fried bangus, grilled pork, or chicken adobo.
Use the vegetables soon after purchasing for maximum freshness.

name: Ginisang Labanos (Sautéed White Radish)
description: Ginisang labanos is a Filipino vegetable side dish featuring white radish sautéed with garlic, onions, and tomatoes. Its mild peppery taste becomes softer during cooking, creating a tender and savory dish that complements fried fish and meat.
ingredients: 500 g white radish, peeled and sliced
steps: Wash, peel, and slice the radish into thin rounds.
Heat oil in a pan over medium heat.
Sauté garlic and onions until fragrant.
Add tomatoes and cook until soft.
Add the radish and stir-fry for 2 minutes.
Pour in water and fish sauce.
Cover and simmer for 7–9 minutes until the radish becomes tender.
Season with black pepper and serve.
tips: Choose firm, smooth radishes with fresh-looking leaves if attached.
Slice uniformly for consistent cooking.
Add carrots for a slightly sweeter flavor.
Pair with fried tilapia, grilled chicken, or pork barbecue.
Avoid overcooking because radish can become excessively soft.

name: Tortang Talong With Tomatoes And Onions
description: This variation of tortang talong incorporates chopped tomatoes and onions into the beaten egg mixture before frying. It combines the smoky flavor of grilled eggplant with the sweetness of vegetables, creating a colorful Filipino side dish.
steps: Wash the eggplants and grill over medium heat for 10–12 minutes until tender.
Allow them to cool and peel off the charred skin.
Flatten each eggplant gently with a fork.
Beat the eggs in a bowl.
Add chopped tomatoes, onions, salt, and black pepper.
Dip each eggplant into the egg mixture, coating it thoroughly.
Heat oil in a frying pan over medium heat.
Fry each eggplant for approximately 2–3 minutes per side until golden and fully cooked.
Transfer to a serving plate and serve warm.
tips: Remove excess tomato liquid before mixing to prevent a watery egg coating.
Grill eggplants until completely tender before flattening.
Maintain medium heat for even browning.
Serve with rice, fried fish, or chicken adobo.
Cook the egg mixture thoroughly before serving.

name: Nilagang Saging Na Saba (Boiled Cardaba Bananas)
description: Nilagang saging na saba is a simple Filipino preparation made by boiling whole or sliced cardaba bananas until tender. Although naturally sweet, it is commonly served as an inexpensive carbohydrate-rich accompaniment to certain savory meals, particularly in regional and home-style cooking.
steps: Wash the saba bananas thoroughly.
Trim the ends but keep the peel intact to help maintain their shape.
Place the bananas in a cooking pot.
Add water until the bananas are mostly submerged.
Add salt if desired.
Bring to a boil over medium-high heat.
Lower the heat and simmer for 15–20 minutes.
Check doneness by inserting a fork into the flesh; it should be tender.
Drain and allow to cool slightly before serving.
tips: Select ripe but firm saba bananas for a naturally sweet flavor without excessive softness.
Boiling with the peel helps prevent the flesh from breaking apart.
Serve with grilled fish or certain traditional savory meals.
This dish can also be served as a light snack, although it is presented here as a meal accompaniment.
Refrigerate peeled leftovers and consume within 2–3 days.

name: Nilagang Kamote (Boiled Sweet Potatoes)
description: Nilagang kamote is a traditional Filipino preparation of sweet potatoes boiled until soft and tender. Its natural sweetness and starchy texture make it a practical accompaniment to savory vegetable, fish, and meat dishes.
steps: Wash the sweet potatoes thoroughly under running water.
Peel if desired and cut large pieces into equal portions.
Place the sweet potatoes in a pot and add water.
Add salt if desired.
Bring to a boil over medium-high heat.
Lower the heat and simmer for 15–20 minutes.
Test with a fork; the sweet potatoes should be tender without falling apart.
Drain and arrange on a serving plate.
tips: Choose firm sweet potatoes without bruises or soft spots.
Cut into equal-sized portions for uniform cooking.
Avoid overboiling to preserve the shape.
Pair with grilled fish, roasted chicken, or savory vegetable dishes.
Use leftover boiled sweet potatoes in other preparations to reduce food waste.

name: Ginataang Papaya (Green Papaya In Coconut Milk)
description: Ginataang papaya is a Filipino vegetable dish made with unripe green papaya simmered in coconut milk with garlic, onions, and ginger. It has a mildly sweet flavor and creamy texture that complements grilled and fried main dishes.
ingredients: 500 g unripe green papaya, peeled and sliced
steps: Wash, peel, and remove the seeds from the green papaya.
Slice the flesh into uniform strips.
Heat oil in a pot over medium heat.
Sauté garlic, onions, and ginger until fragrant.
Add the papaya and stir-fry for 2 minutes.
Pour in coconut milk and fish sauce.
Simmer for 10–12 minutes until the papaya softens.
Add coconut cream, black pepper, and chilies.
Simmer for another 5 minutes until creamy.
Serve warm.
tips: Use completely unripe papaya to maintain the dish's savory flavor.
Slice the papaya evenly to ensure uniform tenderness.
Do not boil coconut milk too vigorously.
Serve with fried tilapia, grilled pork, or chicken barbecue.
Refrigerate leftovers promptly because coconut milk spoils quickly in warm conditions.

name: Ginisang Kundol (Sautéed Winter Melon)
description: Ginisang kundol is a Filipino vegetable preparation made by sautéing winter melon with garlic, onions, and tomatoes. It has a mild, slightly sweet flavor and soft texture that makes it a light accompaniment to fried fish and grilled meat.
steps: Wash the kundol, remove the skin and seeds, and cut into thin slices.
Heat cooking oil in a pan over medium heat.
Sauté garlic and onions until fragrant.
Add tomatoes and cook until softened.
Add the sliced kundol and stir-fry for 2 minutes.
Pour in water and fish sauce.
Cover and simmer for 7–9 minutes until tender.
Season with black pepper and serve warm.
tips: Choose firm kundol with clean, undamaged skin.
Remove mature seeds and fibrous portions.
Avoid overcooking because winter melon softens quickly.
Serve with fried bangus, pork barbecue, or chicken adobo.
Add malunggay leaves during the final minutes for added color.

name: Tortang Gulay (Filipino Mixed Vegetable Omelette)
description: Tortang gulay is a Filipino vegetable side dish made by combining finely chopped vegetables with beaten eggs and pan-frying the mixture until golden. It is a practical way to use leftover vegetables while adding variety and color to everyday meals.
ingredients: ½ cup green beans, finely chopped
steps: Wash all vegetables thoroughly and chop or grate them finely.
Heat 1 tablespoon oil in a pan over medium heat.
Sauté garlic and onions until fragrant.
Add carrots, sayote, cabbage, and green beans.
Cook for 3–4 minutes until the vegetables soften slightly. Allow the mixture to cool.
Beat the eggs in a bowl and season with salt and pepper.
Add the cooled vegetables and mix thoroughly.
Heat the remaining oil in a nonstick pan over medium-low heat.
Pour the mixture into the pan and spread evenly.
Cook for 3–4 minutes until the bottom sets.
Carefully flip and cook the other side until golden and the egg is fully cooked.
Slice into portions and serve.
tips: Drain vegetables properly to avoid a watery omelet.
Use medium-low heat to ensure the center cooks completely.
Use a nonstick pan for easier flipping.
Pair with fried fish, chicken barbecue, or pork adobo.
This recipe is suitable for using small quantities of leftover vegetables safely stored in the refrigerator.

name: Inihaw Na Mais (Filipino Grilled Corn)
description: Inihaw na mais is a traditional Filipino grilled corn preparation made by cooking fresh corn over direct heat until lightly charred and tender. Its naturally sweet kernels and smoky aroma make it a simple accompaniment to grilled meat and seafood.
ingredients: 4 medium ears of fresh sweet corn
steps: Remove the husks and silk from the corn.
Wash each ear thoroughly and pat dry.
Preheat a grill to medium heat.
Place the corn directly on the grill.
Turn every 2–3 minutes for approximately 12–15 minutes until the kernels are tender and lightly charred.
Brush the grilled corn with melted butter.
Sprinkle with salt and black pepper.
Arrange on a serving plate and serve warm.
tips: Choose fresh corn with plump kernels and green husks.
Turn regularly to prevent uneven charring.
Brush with butter only after grilling to prevent excessive burning.
Serve with grilled pork, chicken inasal, or seafood.
Corn can also be boiled before grilling for a shorter final cooking time.

name: Ensaladang Kamatis At Sibuyas (Tomato And Onion Salad)
description: Ensaladang kamatis at sibuyas is a simple Filipino side salad made from fresh tomatoes and onions tossed in vinegar, calamansi juice, and seasonings. Its refreshing acidity and natural sweetness balance the rich flavors of fried and grilled dishes.
steps: Wash the tomatoes, onions, and spring onions thoroughly.
Slice the tomatoes into wedges or rounds.
Thinly slice the red onion.
Combine vinegar, calamansi juice, sugar, salt, and black pepper in a bowl.
Add the tomatoes and onions.
Toss gently until the dressing coats the vegetables.
Sprinkle with chopped spring onions.
Chill briefly and serve fresh.
tips: Choose ripe but firm tomatoes to prevent the salad from becoming watery.
Slice the onions thinly for a milder texture.
Adjust the vinegar and sugar to balance the natural acidity of the tomatoes.
Serve with grilled bangus, fried tilapia, pork barbecue, or chicken inasal.
Prepare shortly before serving and refrigerate leftovers promptly.

name: Lumpiang Shanghai
description: Lumpiang Shanghai is a popular Filipino appetizer made of ground pork, vegetables, and seasonings wrapped in thin spring roll wrappers and deep-fried until golden brown. It is commonly served at celebrations and family gatherings.
steps: Combine the ground pork, carrots, onion, garlic, egg, soy sauce, salt, and pepper in a bowl.
Mix thoroughly until all ingredients are evenly distributed.
Place approximately 1 tablespoon of filling near the edge of each wrapper.
Fold the sides inward and roll tightly. Seal the edge with a little water.
Heat the cooking oil in a deep pan over medium heat.
Fry the lumpia in batches until golden brown and the pork filling is thoroughly cooked.
Drain on a wire rack or paper towels.
Serve hot with sweet chili sauce or banana ketchup.
tips: Avoid overfilling the wrappers to prevent them from tearing.
Keep unused wrappers covered with a clean, damp cloth to prevent drying.
Ensure the filling reaches an internal temperature of 71°C.

name: Lumpiang Gulay
description: Lumpiang Gulay is a vegetable-filled Filipino spring roll commonly prepared with bean sprouts, carrots, cabbage, and other vegetables. It is a lighter alternative to meat-filled lumpia.
ingredients: ½ cup green beans, thinly sliced
steps: Heat 1 tablespoon of oil in a pan.
Sauté the garlic and onion until fragrant.
Add the carrots, green beans, cabbage, and bean sprouts.
Season with salt and pepper. Cook until the vegetables are just tender.
Transfer the filling to a plate and allow it to cool.
Place 1 to 2 tablespoons of filling on each wrapper.
Fold the sides and roll tightly, sealing the edges with water.
Heat the frying oil and cook the rolls until golden brown.
Drain excess oil and serve with vinegar dipping sauce.
tips: Drain excess liquid from the vegetable filling before wrapping.
Avoid overcooking the vegetables because they will cook further during frying.

name: Lumpiang Sariwa
description: Lumpiang Sariwa is a fresh Filipino spring roll filled with sautéed vegetables and sometimes meat. It is wrapped in a soft homemade crepe and served with a sweet-savory garlic sauce.
ingredients: 1 tbsp cornstarch mixed with 2 tbsp water
steps: Heat oil in a pan and sauté garlic and onion.
Add pork and cook until no longer pink.
Add sweet potato, green beans, carrots, cabbage, and water.
Season with salt and pepper. Simmer until the vegetables are tender and the pork is cooked.
To prepare the wrapper, whisk flour, egg, water, and oil until smooth.
Pour a thin layer of batter into a lightly greased nonstick pan. Cook over low heat until set, then carefully remove.
For the sauce, combine water, soy sauce, sugar, and garlic in a saucepan.
Bring to a simmer, then add the cornstarch slurry. Stir until thickened.
Place vegetable filling on each wrapper and fold the sides inward.
Drizzle with sauce and serve with crushed peanuts, if desired.
tips: Cook the wrappers over low heat to prevent browning.
Allow the filling to cool slightly before assembling.
Keep the finished rolls refrigerated if not serving immediately.

name: Tokwa't Baboy
description: Tokwa't Baboy combines fried tofu and boiled pork, usually ears or belly, with a tangy vinegar-based sauce. It is a familiar Filipino pulutan and appetizer.
steps: Place the pork in a pot with enough water to cover it. Simmer until tender and thoroughly cooked.
Remove the pork and allow it to cool slightly. Cut into bite-sized pieces.
Pat the tofu dry and cut into cubes.
Heat the oil and fry the tofu until golden brown. Drain.
In a bowl, combine vinegar, soy sauce, water, onion, garlic, chili, and pepper.
Add the pork and fried tofu.
Toss gently and allow the flavors to combine for several minutes.
Serve at room temperature or slightly warm.
tips: Dry tofu thoroughly before frying to reduce oil splatter.
Adjust the vinegar and soy sauce according to taste.
Refrigerate leftovers promptly.

name: Kinilaw na Isda
description: Kinilaw na Isda is a Filipino dish made from fresh fish dressed with vinegar or citrus juice, onions, ginger, and chili. It is especially popular in coastal communities.
ingredients: 400 g very fresh, sashimi-grade fish, such as tuna or tanigue
steps: Keep the fish chilled until preparation.
Using a clean knife and cutting board, cut the fish into small cubes.
Place the fish in a clean glass or food-safe bowl.
Add vinegar and calamansi juice, then gently mix.
Add onion, ginger, cucumber, chili, salt, and pepper.
Refrigerate briefly while the flavors combine.
Serve immediately while cold.
tips: Use fish intended for raw consumption from a reputable supplier. Acid does not reliably kill parasites or all harmful microorganisms.
Keep the fish at 4°C or below during preparation.
Pregnant people, young children, older adults, and immunocompromised individuals should avoid raw or undercooked fish.

name: Kilawing Puso ng Saging
description: Kilawing Puso ng Saging is a Filipino appetizer made from banana blossom dressed with vinegar, onion, ginger, and seasonings. Some versions include pork or seafood, but this version focuses on banana blossom.
steps: Remove the tough outer bracts from the banana blossom.
Slice the blossom thinly and soak in salted water to reduce discoloration and bitterness.
Drain and rinse thoroughly.
Boil in water until tender, then drain.
Heat oil in a pan and sauté garlic, onion, and ginger.
Add the banana blossom and cook for several minutes.
Pour in the vinegar and allow it to simmer briefly before stirring.
Season with salt and pepper. Add chili if desired.
Cool slightly and serve.
tips: Wear gloves when preparing the blossom because its sap can be sticky.
Remove tough outer layers and discard any hard portions.

name: Ensaladang Talong
description: Ensaladang Talong is a Filipino eggplant salad made from grilled or boiled eggplant mixed with tomatoes, onions, vinegar, and seasonings.
steps: Grill the eggplants over medium heat until the skin is charred and the flesh is soft.
Allow them to cool, then peel away the charred skin.
Place the eggplant flesh in a bowl and gently mash.
Add tomatoes and onion.
Pour in the vinegar and calamansi juice.
Season with salt and pepper.
Mix gently and serve.
tips: Grilling gives the eggplant a smoky flavor.
Avoid over-mashing if you prefer a salad with more texture.

name: Ensaladang Mangga
description: Ensaladang Mangga is a refreshing green mango salad typically combined with tomatoes, onions, and a salty component such as bagoong.
ingredients: 1 tbsp bagoong alamang, or to taste
steps: Wash and peel the mangoes.
Slice the mangoes into thin strips or small pieces.
Place the mangoes in a mixing bowl.
Add the tomatoes and onion.
Add bagoong and calamansi juice.
Mix gently until evenly combined.
Add chili if desired and serve immediately.
tips: Choose firm, sour green mangoes for the best texture.
Taste before adding extra salt because bagoong is already salty.

name: Atchara
description: Atchara is a Filipino pickled green papaya dish prepared with vinegar, sugar, carrots, ginger, and other vegetables. It is commonly served as an accompaniment to rich or fried foods.
ingredients: ½ red bell pepper, thinly sliced
¼ cup ginger, cut into thin strips
steps: Place the shredded papaya in a bowl and sprinkle with salt.
Let it stand for approximately 30 minutes.
Squeeze out excess liquid and rinse lightly if needed.
Combine vinegar, sugar, and water in a saucepan.
Heat until the sugar dissolves, then allow the mixture to cool.
Combine papaya, carrots, bell pepper, raisins, and ginger in a clean container.
Pour the cooled vinegar mixture over the vegetables.
Refrigerate and allow the flavors to develop before serving.
tips: Use a clean, food-safe container.
Keep the atchara refrigerated. This quick recipe is not a validated shelf-stable canning process.
Use clean utensils whenever serving.

name: Adobong Mani
description: Adobong Mani is a Filipino snack made from fried peanuts seasoned with garlic and salt. It is commonly sold by street vendors and served during gatherings.
ingredients: ½ tsp salt, or to taste
steps: Heat the oil in a deep pan over medium-low heat.
Add the peanuts and cook slowly, stirring occasionally.
Add the garlic when the peanuts are nearly cooked.
Continue frying until the peanuts are lightly golden and the garlic is crisp.
Remove the peanuts and garlic using a slotted spoon.
Drain excess oil.
Sprinkle with salt while still warm.
Cool completely before serving or storing.
tips: Peanuts continue cooking from residual heat, so remove them before they become too dark.
Watch the garlic carefully because it burns quickly.
Allow the peanuts to cool completely before placing them in an airtight container.
PART 2: FRIED AND CRISPY FILIPINO APPETIZERS

name: Ukoy
description: Ukoy is a crispy Filipino fritter commonly made with small shrimp and vegetables held together by a light batter.
steps: Combine flour, cornstarch, egg, water, garlic, salt, and pepper in a bowl.
Mix until a relatively smooth batter forms.
Add shrimp, bean sprouts, and carrots.
Heat oil in a pan over medium heat.
Spoon portions of the mixture into the hot oil and flatten slightly.
Fry until crisp and golden brown.
Turn carefully and cook the other side.
Drain on a wire rack.
Serve with vinegar dipping sauce.
tips: Do not overcrowd the pan.
Make the fritters relatively thin so they cook evenly.
Ensure shrimp are thoroughly cooked.

name: Kwek-Kwek
description: Kwek-kwek is a popular Filipino street food made from hard-boiled quail eggs coated in orange-colored batter and deep-fried.
ingredients: 1 tsp annatto powder or orange food coloring
steps: Hard-boil the quail eggs, cool them, and peel.
Pat the eggs dry.
Combine flour, cornstarch, annatto powder, salt, and pepper.
Gradually add water until a thick but pourable batter forms.
Dip each egg into the batter, coating it evenly.
Carefully lower the coated eggs into hot oil.
Fry until the coating is crisp.
Drain and serve with vinegar, sweet sauce, or cucumber-onion dipping sauce.
tips: Dry the eggs well so the batter adheres.
Maintain a consistent oil temperature to prevent the coating from becoming greasy.

name: Fish Balls
description: Fish balls are a popular Filipino street-food snack made from seasoned fish paste formed into balls and fried or simmered.
steps: Ensure the fish is boneless and well chilled.
Process the fish in a food processor until finely minced.
Add cornstarch, flour, egg white, garlic, salt, and pepper.
Mix until the paste becomes cohesive. Add a little cold water if needed.
Shape the mixture into small balls using clean hands or two spoons.
Heat oil in a pan.
Fry the fish balls in batches until golden and thoroughly cooked.
Drain and serve with sweet brown sauce or spicy vinegar.
tips: Keep the mixture cold while shaping.
Cook a small test portion first to check seasoning and texture.
Ensure the fish reaches an internal temperature of 63°C.

name: Squid Balls
description: A Filipino street-food-style seafood snack made from seasoned squid paste shaped into balls, fried, and served with a sweet or spicy dipping sauce.
steps: Pat the cleaned squid dry and cut into small pieces.
Process the squid until finely minced.
Add cornstarch, flour, egg white, garlic, salt, and pepper.
Mix until the ingredients form a thick paste.
Shape the mixture into small balls.
Heat the oil in a deep pan.
Fry the squid balls in batches until cooked through and lightly golden.
Drain and serve with dipping sauce.
tips: Avoid adding too much water because it makes shaping difficult.
Do not overcrowd the pan.
Cook squid thoroughly, but avoid excessive frying that may make it tough.

name: Dynamite Lumpia
