name: Leche Flan
description: A well-known Filipino steamed custard made with egg yolks, evaporated milk, and condensed milk, finished with a smooth layer of caramel.
steps: Melt sugar in a llanera over low heat until amber.
Swirl to coat the bottom and cool.
Gently combine egg yolks, evaporated milk, condensed milk, and vanilla.
Strain twice.
Pour into the llanera and cover with foil.
Steam over low heat for 35–45 minutes, or until set.
Cool, chill, then unmold.
tips: Strain the custard to remove egg strands and help create a smooth texture.
Keep the water at a gentle simmer; strong boiling can create bubbles in the flan.

name: Halo-Halo
description: A popular Filipino shaved-ice dessert that combines sweetened fruits, beans, jellies, and creamy milk with toppings such as leche flan and ube halaya.
ingredients: leche flan and ube halaya for topping
steps: Place assorted sweetened ingredients in tall glasses.
Add shaved ice and pour evaporated milk over it.
Top with leche flan and ube halaya.
Serve immediately.
tips: Drain sweetened ingredients before layering so the dessert does not become watery.
Add the shaved ice and milk just before serving to keep the texture refreshing.

name: Buko Pandan
description: A chilled Filipino dessert made with young coconut, pandan-flavored gelatin, nata de coco, and a creamy milk mixture.
steps: Cook gulaman with water and sugar according to package directions.
Pour into a tray and let it set, then cut into cubes.
Combine gulaman, buko, and nata de coco.
Fold in cream and condensed milk.
Chill before serving.
tips: Cool the gulaman completely before mixing it with the cream.
Chill the dessert for at least 2 hours so the flavors combine.

name: Mais con Yelo
description: A refreshing Filipino merienda dessert of sweet corn, shaved ice, and evaporated milk, often finished with pinipig or cornflakes.
steps: Divide corn kernels among serving glasses.
Add shaved ice, then pour evaporated milk over it.
Sweeten to taste and add cornflakes or pinipig if desired.
Serve cold.
tips: Use well-drained corn and adjust the sugar depending on its sweetness.
Assemble just before serving to prevent the ice from melting too quickly.

name: Suman Malagkit
description: A traditional Filipino rice cake made from glutinous rice and coconut milk, wrapped in banana leaves and steamed until tender.
steps: Rinse rice and soak for 2 hours, then drain.
Combine rice, coconut milk, and salt.
Cook over low heat, stirring, until partially absorbed.
Wrap portions in softened banana leaves.
Steam for 45–60 minutes until tender.
tips: Soften banana leaves briefly over heat so they become flexible and less likely to tear.
Wrap the rice securely but leave a little room for expansion during steaming.

name: Kutsinta
description: A soft, chewy Filipino steamed rice cake with a characteristic brown-sugar color, commonly served with grated coconut.
ingredients: 1/2 tsp annatto powder dissolved in water
steps: Dissolve sugar in water.
Whisk in both flours, lye water, and annatto mixture until smooth; strain.
Pour into lightly greased small molds.
Steam for 20–25 minutes until translucent and set.
Cool and serve with grated coconut.
tips: Strain the batter to remove lumps and achieve a smooth surface.
Grease the molds lightly and allow the kutsinta to cool before removing.

name: Puto
description: A Filipino steamed rice cake with a soft, tender texture, often served as a snack or accompaniment and sometimes topped with cheese.
steps: Mix rice flour, sugar, and baking powder.
Add water and coconut milk; whisk until smooth.
Pour into greased puto molds, filling each about three-fourths full.
Steam for 12–15 minutes.
Add cheese near the end if desired.
Cool slightly before unmolding.
tips: Avoid overmixing the batter to help keep the rice cakes tender.
Keep the steamer covered and maintain steady steam while cooking.

name: Bibingka
description: A Filipino rice cake traditionally associated with the Christmas season, baked in banana-leaf-lined pans and topped with salted egg and cheese.
steps: Line round pans with softened banana leaves and brush lightly with butter.
Whisk rice flour, sugar, and baking powder.
Mix in coconut milk, eggs, and melted butter.
Pour into pans, top with salted egg and cheese, and bake at 190°C for 20–25 minutes.
Brush with butter and serve.
tips: Use softened banana leaves to line the pan without tearing.
Check the center for doneness; it should be set before brushing with butter.

name: Pichi-Pichi
description: A chewy Filipino cassava delicacy made by steaming grated cassava with sugar, then coating or topping it with coconut or cheese.
steps: Combine cassava, sugar, water, and pandan extract.
Pour into small greased molds and steam for 30–40 minutes until translucent.
Prepare the ingredients and equipment before starting so the mixture can be handled without interruption.
Cool, unmold, and roll in grated coconut or top with cheese.
tips: Drain excess liquid from freshly grated cassava if the mixture is too watery.
Let the pieces cool before unmolding so they hold their shape.

name: Cassava Cake
description: A Filipino baked cassava dessert enriched with coconut milk and condensed milk, commonly finished with a creamy topping.
steps: Mix cassava, coconut milk, condensed milk, sugar, egg, and cheese.
Pour into a greased baking dish.
Bake at 180°C for 35–45 minutes until nearly set.
Mix topping ingredients, spread over the cake, and bake another 10–15 minutes until lightly golden.
Cool before slicing.
tips: Spread the mixture evenly so the cake cooks at a consistent rate.
Allow the cake to cool before slicing for cleaner portions.

name: Maja Blanca
description: A Filipino coconut pudding thickened with cornstarch and commonly prepared with sweet corn and toasted latik.
steps: Combine coconut milk, condensed milk, sugar, and corn in a saucepan.
Bring to a gentle simmer.
Dissolve cornstarch in water.
Pour into the pan while stirring continuously.
Cook until very thick.
Transfer to a dish, cool, and top with latik.
tips: Stir continuously after adding the cornstarch slurry to prevent lumps.
Toast the latik gently and use it as a topping just before serving.

name: Buko Salad
description: A chilled Filipino party dessert combining young coconut, nata de coco, kaong, fruit cocktail, and a sweet cream dressing.
steps: Drain the fruit cocktail, nata de coco, and kaong well.
Combine with young coconut in a large bowl.
Fold in cream and condensed milk.
Refrigerate for at least 2 hours before serving.
tips: Drain the fruit, nata de coco, and kaong thoroughly to keep the dressing creamy.
Keep refrigerated until serving because the dessert contains dairy and fresh coconut.

name: Fruit Salad
description: A familiar Filipino celebration dessert made by combining canned fruits and chewy add-ins with a creamy condensed-milk dressing.
steps: Drain canned fruits and mix with nata de coco and kaong.
Fold in cream and condensed milk.
Add cheese if desired.
Chill for at least 2 hours before serving.
tips: Chill the cream before mixing for a thicker dressing.
Drain canned fruits well to prevent excess liquid from thinning the mixture.

name: Ube Halaya
description: A rich Filipino purple-yam jam slowly cooked with coconut milk, condensed milk, and sugar until thick and smooth.
steps: Combine yam, coconut milk, condensed milk, and sugar in a heavy saucepan.
Cook over low to medium-low heat, stirring often, until thick and pulling away from the sides.
Stir in butter.
Transfer to a greased dish and cool.
tips: Stir frequently and scrape the bottom of the pan to prevent scorching.
Cook over low heat; the mixture thickens as moisture evaporates.

name: Turon
description: A popular Filipino merienda snack of banana and jackfruit wrapped in lumpia wrapper, coated with sugar, and fried until crisp.
steps: Place banana and jackfruit on each wrapper.
Sprinkle with a little brown sugar and roll tightly, sealing the edge with water.
Heat oil over medium heat.
Fry turon until crisp and golden.
Drain and serve warm.
tips: Seal the wrapper firmly so the filling does not leak into the hot oil.
Fry in batches and avoid overcrowding the pan to keep the wrappers crisp.

name: Banana Cue
description: A classic Filipino street-food snack made by frying saba bananas with brown sugar until coated in a glossy caramelized layer.
steps: Heat enough oil in a pan for shallow frying.
Add bananas and cook until lightly browned.
Sprinkle in brown sugar and turn bananas until the sugar melts and coats them.
Remove carefully and allow excess oil to drain.
tips: Measure ingredients before cooking and follow the stated quantities to help achieve a consistent texture.
Maintain a steady frying temperature and cook in batches so the pieces brown evenly without absorbing excess oil.
Allow hot desserts to cool safely, then refrigerate perishable items in clean, covered containers until serving.

name: Camote Cue
description: A Filipino street-food favorite made from sweet-potato pieces fried and coated with caramelized brown sugar.
ingredients: 500 g sweet potatoes, peeled and cut into thick pieces
steps: Pat sweet potatoes dry.
Fry in hot oil over medium heat until tender and lightly browned.
Add brown sugar and stir carefully until melted and caramelized around the pieces.
Drain before serving.
tips: Use firm, ripe saba bananas so they hold their shape while frying.
Add the brown sugar after the bananas begin to brown and turn gently to coat.
Allow hot desserts to cool safely, then refrigerate perishable items in clean, covered containers until serving.

name: Minatamis na Saging
description: A Filipino sweet banana dessert simmered in brown-sugar syrup, sometimes flavored with pandan and served warm or chilled.
steps: Combine water, brown sugar, pandan, and salt in a saucepan.
Bring to a boil.
Add saba bananas and simmer gently until tender and the syrup thickens.
Cool slightly and serve warm or chilled.
tips: Cut sweet potatoes into similar-sized pieces for even cooking.
Keep the heat moderate so the sugar caramelizes without burning.
Measure ingredients before cooking and follow the stated quantities to help achieve a consistent texture.
Use low or moderate heat when cooking sugar, coconut milk, or thick mixtures; stir as needed to prevent scorching.
Allow hot desserts to cool safely, then refrigerate perishable items in clean, covered containers until serving.

name: Ginataang Bilo-Bilo
description: A comforting Filipino dessert soup of glutinous-rice balls, saba banana, sweet potato, sago, and jackfruit simmered in coconut milk.
steps: Mix rice flour with water gradually and form small balls.
Simmer sweet potato in water until nearly tender.
Add coconut milk and sugar.
Add rice balls and saba.
Cook until the balls float and are cooked through.
Stir in sago and jackfruit.
tips: Make the rice balls small and uniform so they cook evenly.
Stir gently after adding the rice balls to prevent them from sticking together.

name: Palitaw
description: A traditional Filipino rice cake made from glutinous rice dough, boiled until it floats, then coated with coconut, sugar, and sesame seeds.
steps: Mix rice flour with water gradually to form a soft dough.
Shape into small flat discs.
Drop into boiling water.
When the pieces float, cook for another minute, then remove and drain.
Coat with grated coconut and sprinkle with sugar and sesame seeds.
tips: Add water gradually until the dough is soft but no longer sticky.
Remove the pieces soon after they float and finish cooking to avoid a tough texture.

name: Espasol
description: A Filipino delicacy associated with Laguna, made from toasted rice flour cooked with sweetened coconut milk and coated in toasted rice flour.
ingredients: 1 cup toasted rice flour for coating
steps: Toast glutinous rice flour in a pan over low heat until fragrant.
Set aside.
Heat coconut milk, sugar, and salt until dissolved.
Gradually add toasted flour, stirring until a thick dough forms.
Cool slightly, shape into logs, and coat with toasted rice flour.
Slice and serve.
tips: Toast the flour over low heat and stir often so it does not burn.
Add the flour gradually to the coconut mixture to control the dough thickness.

name: Sapin-Sapin
description: A colorful Filipino layered rice cake made with rice flour, glutinous rice flour, coconut milk, and distinct flavors such as ube and jackfruit.
steps: Combine rice flour, glutinous rice flour, condensed milk, coconut milk, and sugar.
Divide into three portions.
Flavor one portion with ube and another with langka; leave the third plain.
Pour one layer into a greased pan and steam until partly set.
Add remaining layers one at a time, steaming each until set.
Cool and top with latik.
tips: Steam each layer until partly set before adding the next layer.
Allow the finished cake to cool completely before slicing.

name: Suman sa Lihiya
description: A Filipino sticky-rice delicacy prepared with lye water and coconut milk, wrapped in banana leaves and simmered until cooked.
steps: Wash and soak rice for 2 hours, then drain.
Mix rice with coconut milk, lye water, and salt.
Spoon onto softened banana leaves and wrap securely.
Arrange in a pot, cover with water, and simmer for 1 1/2–2 hours until sticky and cooked.
Drain and cool.
tips: Measure ingredients before cooking and follow the stated quantities to help achieve a consistent texture.
Avoid opening the steamer or oven too often; check doneness near the end of the cooking time to help maintain an even texture.
Allow hot desserts to cool safely, then refrigerate perishable items in clean, covered containers until serving.

name: Suman sa Ibos
description: A traditional Filipino sticky-rice cake cooked with coconut milk and salt in palm-leaf or ibos wrappers.
steps: Rinse rice and soak for 2 hours.
Drain well.
Mix rice with coconut milk and salt.
Fill prepared ibos wrappers, leaving room for expansion, and secure.
Steam or boil for about 1 hour until rice is tender and sticky.
tips: Use only the stated amount of lye water because too much can affect flavor and texture.
Wrap the rice tightly and simmer gently until fully cooked.
Allow hot desserts to cool safely, then refrigerate perishable items in clean, covered containers until serving.

name: Puto Bumbong
description: A Filipino purple-glutinous-rice cake traditionally steamed in bamboo tubes and served with butter, grated coconut, and muscovado sugar.
ingredients: 2 cups pirurutong or purple glutinous rice, soaked overnight and drained
steps: Grind soaked rice into a damp fine mixture and press out excess moisture.
Fill puto-bumbong tubes loosely and steam until cooked, about 5–8 minutes.
Push onto banana leaves.
Brush with butter and serve with grated coconut and muscovado sugar.
tips: Do not overfill the wrappers because the rice expands as it cooks.
Check that the rice is tender throughout before removing from the steamer.
Allow hot desserts to cool safely, then refrigerate perishable items in clean, covered containers until serving.

name: Bibingkang Malagkit
description: A Filipino baked sticky-rice cake cooked with coconut milk and brown sugar, finished with a rich caramelized coconut topping.
steps: Cook glutinous rice with coconut milk and salt until tender and liquid is absorbed.
Stir in brown sugar until evenly mixed.
Transfer to a greased baking dish.
Simmer topping ingredients until thick, spread over rice, and bake at 180°C for 15–20 minutes until glossy.
tips: Soak the purple glutinous rice long enough to soften it for grinding.
Serve while warm with butter, coconut, and muscovado sugar.
Measure ingredients before cooking and follow the stated quantities to help achieve a consistent texture.
Avoid opening the steamer or oven too often; check doneness near the end of the cooking time to help maintain an even texture.
Allow hot desserts to cool safely, then refrigerate perishable items in clean, covered containers until serving.

name: Biko
description: A traditional Filipino sticky-rice cake cooked with coconut milk and brown sugar, usually topped with latik.
steps: Rinse rice and cook with 1 1/2 cups water until tender.
In a pan, simmer coconut milk, sugar, and salt until slightly thickened.
Add cooked rice.
Stir over low heat until sticky and thick.
Transfer to a lined tray and top with latik.
tips: Measure ingredients before cooking and follow the stated quantities to help achieve a consistent texture.
Avoid opening the steamer or oven too often; check doneness near the end of the cooking time to help maintain an even texture.
Allow hot desserts to cool safely, then refrigerate perishable items in clean, covered containers until serving.

name: Kalamay Hati
description: A sticky Filipino rice delicacy made by cooking glutinous rice flour with coconut milk and brown sugar until thick and glossy.
steps: Whisk rice flour, coconut milk, brown sugar, and salt until smooth.
Cook in a thick-bottomed pan over low heat, stirring continuously until very thick and glossy.
Transfer to a banana-leaf-lined container and top with latik.
Cool before serving.
tips: Measure ingredients before cooking and follow the stated quantities to help achieve a consistent texture.
Use low or moderate heat when cooking sugar, coconut milk, or thick mixtures; stir as needed to prevent scorching.
Allow hot desserts to cool safely, then refrigerate perishable items in clean, covered containers until serving.

name: Kalamay Ube
description: A Filipino variation of kalamay flavored with ube, coconut milk, and sugar for a chewy, rich dessert.
steps: Whisk rice flour and coconut milk until smooth.
Stir in ube halaya, sugar, and condensed milk.
Cook over low heat, stirring constantly until thick, glossy, and pulling away from the pan.
Transfer to a greased dish and top with latik.
Cool before slicing.
tips: Keep the heat low and stir continuously as the mixture thickens.
Cool completely before slicing to help the kalamay hold its shape.

name: Tibok-Tibok
description: A Pampanga specialty traditionally made with carabao's milk, rice flour, and sugar, then topped with latik.
ingredients: 4 cups fresh carabao milk or whole milk
steps: Whisk milk, rice flour, sugar, and salt until no lumps remain.
Cook over medium-low heat, stirring continuously until thick and smooth.
Prepare the ingredients and equipment before starting so the mixture can be handled without interruption.
Pour into a shallow dish, cool until set, and top with latik.
tips: Measure ingredients before cooking and follow the stated quantities to help achieve a consistent texture.
Use low or moderate heat when cooking sugar, coconut milk, or thick mixtures; stir as needed to prevent scorching.
Allow hot desserts to cool safely, then refrigerate perishable items in clean, covered containers until serving.

name: Mango Float
description: A popular Filipino refrigerator cake layered with ripe mangoes, graham crackers, and sweetened cream.
steps: Mix chilled cream and condensed milk until combined.
Arrange graham crackers in a dish, spread with cream mixture, and add mango slices.
Repeat layers.
Finish with cream and crushed crackers.
Refrigerate at least 6 hours or overnight before slicing.
tips: Whisk the rice flour with milk before heating to prevent lumps.
Cook while stirring until the pudding is thick and smooth, then cool to set.
Use low or moderate heat when cooking sugar, coconut milk, or thick mixtures; stir as needed to prevent scorching.
Allow hot desserts to cool safely, then refrigerate perishable items in clean, covered containers until serving.

name: Graham Balls
description: A no-bake Filipino-style sweet snack made from crushed graham crackers and condensed milk, shaped into bite-sized balls.
ingredients: 1/2 cup desiccated coconut or extra crumbs
steps: Place crushed graham crackers in a bowl.
Add condensed milk gradually until the mixture holds together.
Scoop and flatten a portion; place a small marshmallow in the center if using.
Roll into balls.
Coat with coconut or graham crumbs.
Chill until firm.
tips: Measure ingredients before cooking and follow the stated quantities to help achieve a consistent texture.
Use low or moderate heat when cooking sugar, coconut milk, or thick mixtures; stir as needed to prevent scorching.
Allow hot desserts to cool safely, then refrigerate perishable items in clean, covered containers until serving.

name: Polvoron
description: A Filipino molded shortbread-like confection made from toasted flour, powdered milk, sugar, and butter, sometimes mixed with pinipig or nuts.
steps: Toast flour in a dry pan over low heat, stirring until lightly golden.
Cool.
Combine toasted flour, powdered milk, sugar, and optional pinipig or peanuts.
Pour in melted butter and mix until crumbly but moldable.
Press into polvoron molds and release carefully.
tips: Measure ingredients before cooking and follow the stated quantities to help achieve a consistent texture.
Use low or moderate heat when cooking sugar, coconut milk, or thick mixtures; stir as needed to prevent scorching.
Allow hot desserts to cool safely, then refrigerate perishable items in clean, covered containers until serving.

name: Yema
description: A Filipino milk-and-egg-yolk confection cooked until thick, then shaped into small sweets and optionally coated with sugar.
steps: Combine condensed milk and egg yolks in a nonstick pan.
Cook over low heat, stirring continuously.
Add butter and vanilla.
Continue cooking until thick and able to hold its shape.
Cool, shape into small balls or pyramids, and roll in sugar if desired.
tips: Measure ingredients before cooking and follow the stated quantities to help achieve a consistent texture.
Use low or moderate heat when cooking sugar, coconut milk, or thick mixtures; stir as needed to prevent scorching.
Allow hot desserts to cool safely, then refrigerate perishable items in clean, covered containers until serving.

name: Pastillas de Leche
description: A Filipino milk candy traditionally made with milk and sugar, shaped into small pieces and often wrapped individually.
steps: Place powdered milk in a bowl.
Add condensed milk gradually and mix into a soft dough.
Knead lightly until smooth, then shape into small cylinders.
Roll in sugar and wrap individually in paper.
tips: Use low heat and stir continuously to prevent the milk and egg mixture from scorching.
Cool the mixture before shaping to make it easier to handle.
Use low or moderate heat when cooking sugar, coconut milk, or thick mixtures; stir as needed to prevent scorching.
Allow hot desserts to cool safely, then refrigerate perishable items in clean, covered containers until serving.

name: Minatamis na Langka
description: A Filipino sweet preserve of jackfruit simmered in sugar syrup, served on its own or as a topping for other desserts.
steps: Combine water, brown sugar, and pandan in a saucepan.
Bring to a simmer.
Add jackfruit and cook gently until tender and syrupy.
Cool and serve as a dessert or topping for halo-halo.
tips: Add condensed milk gradually and stop when the dough is soft but manageable.
Keep the finished pieces in a clean, airtight container.
Measure ingredients before cooking and follow the stated quantities to help achieve a consistent texture.
Use low or moderate heat when cooking sugar, coconut milk, or thick mixtures; stir as needed to prevent scorching.
Allow hot desserts to cool safely, then refrigerate perishable items in clean, covered containers until serving.

name: Minatamis na Kamote
description: A Filipino dessert of sweet-potato cubes gently simmered in brown-sugar syrup with pandan.
ingredients: 500 g sweet potatoes, peeled and cubed
steps: Combine water, sugar, pandan, and salt in a saucepan.
Bring to a boil.
Add sweet potatoes and simmer until tender but not falling apart.
Continue simmering until syrup lightly thickens.
Serve warm or chilled.
tips: Cut the sweet potatoes evenly so they become tender at the same time.
Avoid over-stirring to keep the cubes from breaking apart.

name: Ube Turon
description: A Filipino-inspired turon variation filled with ube halaya and banana, wrapped and fried until crisp.
steps: Place a spoonful of ube halaya and a few banana slices on each wrapper.
Fold and roll tightly, sealing the edge with water.
Fry over medium heat until crisp and golden.
Drain and serve warm.
tips: Use a moderate amount of filling so the wrappers can be sealed securely.
Drain on a rack or paper towels and serve soon after frying for the best crispness.

name: Pandan Jelly
description: A simple Filipino-style gelatin dessert flavored with fragrant pandan and served chilled.
steps: Combine gulaman, water, and sugar in a saucepan.
Bring to a boil while stirring until dissolved.
Add pandan extract and pour into a shallow dish.
Cool until firm, cut into cubes, and serve chilled or add to buko pandan.
tips: Measure ingredients before cooking and follow the stated quantities to help achieve a consistent texture.
Use low or moderate heat when cooking sugar, coconut milk, or thick mixtures; stir as needed to prevent scorching.
Allow hot desserts to cool safely, then refrigerate perishable items in clean, covered containers until serving.

name: Agar-Agar Gulaman
description: A Filipino chilled gelatin dessert made with gulaman and sugar, sometimes set with pieces of fruit cocktail.
steps: Dissolve gulaman and sugar in water according to package directions.
Arrange fruit cocktail in a mold and pour in the gulaman mixture.
Prepare the ingredients and equipment before starting so the mixture can be handled without interruption.
Cool until set, refrigerate, and unmold or cut into squares.
tips: Stir until the gulaman is fully dissolved before pouring it into the mold.
Cool at room temperature before refrigerating to help it set evenly.
Measure ingredients before cooking and follow the stated quantities to help achieve a consistent texture.
Use low or moderate heat when cooking sugar, coconut milk, or thick mixtures; stir as needed to prevent scorching.
Allow hot desserts to cool safely, then refrigerate perishable items in clean, covered containers until serving.

name: Sago't Gulaman
description: A popular Filipino refreshment combining chewy tapioca pearls and gulaman cubes in a sweet syrup.
steps: Cook sago in boiling water until translucent, then drain and rinse.
Prepare gulaman according to package directions, let it set, and cut into cubes.
Boil brown sugar with 1 cup water and vanilla to make arnibal.
Serve sago and gulaman with arnibal and cold water or ice.
tips: Rinse cooked sago to remove excess starch and prevent clumping.
Prepare the arnibal to taste and add it gradually when serving.

name: Mais Pudding
description: A Filipino-style corn dessert pudding with a soft, creamy texture and familiar sweet-corn flavor.
steps: Blend half of the corn with milk until partly smooth.
Pour into a saucepan and add remaining corn and sugar.
Dissolve cornstarch in water and stir into the pan.
Cook over medium-low heat until thick.
Stir in butter, pour into cups, and chill.
tips: Stir the cornstarch mixture continuously as it heats to prevent lumps.
Chill in individual cups and serve cold for a firmer texture.

name: Pandan Maja Blanca
description: A pandan-flavored variation of the Filipino coconut pudding maja blanca, with a fragrant aroma and smooth texture.
steps: Combine coconut milk, condensed milk, sugar, and pandan extract in a saucepan; heat gently.
Dissolve cornstarch in water.
Add gradually while stirring continuously.
Cook until thick, transfer to a dish, cool, and top with latik.
tips: Dissolve the cornstarch fully in water before adding it to the coconut mixture.
Keep stirring over moderate-low heat until the pudding is thick and smooth.

name: Ube Puto
description: A Filipino steamed rice cake variation flavored with ube, giving the soft puto a distinctive purple color and yam flavor.
steps: Mix rice flour, all-purpose flour, sugar, and baking powder.
Whisk coconut milk and ube halaya, then combine with dry ingredients until smooth.
Pour into greased molds and steam for 12–15 minutes.
Add cheese if desired.
tips: Mix only until the batter is smooth to help keep the puto tender.
Do not open the steamer too early because a sudden temperature change may affect the rise.

name: Puto Cheese
description: A Filipino steamed rice cake topped with cheese, combining a mildly sweet, soft base with a savory finish.
steps: Whisk flour, sugar, and baking powder.
In another bowl, combine egg, milk, and melted butter.
Mix wet and dry ingredients just until combined.
Pour into greased molds.
Steam for 10 minutes, add cheese on top, and steam another 2–3 minutes until cooked.
tips: Fill molds evenly and leave room for the batter to rise.
Add cheese near the end so it softens without sinking into the batter.

name: Karioka
description: A Filipino street-food sweet made from glutinous-rice dough formed into balls, fried, and coated with a sweet syrup.
steps: Combine rice flour and coconut.
Add water gradually until a soft dough forms.
Shape into small balls.
Fry over medium-low heat until golden and cooked through.
Drain.
Boil brown sugar and water until syrupy.
Toss karioka in syrup or dip before serving.
tips: Make the balls uniform in size so they cook evenly.
Fry over moderate-low heat until cooked through before coating with syrup.

name: Buchi
description: A Filipino-Chinese-inspired sesame ball with a chewy glutinous-rice exterior and sweet filling, commonly served as a snack or dessert.
steps: Mix rice flour and sugar.
Add water gradually to form a pliable dough.
Divide, flatten each portion, fill with mung bean paste, and seal into balls.
Roll in sesame seeds.
Fry over medium-low heat, turning until golden and cooked through.
Drain.
tips: Measure ingredients before cooking and follow the stated quantities to help achieve a consistent texture.
Maintain a steady frying temperature and cook in batches so the pieces brown evenly without absorbing excess oil.
Allow hot desserts to cool safely, then refrigerate perishable items in clean, covered containers until serving.

name: Taho
description: A popular Filipino warm snack or dessert made with soft silken tofu, sago pearls, and arnibal syrup.
steps: Simmer brown sugar, water, and vanilla until dissolved and slightly syrupy.
Warm tofu gently and spoon into serving cups.
Add cooked sago and pour arnibal over the tofu.
Serve warm.
tips: Seal the filling completely to prevent it from escaping during frying.
Fry in small batches and turn gently for even browning.

name: Banana Maruya
description: A Filipino banana fritter made by coating banana pieces in batter and frying until golden, often served with sugar.
steps: Mash or slice bananas.
Combine flour, sugar, egg, and water into a thick batter; fold in bananas.
Spoon portions into a lightly oiled pan and flatten slightly.
Fry both sides until golden and cooked through.
Drain and sprinkle with sugar.
tips: Warm the tofu gently; avoid boiling because it can break apart.
Pour the arnibal over the tofu and sago immediately before serving.
Maintain a steady frying temperature and cook in batches so the pieces brown evenly without absorbing excess oil.
Allow hot desserts to cool safely, then refrigerate perishable items in clean, covered containers until serving.

name: Pilipit
description: A Filipino twisted or ring-shaped fried dough delicacy, commonly finished with sugar syrup or sesame seeds.
steps: Combine flour, baking powder, and sugar.
Add egg and coconut milk gradually to form a firm dough.
Roll into thin ropes and shape into rings or twists.
Fry until golden and crisp.
Drain, then coat lightly with syrup or sesame seeds.
tips: Use ripe bananas for flavor, but avoid overripe fruit that makes the batter too wet.
Cook over medium heat so the fritters brown outside and cook through inside.
Measure ingredients before cooking and follow the stated quantities to help achieve a consistent texture.
Maintain a steady frying temperature and cook in batches so the pieces brown evenly without absorbing excess oil.
Allow hot desserts to cool safely, then refrigerate perishable items in clean, covered containers until serving.
Food Safety and Storage Notes
Wash hands, utensils, and work surfaces before and after food preparation. Use clean, food-grade containers and fresh ingredients.
Refrigerate desserts containing milk, cream, eggs, or fresh fruit promptly. Keep chilled desserts cold until serving.
Do not leave perishable desserts at room temperature for extended periods. Store leftovers in clean, covered containers.
Allow hot desserts to cool safely before covering and refrigerating. Follow safe handling practices when steaming, frying, or preparing hot sugar syrup.
Traditional recipes vary by region and household. Adjustments in ingredients, texture, and cooking time are common.

name: Sago'T Gulaman
description: Classic Filipino street cooler with chewy sago pearls, gulaman cubes, and brown-sugar arnibal.
steps: Cook sago in boiling water until translucent; drain and rinse with cold water.
Prepare gulaman according to package directions, let it set, then cut into cubes.
Simmer brown sugar, 1 cup water, and pandan for 5–7 minutes; cool and strain.
Combine cold water and arnibal in a pitcher; adjust sweetness.
Add sago and gulaman, stir, and serve over ice.
tips: Cook sago fully and rinse it to remove excess starch. Keep it chilled until serving.

name: Calamansi Juice
description: A bright, tangy Filipino citrus drink made with freshly squeezed calamansi.
ingredients: ½–¾ cup sugar or simple syrup
steps: Wash calamansi and cut each fruit across the middle.
Squeeze and strain the juice to remove seeds.
Dissolve sugar in a little warm water, then cool.
Combine calamansi juice, cold water, and syrup in a pitcher.
Taste, adjust sweetness, and serve over ice.
tips: Add the juice after the syrup cools to keep its fresh citrus aroma.

name: Buko Juice With Young Coconut
description: Fresh young-coconut water served with tender strips of coconut meat.
ingredients: 1 cup tender buko meat, scraped into strips
steps: Open fresh young coconuts and collect the water in a clean bowl.
Strain the coconut water to remove shell fragments.
Scrape the tender coconut meat into thin strips.
Combine coconut water and meat in a pitcher.
Sweeten only if needed, chill, and serve with ice.
tips: Use fresh, clean coconuts and refrigerate the drink promptly.

name: Melon Juice
description: A popular Filipino refreshment made with finely scraped cantaloupe, water, and sugar.
steps: Cut the melon, remove seeds, and scrape the flesh into thin strands.
Dissolve sugar in ½ cup warm water and cool.
Combine shredded melon, cold water, and syrup in a pitcher.
Chill for at least 30 minutes.
Stir before serving over ice.
tips: Use a melon scraper for long, thin strands and taste before adding all the syrup.

name: Mango Shake
description: A creamy shake using ripe Philippine mangoes, milk, and ice.
steps: Place mango cubes, milk, and condensed milk in a blender.
Blend until smooth.
Add ice and blend again until thick.
Taste and adjust sweetness.
Pour into chilled glasses and serve immediately.
tips: Use fully ripe mangoes so less added sugar is needed.

name: Guyabano Juice
description: A sweet-tart fruit drink made from ripe guyabano pulp.
ingredients: 2 cups ripe guyabano pulp, seeds removed
⅓ cup sugar or to taste
steps: Separate the ripe pulp from the seeds and fibrous core.
Blend pulp with 2 cups water briefly.
Strain through a fine sieve, pressing gently.
Add remaining water, sugar, and optional calamansi.
Chill and serve over ice.
tips: Remove seeds before blending; crushed seeds can make the drink gritty.

name: Avocado Milk Shake
description: A thick Filipino-style avocado drink blended with milk and a little sugar.
steps: Scoop avocado flesh into a blender.
Add milk and condensed milk.
Blend until smooth and creamy.
Add ice and blend to the desired thickness.
Serve immediately.
tips: Choose an avocado that yields gently to pressure but is not overripe.

name: Buko Pandan Drink
description: A chilled coconut-and-pandan drink with gulaman and young coconut strips.
ingredients: 1 pack pandan gulaman, prepared and cubed
steps: Prepare pandan gulaman according to package directions; cool and cut into cubes.
Combine coconut water, evaporated milk, condensed milk, and pandan extract.
Stir in buko strips and gulaman cubes.
Chill until cold.
Serve in glasses with ice.
tips: Use pandan extract sparingly; too much can overpower the coconut flavor.

name: Buko Lychee Juice
description: A refreshing coconut drink with lychee pieces and light syrup.
ingredients: 1 cup canned lychees with ¼ cup syrup
steps: Drain lychees, reserving a little syrup.
Combine buko water and cold water in a pitcher.
Add buko strips and lychees.
Sweeten with a little reserved syrup if needed.
Chill and serve over ice.
tips: Add lychees gradually because canned syrup is already sweet.

name: Tsokolate Tablea (Sikwate)
description: Traditional Filipino hot chocolate made by dissolving cacao tablea in water or milk.
steps: Heat water in a saucepan until steaming.
Add tablea and whisk until completely dissolved.
Pour in milk if using and continue heating gently.
Add sugar and a pinch of salt; stir until smooth.
Serve hot.
tips: Whisk continuously over low heat to prevent the cacao from settling or scorching.

name: Salabat (Ginger Tea)
description: A traditional Filipino ginger infusion commonly served warm.
ingredients: 100 g fresh ginger, sliced and lightly crushed
steps: Wash and slice the ginger; lightly crush the slices.
Bring water to a boil in a saucepan.
Add ginger and simmer for 10–15 minutes.
Strain into cups.
Sweeten with honey or brown sugar and add citrus if desired.
tips: Simmer longer for a stronger ginger flavor.

name: Kapeng Barako
description: Strong Batangas-style coffee traditionally brewed from Liberica coffee beans.
steps: Bring water to a near boil.
Add ground coffee to a French press, coffee sock, or filter.
Pour hot water over the grounds and steep for 4–5 minutes.
Strain or press slowly.
Serve hot, black or with sugar and milk.
tips: Use freshly ground beans and avoid boiling the coffee grounds for a cleaner cup.

name: Iced Kapeng Barako
description: A chilled version of strong Batangas coffee served with milk and ice.
steps: Brew the coffee strongly using hot water and strain.
Stir in brown sugar syrup while the coffee is warm.
Cool, then refrigerate until cold.
Fill glasses with ice and pour in the coffee.
Add milk, stir, and serve.
tips: Brew stronger than usual because ice will dilute the coffee.

name: Duman Sikwate (Kapampangan-Style)
description: Hot tablea chocolate served with toasted Pampanga duman, a fragrant young-rice delicacy.
ingredients: 4 cups water or 3 cups water plus 1 cup milk
steps: Toast duman briefly in a dry pan over low heat; set aside.
Heat water or water-and-milk mixture until steaming.
Add tablea and whisk until dissolved.
Sweeten with muscovado and add a pinch of salt.
Pour into cups and serve with toasted duman on top or on the side.
tips: Toast duman gently; do not cook it in the chocolate for a long time.

name: Benguet Strawberry Shake
description: A cool fruit shake inspired by the strawberries widely grown in Benguet.
steps: Wash strawberries thoroughly and remove the leaves.
Place strawberries, milk, and sweetener in a blender.
Blend until smooth.
Add ice and blend until thick.
Serve immediately.
tips: Use ripe berries and adjust sweetness after blending.

name: Strawberry Calamansi Cooler
description: A tart-sweet cooler combining strawberries and calamansi.
steps: Wash and hull the strawberries.
Blend strawberries with 1 cup water, then strain if desired.
Combine strawberry puree, calamansi juice, and remaining water.
Add sugar syrup gradually and stir.
Chill and serve over ice.
tips: Add calamansi gradually to balance the fruit without making the drink too sour.

name: Pinya Juice (Pineapple Juice)
description: A tropical Filipino refreshment made from ripe pineapple.
steps: Remove the pineapple skin and hard core; cut the flesh into chunks.
Blend pineapple with 2 cups water until smooth.
Strain for a lighter juice, if preferred.
Add remaining water and sweetener to taste.
Chill and serve over ice.
tips: Use ripe pineapple and taste before adding sweetener.

name: Dalandan Juice
description: A fragrant citrus drink made with fresh dalandan, a local green mandarin.
steps: Wash dalandan and cut in half.
Squeeze the juice and strain out seeds.
Combine juice and cold water in a pitcher.
Stir in sugar syrup and adjust to taste.
Serve chilled over ice.
tips: Avoid squeezing the peel too hard because it may add bitterness.

name: Tamarind Juice (Sampalok)
description: A sweet-and-sour drink made by extracting the flavor of ripe tamarind pulp.
steps: Place tamarind pulp and 2 cups water in a saucepan.
Simmer for 8–10 minutes, then cool slightly.
Mash the pulp and strain through a sieve.
Add remaining water, sugar, and a pinch of salt.
Chill and serve over ice.
tips: Strain well to remove fibers and seeds.

name: Pandan Cooler
description: A lightly sweetened chilled drink infused with fragrant pandan leaves.
steps: Rinse pandan leaves and tie them into a knot.
Bring water to a boil and add pandan.
Simmer for 8–10 minutes, then turn off the heat.
Stir in sugar until dissolved; cool and strain.
Add calamansi if desired, chill, and serve over ice.
tips: Do not boil pandan for too long or the infusion may taste grassy.

name: LEMONGRASS TEA (TANGlad TEA)
description: A fragrant herbal infusion made from fresh lemongrass stalks.
ingredients: Honey or brown sugar to taste
steps: Wash lemongrass and bruise the stalks with the back of a knife.
Bring water to a boil.
Add lemongrass and simmer for 10 minutes.
Strain into cups and sweeten to taste.
Serve hot or chill and pour over ice.
tips: Bruising the stalks helps release their citrus-like aroma.

name: Ginger Calamansi Tea
description: A warm Filipino-style drink combining ginger infusion and calamansi.
steps: Simmer ginger in water for 10–12 minutes.
Turn off the heat and strain the infusion.
Allow it to cool slightly before adding calamansi juice.
Sweeten with honey or brown sugar.
Serve warm.
tips: Add calamansi after removing the pot from the heat for a fresher flavor.

name: Cucumber Calamansi Cooler
description: A light, refreshing drink made with cucumber, calamansi, and cold water.
steps: Wash and slice the cucumber.
Blend cucumber with 1 cup water until smooth.
Strain the cucumber mixture into a pitcher.
Add calamansi juice, remaining water, and syrup.
Stir, chill, and serve over ice.
tips: Strain the cucumber puree for a smoother drink.

name: Watermelon Juice
description: A naturally sweet Filipino summer drink made from ripe watermelon.
steps: Remove the rind and cut watermelon into cubes.
Blend watermelon until smooth.
Strain if a lighter texture is preferred.
Stir in calamansi juice and add water if too thick.
Serve chilled over ice.
tips: Use cold watermelon to reduce the amount of ice needed.

name: Papaya Milk Shake
description: A creamy fruit shake made with ripe papaya and chilled milk.
steps: Peel papaya, remove seeds, and cut into cubes.
Place papaya, milk, and condensed milk in a blender.
Blend until smooth.
Add ice and blend again.
Serve immediately.
tips: Use ripe papaya for a naturally sweet and smooth shake.

name: Banana Milk Shake
description: A simple Filipino-style banana shake with milk and ice.
steps: Peel and slice the bananas.
Place bananas, milk, and sweetener in a blender.
Blend until creamy.
Add ice and blend until smooth.
Pour into glasses and serve.
tips: Use ripe bananas with brown speckles for better sweetness.

name: Ube Milk Drink
description: A creamy purple drink flavored with cooked ube and milk.
steps: Place cooked ube, milk, condensed milk, and vanilla in a blender.
Blend until completely smooth.
Strain if needed to remove lumps.
Chill and stir before serving.
Pour over ice.
tips: Use fully cooked ube and blend thoroughly for a smooth texture.

name: Ube Shake
description: A thick Filipino-inspired shake made with ube, milk, and crushed ice.
steps: Combine ube, milk, and condensed milk in a blender.
Blend until smooth.
Add ice and blend until thick.
Taste and adjust sweetness.
Serve immediately.
tips: Cool the cooked ube completely before blending.

name: Mais Milk Cooler
description: A chilled sweet-corn drink with milk, inspired by familiar Filipino merienda flavors.
steps: Reserve ½ cup corn kernels for serving.
Blend remaining corn with milk and water until smooth.
Strain for a smoother drink, if desired.
Stir in condensed milk and reserved kernels.
Chill and serve over ice.
tips: Use cooked corn and refrigerate the drink until serving.

name: Mais Con Yelo Drinkable Style
description: A pourable corn-and-milk cooler inspired by the Filipino shaved-ice merienda.
steps: Blend 1 cup corn with milk until smooth.
Stir in condensed milk and a pinch of salt.
Divide remaining corn among glasses.
Pour the milk mixture over the corn.
Add crushed ice and serve with a spoon or wide straw.
tips: Keep it pourable by adding milk rather than using too much crushed ice.

name: ISKRambol (PINK STREET-STYLE SLUSH)
description: A sweet pink shaved-ice drink commonly sold as a street-side treat.
steps: Place shaved ice in a large chilled bowl.
Drizzle in the syrup and gently mix to color the ice.
Add evaporated milk and condensed milk.
Scoop into cups and top with sprinkles or pinipig.
Serve immediately.
tips: Assemble just before serving so the shaved ice does not melt.

name: Guinomis
description: A traditional cold Filipino merienda drink with sago, gulaman, pinipig, coconut milk, and syrup.
ingredients: ½ cup panutsa or brown-sugar syrup
steps: Prepare and chill the sago and gulaman cubes.
Toast pinipig in a dry pan over low heat.
Dissolve panutsa in a little hot water to make syrup; cool.
Divide sago, gulaman, and pinipig among glasses.
Add coconut milk and syrup, top with crushed ice, and serve.
tips: Toast pinipig lightly and keep it dry until serving.

name: Buko Salad Samalamig
description: A creamy, pourable party drink with buko, fruit cocktail, nata de coco, and gulaman.
ingredients: 3 cups cold buko water or milk
steps: Whisk evaporated milk, condensed milk, and buko water until combined.
Add buko strips, drained fruit cocktail, nata de coco, gulaman, and sago.
Stir gently and adjust thickness with more cold liquid.
Chill for at least 1 hour.
Serve in glasses over ice.
tips: Drain canned fruit and nata well to prevent the drink from becoming watery.

name: Mango Sago Drink
description: A chilled mango drink with tapioca pearls and milk.
steps: Blend one mango with milk, water, and condensed milk.
Dice the second mango into small cubes.
Divide cooked sago and mango cubes among glasses.
Pour in the mango milk mixture.
Stir, chill, and serve over ice.
tips: Rinse cooked sago under cold water and drain well before adding.

name: Coffee Jelly Milk Drink
description: A chilled coffee-and-milk drink with soft coffee jelly cubes.
steps: Dissolve coffee in hot water and stir in gulaman powder and sugar.
Bring to a boil while stirring according to package directions.
Pour into a shallow dish and chill until firm.
Cut the coffee jelly into cubes.
Combine milk and condensed milk; add jelly and serve over ice.
tips: Let the jelly set fully before cutting so the cubes hold their shape.

name: Milo Sago Drink
description: A chocolate malt drink served cold with chewy sago pearls.
ingredients: 4 tbsp Milo or malt chocolate powder
steps: Cook sago until translucent, then rinse and drain.
Whisk malt chocolate powder with a little warm milk until dissolved.
Add remaining cold milk and condensed milk.
Divide sago among glasses and pour in the chocolate milk.
Add ice and serve.
tips: Dissolve the powder first in a small amount of warm liquid to avoid lumps.

name: Pineapple Ginger Cooler
description: A tropical pineapple drink with a mild ginger note.
steps: Blend pineapple with 2 cups water until smooth.
Strain the juice into a pitcher.
Steep grated ginger in ½ cup hot water for 5 minutes, then strain and cool.
Combine pineapple juice, ginger infusion, remaining water, sweetener, and calamansi.
Chill and serve over ice.
tips: Use ginger infusion sparingly so it complements rather than masks the pineapple.

name: Pomelo Juice (Suha)
description: A refreshing citrus drink using sweet pomelo segments.
ingredients: 2 cups pomelo segments, seeds and membranes removed
steps: Separate pomelo segments and remove seeds and tough membranes.
Lightly crush half of the segments to release juice.
Combine with cold water and sugar syrup.
Add remaining segments and optional calamansi.
Chill and serve over ice.
tips: Remove as much white pith as possible to avoid bitterness.

name: Bignay Juice
description: A ruby-colored fruit drink made by simmering ripe bignay berries and balancing their tartness.
ingredients: 4 cups ripe bignay berries, stems removed
½ cup sugar, or to taste
steps: Sort and wash ripe bignay berries; discard unripe or damaged fruit.
Simmer berries in water for 8–10 minutes until softened.
Mash gently and strain without crushing the seeds.
Dissolve sugar and salt in a little warm strained juice.
Cool, add calamansi, dilute to taste, and serve chilled.
tips: Mash gently; crushing the seeds can make the juice harsh.

name: Pili Nut Milk Drink (Bicol-Inspired)
description: A creamy nut drink using pili, a well-known nut from the Bicol region.
ingredients: 1 cup shelled roasted pili nuts, unsalted
steps: Soak roasted pili nuts in warm water for 20 minutes.
Blend nuts with 4 cups fresh water until very smooth.
Strain through a nut-milk bag or fine cloth.
Stir in honey, salt, and vanilla if using.
Chill and shake before serving.
tips: Use unsalted roasted pili and keep the finished nut milk refrigerated.

name: Bicol Pandan-Lime Cooler
description: A simple chilled pandan and citrus drink with a bright, refreshing finish.
steps: Simmer pandan leaves in water for 8–10 minutes.
Turn off the heat, cover, and steep for another 5 minutes.
Strain and cool the pandan infusion.
Stir in sugar syrup and calamansi juice.
Chill and serve over ice.
tips: Add calamansi only after the infusion has cooled.

name: Turmeric Ginger Tea
description: A warm golden drink made with turmeric and ginger, inspired by familiar Filipino herbal brews.
ingredients: 1 tsp grated fresh turmeric or ½ tsp ground turmeric
steps: Bring water to a boil with ginger and turmeric.
Lower heat and simmer for 10 minutes.
Turn off the heat and strain into cups.
Sweeten with honey.
Add a little calamansi if desired and serve warm.
tips: Use a stainless-steel pot and wash utensils promptly because turmeric can stain.

name: Malunggay Lemon Tea
description: A mild herbal infusion made with clean malunggay leaves and citrus.
steps: Bring water to a boil and turn off the heat.
Add washed malunggay leaves and cover for 5–7 minutes.
Strain the infusion.
Allow it to cool slightly, then add honey and citrus juice.
Serve warm or chilled.
tips: Use clean, young leaves and avoid boiling them for a long time.

name: Kape With Muscovado
description: A Filipino brewed coffee sweetened with muscovado sugar.
steps: Place ground coffee in a filter, coffee sock, or French press.
Pour hot water over the coffee and steep for 4 minutes.
Strain or press slowly into a pot.
Stir in muscovado until dissolved.
Serve hot, with milk if desired.
tips: Adjust muscovado gradually because its flavor is stronger than white sugar.

name: Iced Calamansi-Mint Tea
description: A chilled tea infused with calamansi and fresh mint.
ingredients: 4 tea bags or 2 tbsp loose black tea
steps: Steep tea in hot water for 3–5 minutes, then remove the tea bags or strain.
Cool the tea completely.
Stir in calamansi juice and sugar syrup.
Add mint leaves and refrigerate for 30 minutes.
Serve over ice.
tips: Do not steep black tea too long or it may become bitter.

name: Papaya Calamansi Juice
description: A tropical fruit drink blending ripe papaya with a little calamansi.
steps: Blend papaya with 2 cups cold water until smooth.
Strain for a lighter texture, if desired.
Pour into a pitcher and add remaining water.
Stir in calamansi and sugar syrup.
Chill and serve over ice.
tips: Add calamansi gradually to keep the papaya flavor balanced.

name: Banana Saba Smoothie
description: A filling chilled drink made with ripe saba bananas and milk.
ingredients: 2 ripe saba bananas, peeled and sliced
steps: Steam or boil saba until tender if it is not fully ripe; cool completely.
Place banana, milk, yogurt, and honey in a blender.
Blend until smooth.
Add ice and blend again.
Serve immediately.
tips: Cook and cool firm saba before blending; raw unripe saba is not suitable for this shake.

name: Mango Calamansi Cooler
description: A fruit cooler balancing ripe mango sweetness with calamansi acidity.
steps: Blend ripe mango flesh into a smooth puree.
Combine mango puree and cold water in a pitcher.
Add calamansi juice and stir.
Sweeten gradually with syrup.
Chill and serve over ice.
tips: Use ripe mangoes and adjust calamansi after tasting.

name: Strawberry Yogurt Shake
description: A creamy shake made with strawberries, yogurt, and milk.
steps: Wash and hull strawberries.
Place strawberries, yogurt, milk, and honey in a blender.
Blend until smooth.
Add ice and blend until thick.
Serve immediately.
tips: Use chilled yogurt and fruit for a thicker shake.

name: Brown Sugar Gulaman Drink
description: A simple samalamig made with grass jelly or gulaman and brown-sugar syrup.
steps: Prepare gulaman according to package directions and let it set firm.
Cut the gulaman into small cubes.
Simmer brown sugar with 1 cup water until dissolved; cool.
Mix syrup with 4 cups cold water in a pitcher.
Add gulaman cubes and serve over ice.
tips: Make the jelly ahead and keep it covered in the refrigerator.
RESEARCH NOTES AND REFERENCES

Ingredient quantities and preparation methods are standardized home versions; household and regional preparations may vary. Regional labels are used where the association is supported by the cited sources; other entries are identified as Filipino-style or regional-inspired. This collection focuses on non-alcoholic drinks.
